Fossil mammal with reptile-like teeth changes picture of our evolution

New Scientist October 02, 2026

A newly discovered, semi-aquatic mammal – which would have lived alongside the dinosaurs – had the streamlined appearance of a water rodent, feet almost identical to a platypus and teeth that grew like a reptile’s.

The researchers who studied the near-complete, 120-million-year-old fossil, named Dongoconodon platycauda, say its disparate anatomy offers a window into early mammal evolution.

D. platycauda was found in 2018 in Liaoning, China. Shundong Bi at Yunnan University, China, and his colleagues studied the fossil after the collector who found it took it to the Mongolia Museum of Natural History. When it was alive, the mammal would have weighed up to 190 grams and measured about 40 centimetres long.

Advertisement

Spectacular feathered dinosaur fossil shows bird-like adaptations

In its overall appearance, it may have looked somewhat like a small nutria, also known as the coypu (Myocastor coypus), say the researchers. Like this modern aquatic mammal, D. platycauda had a streamlined body and a flattened tail adapted for swimming.

D. platycauda also had broad hands and feet “remarkably like” those of the modern platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus), says Bi. Also, several of its finger and toe bones preserve specialised flanges, indicating that the digits supported extensive webbing.

It would have been a strong swimmer, says Bi.

“The broad, webbed forefeet generated much of the propulsive force, while its flattened, tapered tail functioned primarily as a rudder for steering and stability,” he says.

See Alice Roberts at New Scientist Live 2026

But what makes the ancient mammal most interesting is its teeth. For more than a century, he says, biology textbooks have identified that mammals replace some or all of their teeth just once during a lifetime – a condition called diphyodonty.

“Dongoconodon challenges this long-standing view,” says Bi.

The fossil preserves evidence that incisors, canines, premolar-like teeth and even molar-like teeth were replaced multiple times during the animal’s life – a condition called polyphyodonty.

“It is the only known mammal to exhibit polyphyodonty across all four tooth classes, a pattern previously associated with reptiles rather than mammals,” he says.

The specimen also has what the researchers say is one of the most complete preserved middle-ear regions known from an Early Cretaceous mammal. This includes its Meckel’s cartilage, a transient embryonic structure that temporarily connects the developing middle ear to the lower jaw in all mammals.

D. platycauda preserves an intermediate stage in which Meckel’s cartilage maintained only slight contact with the jaw while remaining connected to the tiny ear bones.

“The discovery changes our picture of early mammalian evolution,” says Bi.

Rather than changes to the teeth and ear bones evolving together as a tightly linked suite of characteristics, he says, these important mammalian features evolved independently, producing a remarkable diversity of evolutionary experiments during the age of dinosaurs.

A stunningly intact marine reptile named Austronaga minuta that lived around 245 million years ago may have looked like a miniature version of more famous later ocean predators, like plesiosaurs

“Our discovery shows that early mammalian evolution was considerably more flexible than the traditional textbook picture suggests,” he says.

Mike Benton at the University of Bristol in the UK says the team makes a good case for at least three sets of teeth and an intermediate ear anatomy.

“This is an interesting, quite late-occurring mammal that for some reason has retained hints of the reptilian ancestry more so than many other Mesozoic mammals that had apparently made those two transitions by the end of the Triassic [about 201 million years ago],” says Benton.

Nature Communications DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77339-w

Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true

New Scientist October 02, 2026

AI has made staggering progress in mathematics in recent months, unearthing solutions to thorny puzzles that evaded humans for decades. Key to technology companies being able to announce these complex new findings, confident in their correctness, is a niche field called formalisation.

But recently, the developers behind formalisation tools have realised that the AI models have the potential to cheat their way to success. Now, the battle is on to tighten up the tools and prevent that from happening.

Formalising mathematical theorems essentially turns them into code that allows computers to grapple with them directly, methodically working through the logic and exposing any flaws. The process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt.

Advertisement

A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out

The leading software to do this, Lean, has risen to prominence in the AI world as a convenient way for technology giants to quickly and decisively prove the output of their models. It’s by using Lean that the companies can make bold announcements about solving complex puzzles. Without it, they would only be able to claim they had found a possible solution to the puzzles and then invite human mathematicians to assess the solutions – work that might take weeks or months.

Leonardo de Moura created Lean in the 2010s while working at Microsoft Research. He says that the software was initially a niche tool used only by human mathematicians, and that there were never any attempts at trickery or manipulation.

That all changed in July this year when software engineer Ramana Kumar announced he had disproved the Collatz conjecture – one of the most famous open problems in all of mathematics – and published a Lean formalisation to back up his claim.

See Jim Al-Khalili at New Scientist Live 2026

De Moura was surprised by the breakthrough, but it seemed legitimate. Not least of the reasons for believing so was that the code had been approved by both the standard Lean kernel – the tiny bit of code at the heart of Lean that actually checks the mathematics – and also a separately developed one designed for Lean, called Nanoda. Lean allows for, and actively encourages, the creation of different kernels because variety equals safety; a specific bug that makes something true look false, or vice versa, in one kernel is vanishingly unlikely to appear in another. Formalised code checked by two kernels was as water-tight as things got.

But then it turned out that Kumar’s disproof wasn’t what it seemed. He had used AI to discover and exploit two separate bugs in two separate kernels, within the Lean code.

“[The AI] managed to do something that we thought was impossible,” says de Moura. “It found different bugs and managed to craft a problem that exploited both of them. After that we were really worried. It was clear we had to improve.”

Can mathematicians still refuse to use AI at this point?

Kumar told New Scientist that he thought the stunt would be “useful to throw some cold water on the hype” of formalisation. He didn’t respond to follow-up questions on why he didn’t then disclose the bugs he had found so that they could be fixed. In any case, a fix was published an hour after the bug was officially logged.

Regardless of Kumar’s motivations, it certainly concerned de Moura, the 20 or so full-time developers working on Lean and mathematicians. They feared that malicious actors could use AI to pull such stunts, as Kumar had done.

But they also worried that AI might perform something similar unprompted. When faced with a serious challenge like formalising a fiendishly difficult and complex piece of mathematics, AI might actually find it easier to simply hack Lean and give the appearance of success. This so-called “reward hacking” can occur when AI is given vague instructions, and researchers have already seen evidence of models trying to exploit Lean bugs rather than actually doing their homework.

The first thing Lean’s developers did was to formalise their own kernel, using Lean to check the code at the heart of Lean – an oddly self-referential safety check – and verify that there were no bugs that could be exploited. They then used AI to convert that kernel into a different programming language, and verified that second one as well. A third kernel written from scratch was also verified. This gave developers a greater sense of security, but it didn’t necessarily mean that Lean was infallible.

Fermat’s last theorem formalised by AI agents in just 11 days

Floris van Doorn at the University of Bonn in Germany says there was a vanishingly small chance that Lean had a very unusual bug that caused it to report itself as error-free even when it wasn’t. If such a bug existed, the boot-strapping safety measures would have been meaningless. “That is completely possible, but in practice this would be very weird,” says van Doorn.

To get around this issue, the Lean developers made a lot more kernels, as diverse as possible, built on all types of software and hardware, to increasingly lower the chances of finding a bug that worked universally. These kernels are tested head-to-head in a battle arena website where league tables record how well they’ve done on known true and false proofs, and unusual problems that have been shown to trip up kernels in the past.

The researchers are now also taking steps to push these kernels into wider use – they only help if they’re deployed. Lean, which is open source, currently ships with just one, and it’s on the user to check their code with others if they want more security. But because of the surprising complexity of AI attacks, the next version will ship with four different kernels as standard.

Mathematician discovers rare eight-faced shape

Developers now believe that Kumar’s approach would no longer succeed. “We want to get much closer to this idea of being bulletproof,” says de Moura. “I can tell you that we’re sleeping much better now. We don’t believe the existing AI will be able to break all these layers of defence.”

Even now, though, there are risks. The diversity of kernels makes the chance of a universal bug that works on them all smaller, but not zero – and future AI models may become so capable that they can continue to find convoluted exploits that somehow work across the board on all kernels.

For instance, when working with engineers from OpenAI, the Lean team found a bug in the runtime of their program – the compiled code that is actually executed by a computer, constructed from the source code using a tool called a compiler. Exploiting this bug, they managed to incorrectly prove a conjecture that is false. The error cropped up because the compiler wasn’t perfect, not because Lean’s code had an error.

Dice discovered that solve decade-long mathematical problem

So the ultimate aim is to show that one particular computer setup, with hardware and software of specified standards, is formalised, verified and guaranteed error-free. This would give Lean users the reassurance not only that the kernel is free of mistakes, but also that the compiler, operating system and hardware are error-free, too. Totally trustable from top to bottom. “That’s the dream,” says de Moura. But it will take a vast effort.

There are other problems. Lean code is a programming language, so it can be crafted to do anything the user wants – including malicious trickery, says van Doorn. This could involve simply writing in the output file created by Lean that a theorem was correct, even if it was false, or changing the actual source code that makes up Lean itself to manipulate results, or report that every proof tried from them on was correct.

“You can redefine addition. And then you can prove Fermat’s last theorem, which mentions addition, and you can say you’ve done it,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London. “But then when people actually look at what you’ve really done, you haven’t done it.”

Mathematicians now have a formidable tool for breaking open challenging problems, but working out how best to use it isn’t going to be easy

These loopholes are also now being closed in Lean. Another effort involves Google DeepMind, which maintains a list of open mathematics problems that have been explicitly defined in Lean and then checked carefully by mathematicians. Anyone claiming to have solved one of these problems can take the appropriate definition off the shelf and use it in an unmodified form to test their proposed proof in Lean. Doing so would demonstrate that they are not trying to cheat by subtly altering the definition of the problem to make it far easier to solve.

When OpenAI solved the Navier-Stokes puzzle earlier this month, for example, we knew it was on stable ground because the statement provided to Lean was taken directly from the Formal Conjectures list.

But for some, none of these efforts will ever be enough.

“Computer scientists are, in general, very paranoid people, and probably with good reason because they’ve seen all sorts of things,” says Buzzard. “You can find people that will never believe anything. You say ‘I’ve checked it a million times’ and they say ‘well, what about gamma rays [flipping bits in memory], did you check for them?’ There are some people that you can never convince.”

First week of life seems crucial for future allergy and eczema risk

New Scientist October 02, 2026

Babies who have a strong immune reaction in the first week of life seem to have triple the risk of developing an allergy or eczema by age 1, compared with those who don’t. But the long-term impact of this early immune response, now defined for the first time, seems to be modulated by the microbiome and how babies are fed.

“If you ask 100 immunologists, they would say that immune development begins at birth and continuously develops over time, without discrete phases,” says Petter Brodin at Imperial College London.

But at a talk at an immune conference in London earlier this month, Brodin challenged this idea. He revealed that he and his colleagues have found that if a baby has a strong immune response in the first week of life, this seems to have an oversized impact on how the infant’s immune system subsequently develops. “That’s a novel concept,” he said during the talk.

Advertisement

How older siblings may shape sexual orientation via mother’s immune system

In ongoing research, Brodin and his colleagues have been studying nearly 600 infants in Sweden, collecting and analysing blood and stool samples from the infants throughout their first year of life. The analysis revealed that about half the babies had what the researchers termed a strong “seeding” immune reaction during the first week of life, marked by high levels of inflammatory molecules such as interferon gamma, which activates immune cells. The remaining infants had lower levels of these inflammatory molecules during the first week, which the team called a weak seeding reaction.

Further analysis revealed that babies with a strong seeding reaction had substantially more Bacteroides bacteria in their gut than those who had a weak reaction. “A high abundance of Bacteroides bacteria seems to drive seeding reactions to be very strong,” says Brodin – although it is also possible that the variation in levels of the bacteria actually resulted from differences in the severity of the seeding reaction. Babies can pick up these bacteria via interactions with their mother and family members, he says.

The researchers think the effects of the seeding reaction last for only about a week at the beginning of life because that is when the gut is especially leaky, enabling bacteria like Bacteroides to enter the bloodstream and activate immune cells. “Healthy infants are born with a leaky gut that closes up after about a week,” says Brodin.

See Chris and Xand van Tulleken at New Scientist Live 2026

But the seeding reaction may have lasting effects: by sifting through the infants’ medical records, the researchers found that 39 per cent of those with a strong seeding reaction developed either eczema or a food allergy by age 1. In contrast, just 12 per cent of infants with a weak seeding reaction developed at least one of these conditions, which are caused by excessive inflammation. “What we ideally want is a weak seeding reaction,” says Brodin.

Further analysis revealed that the infants with a strong reaction then followed one of three immune trajectories linked to two main factors: whether they were primarily fed breast or formula milk, and the abundance of bifidobacteria in their gut.

For instance, 50 per cent of babies who had a strong seeding reaction and were breastfed – but had low levels of bifidobacteria – developed eczema or food allergies. Breastfed infants who had a strong seeding reaction and had high bifidobacteria levels were less likely to develop eczema or food allergies, with 25 per cent of them doing so.

Babies are born with the neural foundations for maths

The researchers also found that 33 per cent of infants who had a strong seeding reaction and were fed formula milk developed eczema or an allergy by age 1. In the work presented at the conference, the team didn’t give details of bifidobacteria levels in the guts of these formula-fed babies.

Brodin says the bifidobacteria may be important because they break down certain sugars in breast milk, known as human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), to produce anti-inflammatory molecules called short-chain fatty acids. In turn, these can prevent the immune system from overreacting, he says. The researchers plan to explore why exactly the other links may have emerged in future research, says Brodin.

“This is a really important piece of work. Only a few studies have looked at immune development during the first week after birth,” says Lucy Crouch at the University of Birmingham in the UK. The research could reveal ways to develop personalised medicine for infants, she says.

A revolutionary cancer treatment is now being applied to a wide range of autoimmune disorders. Columnist Michael Le Page finds it is proving to be even more effective than expected

For instance, you could imagine measuring whether a baby has a strong or weak seeding reaction, then, depending on whether they are breastfed or not and their levels of bifidobacteria, you could give them a probiotic that boosts these microbes to cut their allergy or eczema risk, she says.

But further research is needed to establish whether the seeding reaction has effects beyond the first year, says Crouch. Studies should also explore whether the links made in the study really are causal, she says, which could be done by tracking how immune cells within gut organoids – clumps of lab-grown cells that are used to mimic the intestines – react to bacteria in the presence or absence of HMOs.

“The reported differences in allergy and eczema risk are striking, but they show associations rather than demonstrating that particular microbes or immune responses directly cause the later outcomes,” says Lindsay Hall, also at the University of Birmingham.

For now, parents shouldn’t alter how they feed or interact with their infants based on the results. “It is much too early to suggest that the findings should change advice to parents,” says Hall.

New Scientist October 02, 2026

A tiny set of neurons deep inside the brain is fundamental to viable pregnancies in mice. These neurons are also present in human female brains and could provide clues about unexplained recurrent miscarriages and IVF difficulties.

Nirao Shah at Stanford University, California, and his colleagues discovered the neurons while looking for gene expression changes in different parts of the female mouse brain during pregnancy. They observed a small population of neurons that completely transformed.

The levels of gene expression in these neurons changed over 30-fold when mice became pregnant for the first time, converting them to a new class of neurons that functioned in a completely different way by mid-gestation. “This cell type is exclusive to pregnancy,” the researchers write.

Advertisement

The previously unknown set of neurons is in an area deep in the centre of the brain called the preoptic hypothalamus, which is also involved in sexual and parental behaviours. The neurons have receptors for pregnancy-related hormones like progesterone, which may be responsible for switching the neurons on after the initial fertilisation of an egg.

Paracetamol use in early pregnancy linked to smaller ovaries and testes

Once activated, these neurons appear to coordinate the implantation of the embryo in the uterus and maintain the ongoing pregnancy. When Shah’s team created female mice without this special type of neuron, the mice were able to mate and become pregnant, but their pregnancies all ended at an early stage. This was because their embryos couldn’t implant in the lining of the uterus.

“Certainly, the fact that when you get rid of these neurons, you lose these pregnancies, is really suggestive,” says Jennifer O’Chan at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York.

These neurons comprise fewer than 0.001 per cent of all brain cells, making it remarkable that their selective elimination completely blocks the ability to establish viable pregnancies, write Shah and his colleagues.

However, further research will be required to investigate how these neurons actually do this, says O’Chan. “They’ve shown that these neurons change robustly during pregnancy, but then how are they actually communicating with the uterus? Is it hormonal? Are they secreting some kind of factor? If they could identify that, I would be very convinced.”

It would also be interesting to study whether these neurons are permanently changed by pregnancy or eventually return to their original state, says O’Chan, since her own research has found that pregnancy induces long-lasting changes in the brain.

Free newsletter

Shah’s team also analysed an existing atlas of gene expression in the human brain and found that women have the same special set of neurons in their preoptic hypothalamus, hinting these neurons may play a similar role in human pregnancies. “You can’t do these types of experiments in humans, so we have to extrapolate here, but mouse and human brains do tend to be fairly well-conserved,” says O’Chan.

Just over half of miscarriages are known to be caused by genetic errors in the embryo, but the rest can’t be explained. For example, some people undergoing IVF have multiple embryos that appear genetically healthy, but none seem to implant once they are inserted in the uterus, for reasons that are unclear. Some who conceive naturally also have recurrent early pregnancy losses for no detectable reason.

According to Shah and his colleagues, these fertility challenges may relate to the neurons they discovered, potentially paving the way for new treatments. “We speculate that a subset of such events reflects failure of particular neural circuits to recognize, monitor, or adapt to gestation,” they write.

“If, for example, you found that these neurons were releasing a fundamental signalling molecule that was important for implantation, you might be able to turn that into a therapeutic for people with fertility issues,” says O’Chan.

Read an extract from Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel

New Scientist October 02, 2026

In the first spring after the collapse of the United States, the blossoming of the jacaranda trees felt to Ari like grace. The trees bloomed in the same week that international peacekeeping troops withdrew from Los Angeles, and the convergence of flowers with the absence of foreign soldiers brought a delirious kind of hope. Everyone in the spring of 2031 knew the city was one terrorist attack away from disaster, but that peril made the season more vivid, not less.

It was Ari’s first spring outside of prison in nearly two decades, and she spent hours at a time walking the streets. Prison is a wasteland of sensory deprivation, and now the city was overwhelming. She kept expecting that the details of the world would cease to be extraordinary, but that kept not happening. No one around her seemed to notice the jacarandas, because in Los Angeles there are flowers every month of the year, but she walked streets where the trees were lit up by purple blue blossoms and thought, My god. This place. She was forty-eight years old but felt younger, because so much of the world was new.

Free newsletter

The United States had come undone following a coup d’état. Several states had seceded within a week of the coup, either alone or in alliances with neighbours, and war had broken out within the month. Now the fighting had subsided, for the most part, and Ari had been released into an uneasy aftermath.

Advertisement

“When I think of what the city was a year ago,” Gloria said. Gloria was Ari’s roommate in a very small apartment in Echo Park. She was about a decade younger than Ari, a refugee who’d fled fighting between rival militias in Tennessee. Gloria slept in the bedroom. Ari slept in the living room, with an old sheet stapled to the door frame as a makeshift door, and they met one another in the tiny kitchen. Gloria seemed to spend most of her time reading the news online, her eyes wide and blank in the blue light of her laptop. What the city had been like a year ago was Gloria’s favourite topic of conversation.

“I know,” Ari said gently, although she didn’t. Their experiences were not the same. A year ago, Ari had been imprisoned in what was now a different country and Gloria had been holed up in this apartment with a different roommate.

But tonight the curfew had lifted, and when Ari had gone for a walk earlier, her impression from passing conversations was that everyone in Los Angeles was going out tonight. Gloria was going to her friend Kareem’s party, one neighbourhood over, and had invited Ari to come. But now, with dusk approaching, she’d settled into her familiar position with her laptop at the kitchen table, and showed no signs of getting ready.

“What time shall we leave for that party?” Ari asked.

I am a top drone pilot in the Ukrainian Army – this is what it is really like

New Scientist October 02, 2026

I joined the army on the day of the Russian invasion. I’d studied computer science and only recently landed a great internship at a game company. But I saw the news and knew my options were to sit and wait for them to come and kill me or go running into the fight.

Comparing the early days of the war to now, it’s like two different worlds. Back then there were drones, but most of the damage was still done by artillery. Now, drones are everywhere, from the front line all the way back 30 kilometres. It’s terrifying because you used to be able to come a little way back from the fighting for rest and feel completely safe. Now, danger is always looming over you, wherever you are.

Jet-powered drones pose a new threat to Ukraine – can they be stopped?

I occasionally have the chance to get back to Kyiv and then I feel like I’m not losing my mind quite as fast as usual. It’s a partial respite because on the front line we work 24 hours a day and the non-stop fighting is hugely draining, but you’re still aware of the risk of drone strikes even in Kyiv. You just can’t escape it.

Advertisement

On the front line, we spend 90 per cent of our time underground in bunkers because of the threat of enemy drones. Every time you go outside, you risk being spotted and killed. The conditions are like camping, but it obviously has a very different vibe.

I’ve done a lot of different jobs as a drone pilot, but at the end of the day, the mission was always to protect our ground troops. I spent time as a reconnaissance drone pilot, then flying bomber drones and now I’m doing anti-drone missions in a regiment called Aquila under the control of the 3rd Army Corps.

We specialise in shooting down everything from small first-person view (FPV) drones to the long-range kamikaze models heading for Ukraine’s cities. We’ve got short-range anti-aircraft guns, shoulder-launched rockets and drones. But I’m in a small unit that does drone-to-drone warfare in the skies above the front line.

I’m proud to say that I’m a top performer not just in my regiment but in the wider army. I think it’s because I’ve been doing it for a long time, but I’ve taken out 932 enemy drones. Right now I focus on finding smaller FPV drones that are doing reconnaissance or hunting our troops with explosives, and take them out before they can do any damage.

Robots clash in first naval engagement between uncrewed sea drones

Russians often find our positions on the front line and target them with drones and artillery. We get information from our guys that they’re being hunted and we try to take out Russian drones before they can do any damage. Most of the time we find them.

I remember one time we were retaking a village that the Russians had occupied. In a single day, we erased all the progress they’d made in a year, and we drone pilots were helping cover the guys that were advancing on the ground. There was a soldier wounded, and the Russians were trying to bomb him with a drone. At the last minute, we found it, we hit it and the guy is alive because of that. It’s an amazing feeling.

Spotting those tiny drones among miles of open land is as much an art as a science. You need to be able to put yourself in the shoes of the enemy pilot who’s out hunting for your comrades, imagine what interests them, where they’ll be looking. You need to hunt him.

We have a few distinct jobs in my team. Some assemble and arm drones, others pilot them and there are also navigators who direct us to the enemy and keep meticulous logs of what hardware we get through and which targets we take out. Even though we have specialities, we make sure we can all step into any role in case someone is injured.

On my most recent trip to the front line, we hit 180 targets in 20 days. But there are also missions where you don’t spot a target, run low on battery and have to return, so it can be up to 30 flights per day.

Stealth drone spins so fast that it disappears

We’ve all seen the advanced interceptors and various other drones that Ukraine produces, and they are used for all sorts of missions, but most of the drones that I fly, and also that I shoot down, are commercially available models. They’re cheap and they’re available – they’re good enough for war. Both we and the Russians buy the same Chinese models – that’s the world that we live in. I’ve shot down so many of them and they still keep coming.

We work in what used to be beautiful countryside, beautiful cities, that real people lived in. That people had made their own. Now it’s all destroyed. But you can still see so much potential for this land to bring so much happiness and fulfilment to people. It’s disheartening, and heartbreaking, to be perfectly honest.

The war is horrible, it’s horrid, it’s everything that you imagine it being, but it’s also a very unique experience. It’s the sort of experience that foreigners usually only see in movies. The stakes are so high that everything you do matters. Everything you do has a weight to it. It changes your perspective, and you see so many people die and get injured that you begin to realise that every moment that you’re alive, every person that you meet, everything that you do, is important. You could die at any moment. Every moment that you live is important. We don’t get to choose what happens to us, we just get to choose what we do with that.

I used to be much more angry with the Russians, I think. I used to be much more emotional about it. I’m getting to a point now where I’m trying to find my inner peace.

Killing the enemy, from some points of view, it’s horrible. But if you don’t take care of them, if you don’t kill them, they advance towards our troops and then they have to deal with them, and that’s not fair.

I’m not sure what I’m going to do after the war. It’s a very demanding job, both physically and psychologically, and it takes much from you. When the war ends, yes, you’ll get this freedom, but what to do with this freedom is not a question you get to ponder while you’re still serving. I’ll find some way to keep myself busy.

As told to Matthew Sparkes

Will the backlash against AI data centres hit quantum computing too?

New Scientist October 02, 2026

People aren’t happy about data centres. As interest in AI and its use has dramatically increased in the past couple of years, communities across the world have begun protesting against the massive infrastructure needed to support this technology.

We may finally have a way to rate a quantum computer’s usefulness

In the US, data centres are popping up in residential areas, their construction has been proposed on protected natural lands and, in places where they have been built, they have caused havoc. These enormous buildings produce a lot of noise and use huge amounts of electricity and water. In some places, utility bills are rising and water taps are running dry. Community after community has risen up to fight data centres in their neighbourhoods. It made me wonder whether that battle will stay limited to AI, or if the scrutiny will come for quantum computing too.

Consider the south side of Chicago. The Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park (IQMP), a 128-acre research and development campus that will house facilities of several leading quantum computing firms, is being built there – and it’s not entirely welcomed by its neighbours.

Advertisement

The project broke ground in September 2025 with enthusiastic support from the governor of Illinois, JB Pritzker, and Mayor of Chicago Brandon Johnson. The most notable tenant of the park will be PsiQuantum, which is aiming to build the US’s first utility-scale, error-corrected quantum computer there by the end of the decade, and as early as 2028. Other companies, such as Pasqal, Infleqtion, IBM and Diraq, will also have facilities at the park.

So far, more than $1 billion in public and private funding has been invested in this campus, which is situated at a steel mill that was a great source of economic activity for the south side of Chicago in the 1950s and 1960s, but has stood abandoned for decades. In the long run, the IQMP is expected to bring $9 billion in investment. In other words, it would be impossible for residents of the nearby neighbourhoods not to notice that quantum is moving in, and at an ambitious scale.

And some Chicagoans certainly did notice. On 15 August, at an event titled “Community Over Quantum”, Johnson faced jeers and antagonistic chants from the audience. The meeting was organised by community advocacy group Southside Together, which has been consistently protesting the development for the past year. Southside Together didn’t respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.

Other community and environmental groups have been engaged in the matter as well, such as Science for the People Chicago; Environment, Transportation, Health and Open Space; and the Alliance of the Southeast, according to the Hyde Park Herald, a local newspaper. Block Club Chicago reported that, at the event in August, the demands put to Johnson were simple: “Reverse the permits. Shut it down. Mayor Johnson, do it now.”

“This is genuinely exciting technology, and it’s easy to assume everyone will see it that way. But it’s human nature to be uneasy about change, especially change this size,” says Pranav Gokhale at Infleqtion.

“Any project of this scale will draw questions, and we embrace that,” says Rebecca Carroll, a spokesperson for the IQMP. The situation is complicated by the history and context of the IQMP’s location. For one, concerns about environmental damage and toxins in the ground have persisted ever since the steel mill closed in 1992, though there have been remediation efforts through the years. At the end of 2025, the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency approved a new clean-up of the property, and at the event in August, Johnson reaffirmed that these efforts will take place.

Several previous attempts to revive the site failed, letting down the local community, many of whom were excited about the prospect of new investment in their neighbourhoods, says Carroll. But she adds that the project’s developer, Related Midwest, has been meeting with community environmental groups since the IQMP broke ground.

These aren’t the only environmental worries raised by the IQMP’s neighbours, however. Concerns about the water and electricity usage of the new facilities abound, in part spurred by the destructive effects that AI data centres have had on other communities. “Opponents of the quantum campus likened the project to the xAI data center in Memphis,” reported Block Club Chicago.

Josh Sodicoff at the University of Chicago co-chairs the local chapter of Science for the People. They say community members feel that this project has popped up in their backyard at an alarming speed, and worry about its impact on their energy and water prices, as well as access to the jobs that the IQMP promises to bring. “The vast majority of people who now know about this [development] were not informed by the developers. They were not informed by the city. They were informed by people in Southside Together, who have been focused explicitly on just canvassing people in the area to let them know what’s going on. That lack of autonomy, especially when the thing that is being decided on is so substantial [and] does use our taxes, seems to have disgruntled a lot of people,” says Sodicoff.

Many local people who have been speaking out against the development want it to end, and for the federal and state dollars behind it to be put into things that they feel would benefit the community, like grocery stores and pharmacies, says Hanna He, who also co-chairs the Science for the People chapter.

I wondered whether another development at the same scale would face the same pushback if it weren’t related to quantum computing. “When we talk to residents, they don’t know much about the quantum aspect. All they know is that this giant industrial complex is being built in their backyard, and it’s not doing anything for them,” says He.

It is, then, tempting to dismiss the situation in Chicago as a problem of local politics, rather than a quantum one. Yet the opacity of the word “quantum” cannot be extricated from many of the issues at play. As Sodicoff told me, it isn’t well-understood by the public, so all sorts of narratives can stick to it easily. Having reported on the quantum computing industry for almost half a decade, I am keenly aware of this. Whether you want to argue that quantum technology will save or destroy the world, “quantum” lends the claim a type of enabling mystique. In Chicago, it also seems to suffer from the association with the other big tech story of the moment: AI.

Grim warnings of the existential risk posed by AI are all over the news, but there is very little evidence to back them up

“People are asking the same questions about power and water everywhere right now, and it’s possible that they have connected [this with] the IQMP, assuming it’s a data centre,” says Gokhale.

Carroll says there couldn’t be a starker contrast between an AI data centre and the IQMP. Unlike data centres, which are largely filled with machines, she says the quantum park will be filled with people. This means there will be employment opportunities beyond quantum-specific roles, she says, similar to the variety of jobs that are available on college campuses.

Her colleagues are already involved with education and outreach programmes, some in partnership with local public schools and city colleges, that she says could help the neighbourhood’s young people become part of the city’s ambitions to become the leading quantum hub in the country. IBM is also establishing a centre at the IQMP that the firm says will bring 750 full-time jobs in cybersecurity, data science, quantum computing, AI and related technologies.

Quantum computing technology isn’t necessarily dependent on the large data-processing facilities AI uses, but to become more useful, quantum computers will have to become physically larger. Does that also mean that they will gobble up more power?

Earlier this year, Olivier Ezratty at the Quantum Energy Initiative estimated that future quantum computers could draw anywhere between 100 kilowatts to 200 megawatts of power, a range that goes from the current needs of a supercomputer at a moderately large research facility to a figure that tops the energy usage of a small city. In other words, the situation is complicated even for quantum industry watchers and analysts, let alone for people with no prior knowledge of anything quantum.

Recently, many who work in the quantum computing industry have also purposefully compared and conflated their technology with AI. Investors that may have missed out on AI are being urged to not skip quantum as the next big thing. Countless claims circulate online about quantum computers making AI better, despite the scientific reality being a lot less settled. Quantum computing and AI will surely be part of the same scientific workflows, but putting an equals sign between the two, or implying one, isn’t yet fully warranted.

For the past year, quantum technology firms have been switching into higher gears, getting ready to scale up and make their biggest splash yet. If all goes according to their roadmaps, they will be in the news more and more often, and the growing importance of quantum computing as an arena of geopolitical dominance – particularly in the technological race between the US and China – will only exacerbate this.

For activists like Sodicoff, quantum’s connection to the US military, such as through some of the IQMP tenants’ contracts and partnerships with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, is already a reason to be sceptical of the technology and participate in the pushback. So, quantum computing firms really can’t afford miscommunication. The technology can’t risk being confused with AI or any other technology that has already raised electricity bills, caused noise pollution or become attached to ideas like bringing decommissioned coal power plants back online to produce enough energy for computing.

Quantum computing may be facing a replication crisis

Certainly, the quantum computing industry also cannot afford to be a bad neighbour. If successfully scaled up and made useful, the technology stands a chance of making a big difference in the lives of not just those who live near research campuses, but people all over the world too. Whether it be by cracking the chemistry behind more efficient ways to produce fertilisers, advancing our understanding of materials for solar panels or shortening the drug discovery timeline, transformative uses for quantum computers are on the table.

“People get excited about quantum helping us address humanity’s challenges,” says Carroll. She shares a vision of the IQMP as a bustling campus that can be both an economic engine for Chicago’s south side and a place where researchers will work on solving some of today’s most pressing problems. The challenge lies in being accountable to the local community and addressing their concerns about the environment, infrastructure and what quantum technology will be used for.

Everyone I spoke to acknowledged that the IQMP is unlikely to be successful without the support of people who live nearby. “They are the people who are breathing in the dust that’s coming off these construction sites. They’re the people who are just wondering what’s behind this fence,” says Sodicoff. Simply put, it isn’t enough for quantum technology firms to promise that they will make the world better in the future – they have a chance to practise for a better world right now.

National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis has again attacked Labour's fiscal plan, saying it has not funded multiple commitments.

She told Ryan Bridge TODAY with Katie Bradford that she believed Labour "tried to pull the wool over Kiwis' eyes" after seeing the reaction to their "hidden bill".

Labour's Barbara Edmonds said this morning that the Land Transport Fund gap in the plan was because the party needed numbers from the Government Policy Statement.

But Willis refuted that point, saying the Pre-Election Fiscal Update had enough information. Willis said her party's fiscal plan would be released in the next "couple of weeks".

Recent polling suggests Willis may not retain her seat in Parliament, but she told Bradford that was not a concern, adding: "I focus on us growing our party vote because what I'm here for is to see National leading the next government."

Willis said she did not regret running as a list-only candidate.

Split Your Vote - a campaign launched by Zuru co-founder Nick Mowbray, his father Harry and former National leader Don Brash - encourages centre-right voters to split their votes between National and a coalition partner, rather than providing two ticks for National.

Harry Mowbray told Katie Bradford on Ryan Bridge TODAY that ‘people are trying to make it complicated’.

The idea has copped negative feedback from National leader Christopher Luxon, who called it “an insanely stupid idea”.

Mowbray said: “It’s very simple, people are trying to make it complicated. It isn’t.

“If you split your vote and you give National your electorate vote and NZ First or Act your party vote, you will guarantee a centre-right government.”

Mowbray said he had been looking at the process for some time after creating a party called ‘Heartlands’, advocating for farmers in parliament, which didn’t hold up.

“Farmers don’t have a voice in parliament and I’m an organic dairy farmer. The heartlands policy or process does not work when National has a lot of electorate seats and a low party vote.”

National leader Christopher Luxon says the Act Party's KiwiSaver plan looks "quite expensive" and he is unsure how it would help balance the books.

Act announced yesterday it was proposing to abolish the tax paid on investment earnings made through KiwiSaver and other superannuation accounts, as well as removing the Government contribution for members receiving employer contributions.

Luxon told Newstalk ZB's Mike Hosking Breakfast that his party's focus was on repairing the books, and although he had not looked through Act's policy in detail, "it just looks quite expensive".

He said: "I don't know how it would get funded in the context of trying to repair the books."

Luxon said he was proud of Nationals' policy of making the scheme compulsory, adding: "We should be able to, you know, actually get people focused on building out more KiwiSaver wealth rather than just relying on property values."

The Act Party has vowed to remove tax on KiwiSaver contributions if re-elected.

Leader David Seymour told Ryan Bridge TODAY with Katie Bradford it would mean the government wouldn’t contribute the standard $250 each year but would lose about $1 billion of revenue.

He said: “But it’s also a strategic tax cut because if the interest or the investment return on your KiwiSaver every year is all yours then the money staying in your account this year will be compounded on this year and compounded on the year after that and interest on interest year after year…

“It means that, say, if you’re a builder on $60,000 at 20 years old, by the time you retire you’ll be $210,000 better off because you won’t be paying that tax on your interest.”

Seymour said that on Sunday the party would release a fully costed alternative budget to show how the government would deal with the revenue loss.

Green Party transport spokesperson Julie Anne Genter told Katie Bradford on Ryan Bridge TODAY the longer-term plan was to prioritise public transport.

The party’s plan announced at the weekend included cheaper bus fares and rail between cities.

Genter said in the first four years, their policy would cost $4.24 billion - about $1b a year.

She said: “We all know and Auckland Council even said that Mill Rd or roads shouldn’t be a priority, rapid transit has to be a priority.

“What we’ve talked about reprioritising is just from the new state highways activity class there would still be many, many billions going into fixing roads, making sure they’re well-maintained and renewed.”

National yesterday announced it would start construction on Auckland’s highly anticipated Mill Rd if re-elected.

The road, currently planned as a Road of National Significance, is a new four-lane, 21.5km corridor running alongside State Highway 1 from Manukau to Drury.

But Winston Peters said, while the road was needed, he questioned whether trains were the better alternative.

He said: “Rail is getting back on track big time and we’ve got a lot of investment going into it because it’s a no brainer, both here and in other parts of the country.

“I’m the Minister for Rail. Railroad first, Mill Rd second.”

Peters also mentioned he didn’t think Labour’s fiscal plan, announced yesterday, “held up”.

It included using a Capital Gains Tax to fund pay equity.

He said: “I heard Barbara Edmonds and thought, 'Barbara you didn’t write that, someone’s overruled you, because it doesn’t hold up'.

“Their chance of turning around the Capital Gains Tax income to help pay for this is going to take five, six, seven years…”

AgriZero NZ gets funding boost of $117m, new partners come on board

New Zealand Herald October 04, 2026

AgriZero board chairman Rob Hewett. Photo / RNZ, Carol Stiles

By RNZ

Government-industry partnership AgriZero NZ has received a big funding boost, to the tune of $117 million, with two new industry partners all coming aboard.

The new funding is equally split across industry and government, taking the total funds raised to $308m.

Red meat processor and exporter Alliance and rural supplies co-op Farmlands have also joined the partnership, which, alongside other industry investors, the a2 Milk Company, ANZ, ANZCO, ASB, BNZ, Fonterra, Rabobank, Ravensdown, Silver Fern Farms and Synlait, jointly owns half of AgriZero.

AgriZero board chairman Rob Hewett said it reflected both the scale of the challenge and the sector’s growing commitment to address it.

“Many of our major export customers expect progress on emissions reductions across their supply chains, through to New Zealand farms,” he said.

“If we want to maintain New Zealand’s competitive advantage and reputation as a trusted supplier of premium food products to discerning customers around the world, we’d be wise to listen to them.

“This is too big for any one organisation to solve alone, and the collaborative support behind AgriZero NZ shows our partners’ determination to get on with the job.”

Hewett said getting tools into farmers’ hands was critical to this, adding there would be tools available by 2030.

“There should be one to two products each year becoming available between now and 2030.

“By 2030, I would expect the farmers will have five to six products to choose from, depending on their farming system.”

The first AgriZeroNZ-backed tool likely to become available to farmers is a methane-inhibiting bolus developed by Kiwi company Ruminant Biotech, currently undergoing regulatory approval.

Hewett said some of the technologies might be “stackable”, offering greater emissions reductions and possibly even improved productivity on farm.

“We also want to have a portfolio of products so that farmers not only have choice for what’s right for them but also potentially stack products on top of each other.

“We could conceivably have a seed treatment solution that means the grasses the animals consume produce less methane, eaten by an animal that may have a bolus or vaccine to reduce the methanogens in the rumen, which may well be wearing a wearable that can deal with nitrous oxide as well”

Hewett said the new partnerships would also help with supply chains and making these tools available to farmers.

AgriZero chief executive Wayne McNee said the additional funding would give it the capital to build on the momentum achieved so far.

“We’re backing some of the world’s best innovators and scientists, and they need sustained support to get these new technologies through development, testing and approvals so farmers can trust they’re proven, safe and effective.

“Not every technology we invest in will succeed; that’s the reality of innovation.

“But we’re optimistic that, with continued investment and focus, New Zealand farmers will have a range of tools to choose from by 2030.”

Since being established in 2023, AgriZero has invested more than $80m across 21 projects to develop tools for reducing methane and nitrous oxide emissions, including inhibitors, probiotics, genetics, pasture, vaccines and wearables.

Revisiting zombie towns: What happens when the housing supply keeps up

New Zealand Herald October 04, 2026

Kaitangata now has 30 new homes, after organisers initially planned six. Photo / RNZ, Amrita Marks

By Shamubeel Eaqub for RNZ

In many parts of New Zealand houses have become unaffordable. But where housing supply has kept up, the provinces can be a genuinely better deal. After housing costs, you may have more money in your pocket than a higher paying job in Auckland or Wellington.

It’s not enough to have jobs, you must have homes that are warm, dry and affordable. Many provinces have cheap homes, but they are old and cold.

But when you build homes that people want, and help them into it, it can rekindle communities.

Kaitangata, affectionately known as Kai, shows it can be done. I met Amber and Kobe, a nurse and a linesman, both local, both in their twenties.

Two years ago, they bought a brand-new home in Kai. “A little over $500,000 for everything,” Kobe told me. “That’s the land and the whole house.”

They aren’t slaves to their mortgage. They are house proud, settled, and playing netball on a Friday night and cricket on Saturday.

This was possible because locals turned an obstacle into an opportunity. Kai hollowed out after the coal mine closed. Joyce Beck, the former school principal, calls what was left “a bit of a ghost town”. There were serviced sections everywhere, and they were so cheap the banks wouldn’t lend to build on them.

Evan Dick, a third-generation dairy farmer, wanted to do something about it. “I thought even if I get one house out of it, just one house, it’s a success.”

He recruited Joyce, who could write a letter and talk to anyone. Joyce recruited Liz Jenkinson, a legal secretary, to run things. They worked together, informally but tightly and they stuck at it.

Their cunning plan was pretty simple. They went to the local plumbers, electricians, builders and surveyors and asked, in Bryan Cadogan’s telling, not for a best price but for “a Kai Rules price”: a fair margin, not silly city money, in return for steady work if it took off.

Evan’s aim was to take the risk out for everyone. He cornered Sir Stephen Tindall over scones and a cup of tea and got seed money that rolled over as each house sold. Once a house was built, the banks would lend, and young people could use their KiwiSaver first-home withdrawal. The council supported it too.

Joyce had planned for six houses. There are now 30, dotted around Kai. Section prices have tripled. The school roll is growing.

The council is now trying to copy Kai in Balclutha and Milton.

Councils play an unusual role in small communities. As the biggest organisation in town, they alone have the scale and gravity to pull people together and nudge things along.

The market on its own was never going to build in Clutha. Sections sold for $50,000 to $60,000, and the pipes under them cost the same as in Auckland. No developer would bother. So the council subdivided its own land on old forestry blocks above Balclutha.

We hear a lot about councils as bouncers, all rates and red tape. In Clutha I saw ushers, holding the door and guiding things through. Jock Martin, the current mayor, calls the council “the district’s glue”.

Wellington is capping rates and pushing councils towards regional reorganisation. Jock’s retort: “Who knows the communities better than the people that actually live in those communities?” I fear this quiet, local job will be lost in the rush to make councils bigger and do less.

On that subdivision I met Shannon, a builder from Dunedin. He is looking at his first house in Milton, where his Nana lives. “It’s so much more affordable.” He reckons he’ll spend the rest of his life here.

House building in Clutha is the fastest in decades. It’s not Auckland numbers, but it is a flywheel: more homes, more people to fill local vacancies, more homes needed.

Where the people arrived before the houses did, as in Rotorua, provinces became unaffordable too.

Housing supply has to keep pace with the people and leave a path for local kids to stay. Housing is infrastructure and must be an integral part of creating good reasons for people to live there.

- Shamubeel Eaqub is an economist and media commentator who was formerly part of the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research think-tank.

- On today’s episode of Zombie Towns, Bryan Cadogan drives me to Kaitangata, a coal town that had become “a bit of a ghost town”. I meet the dairy farmer and retired principal who got houses built on what were horse paddocks, a young couple who have made a great start in life in one of these Kai homes, and the high school programme that has put nearly 200 students into building apprenticeships.

- RNZ

Three injured, two critically, after stabbing at property in Glendene, West Auckland

New Zealand Herald October 04, 2026

Two people are in hospital with critical injuries after a stabbing at a Glendene property late last night.

Police were called to the property on Kirby St at 11.40pm to reports of a disorder.

Waitematā CIB Acting Detective Inspector Megan Goldie said on arrival, three people had “suffered injuries that appeared to be consistent with knife wounds”.

Hato Hone St John said it was called to a residence on Kirby St at 11.40pm.

Three people have been taken to hospital, two in a critical condition and a third with moderate injuries.

Goldie said that while the investigation was in its early stages, they were not currently looking for anyone else in relation to the incident.

National is promising $800 million in the next Budget to fund Canterbury’s Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and Woodend Bypass, with construction beginning next year if the party is re-elected.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon and Transport spokesman Chris Bishop made the commitment this morning.

In a statement, Bishop pointed to the congestion and safety concerns associated with the current routes.

“SH1 approaching Woodend already carries around 21,500 vehicles a day, around 9% of them freight, and that is expected to increase to around 28,000 vehicles a day by 2048.

“At peak times it can take up to 20 minutes to travel through the town, while heavy through-traffic makes it harder for locals to access shops, schools and other parts of the community.

“There is also a significant safety problem. Between 2014 and 2023 there were 280 crashes on SH1 through Woodend, including three fatalities and 25 serious injuries.”

He cited an estimate from the New Zealand Transport Agency that suggested the project would save motorists up to 10 minutes travel time, reduce traffic through Woodend from around 21,500 vehicles a day to 8000, and reduce deaths and serious injuries by 78%.

The upgrades would extend the Christchurch Northern Motorway around 11km north, from just south of the Waimakariri River to beyond Pegasus and Ravenswood.

Bishop said $800m would be devoted to the project in next year’s Budget if National was re-elected. He said construction would begin next year.

More to come…

Carcasses, trespasses and a ‘Slink Mafia’: The strange and smelly saga of ‘Fast Eddie’ Zhi, ‘The King of Sheepskin’

New Zealand Herald October 04, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Every lamb and calf that dies at birth leaves behind a problem: a body that must be collected, buried or rendered before it becomes a source of contamination and stench. Around three years ago, Eddie Zhi built a business around taking those bodies from Southland farms, stripping away the valuable skins and finding a use for what remained. Now, after council orders halted the operation, Zhi is attempting to burn the hundreds of thousands of accumulated carcasses instead. Ben Tomsett reports.

Da Cheng “Eddie” Zhi says he came to Southland to revive a forgotten industry.

Instead, his Tuturau slink-skin operation has become the subject of repeated Environment Court orders, seven Environment Southland charges, a parallel Southland District Council case, angry protests, a formal trespass notice and thousands of emails.

It began with a practical problem of farming: what to do with lambs and calves that die before they can be sent to the meatworks.

Zhi’s answer was to recover their skins for export and turn the remaining animal material into organic fertiliser.

The councils believe that the business has operated outside its consent, with carcasses, skins, liquid and earthworks creating environmental risks.

Zhi spoke to the Herald by video call, his face marked with the words “SAVE JOBS” and “SOS” as he drove to the Environment Southland offices, where he planned to sticker their signs as a peaceful protest.

He calls the councils the “Slink Mafia”, blaming them for strangling the industry.

Before Zhi arrived, Newton Slinkskins had reduced its Southland service from about 140,000 lambs and 25,000 calves the previous season to an expected 50,000 to 70,000 lambs, amid the collapse of other operators and Lowe Corporation’s withdrawal from the South Island casualty-stock business.

When Newton shut the Tuturau plant in 2023, Zhi established NZAgri Development Ltd and restarted slink-skin processing at the site with help from Newton and former Newton staff.

Before Southland, Zhi was involved in the Australian meat trade where the nickname “Fast Eddie” followed him through a series of high-profile business disputes and legal battles – he tells the Herald he is an experienced international operator: “I was the king of sheepskin”.

“I turned myself into a meat trader.”

Zhi said he graduated from East China Normal University, became a university teacher at 20 and later studied leather technology at Sydney TAFE.

He said he had worked in the leather and meat industries in China, Australia and New Zealand and had been involved in major Australian deals - and that the Southland business was relatively modest by comparison.

“Today it’s a piece of cheesecake,” he said.

Zhi said he became involved in the Southland operation in 2023 after a friend told him there were no longer enough slink-skin operators in New Zealand.

He travelled to Tuturau and visited the existing plant, which he described as “pathetic, dirty” and “very, very, very, very, very sad looking”.

The slink-skin business is seasonal.

Lambs and calves that die around birth are collected, skinned and processed.

Their hides are exported for use in leather goods, while the remaining carcasses have to be disposed of lawfully.

Zhi said the original business model was too seasonal and labour-intensive. He believed it could be modernised.

He said the first year exceeded expectations: “I collected 162,000 lambs - 162,000 lambs,” he told the Herald.

“It’s only because there’s no bloody competition.

“Everybody else died.” One requires a sense of humour to understand Zhi, he explains.

Zhi’s solution for dealing with the remaining animal material was to convert it to organic liquid fertiliser.

He said he had told Environment Southland about the plan and believed council officials had responded positively.

In the second year, Zhi said the operation collected about 182,000 lambs and 33,000 calves.

However, that year two contractors walked off the job, stopping work for five days.

During that time, he said, animals continued arriving and a backlog developed.

“After one stop for five days, you have like 30,000 lambs piling up,” he said.

He said the backlog was worsened by severe weather and that animals had to be stored in different parts of the property.

Alyce Perkins lives with her husband and children about 250m from the plant and says the smell has become part of daily life.

“It’s horrible,” she told the Herald. “It just smells every day.”

Perkins said the previous operator’s season was unpleasant but short – the current operation lasted longer and the fertiliser production changed the experience of living nearby.

“It wrecks your little slice of heaven, really. It’s a pretty nice place here, but you’ve got to live next to that hellhole,” she said.

She said she supported finding a use for casualty animals, but believed the work needed to be done properly.

“There’s got to be a way of doing it that’s not detrimental to the environment and the people around it.”

By October last year, Environment Southland and the Ministry for Primary Industries were investigating Zhi’s operation.

Zhi said the labour dispute had been resolved and that processing was continuing normally.

A worker who has spoken to the Herald said they were owed $1200, which should have been paid by September 21.

They believed other workers were also thousands out of pocket.

Zhi rejected the account as “a total lie from suckers” and sent documents appearing to show contracts to sell 30,000 calf skins for US$450,000 and 40,000 baby lamb skins for US$300,000.

The documents did not show whether workers had been paid or directly address the alleged wage arrears.

Zhi said any smell may have come from the backlog, but denied there was a serious ongoing odour problem.

On October 31, 2025, Southland District Council applied to the Environment Court for interim enforcement orders against NZAgri Development Ltd, Zhi and Hui Xie.

Its evidence alleged offensive odour, blood discharges, possible contamination and vermin.

A monitoring officer described the smell as “overwhelming” and said she had at times been unable to breathe through her nose.

Officers also counted 283 intermediate bulk containers (IBCs) holding organic liquid fertiliser at the Tuturau property.

The court issued interim orders on November 21, requiring fertiliser production to stop, restricting the receipt of new skins and carcasses, and requiring existing animal material to be lawfully disposed of.

The orders were extended in December after a substantive hearing was delayed.

The parties later disagreed over whether Zhi could continue processing the material in the containers, with Zhi arguing further chemicals were needed before the fertiliser could be exported and the council arguing that would amount to an unconsented industrial activity.

Further orders were made in March after the council raised concerns about earthworks and a proposal to mix liquid fertiliser with soil to make a solid product.

The court ordered the fertiliser businesses to cease and required action over the earthworks and animal remains.

Initially, the judge declined to order the removal of the 283 containers, saying there was insufficient evidence of a likely adverse environmental effect from their continued presence.

But after council officers provided further evidence, including photographs showing dark marks around some containers, Judge Reid found that a number of the IBCs were leaking.

Leaving them represented a “significant ongoing risk to the environment”, the judge found, and the orders were amended to require their removal.

Zhi sought more time, citing wet and unstable ground, unsuitable lifting equipment and difficulties scheduling council staff.

The council opposed the application, saying officers had repeatedly attended the site but there had been “very limited progress”.

The court rejected the extension in June.

In July, Zhi applied to receive slink calves for skin recovery, arguing that the short season was important to farmers, collectors and seasonal workers.

The council said existing skins, carcasses and fertiliser containers had not been cleared.

On August 13, the court refused the application. Although Zhi framed the proposal as skin recovery rather than fertiliser production, the judge said it would still bring more animal material onto the site.

The court found the seasonal urgency was foreseeable and that any commercial harm arose while the respondents remained subject to orders they had not complied with.

Despite the decision, Zhi told the Herald the business had collected animals during the 2026 season.

This week, Zhi begun burning the the thousands of carcasses piled at Tuturau - which proved difficiult, as there was “too much moisture,” he said.

Asked why he was burning the carcasses, Zhi said it was intended to sterilise the surface, kill bacteria, reduce oxygen and encourage gradual degradation.

He said carbonisation would adsorb ammonia and claimed the process would deter rats.

He also said the burn was intended to draw international attention and condemnation, express his “freedom of scientific expressions”, mock what he called the “ignorant two fat rats”(ES and SDC), and celebrate China’s national day.

Zhi has also filed a judicial-review proceeding in the High Court against Environment Southland and Southland District Council.

In the filing, dated July 30, he alleges the councils failed to properly investigate historic offal pits, including their lining, construction, location and potential impact on groundwater.

He also alleges the councils failed to properly consider laboratory results, historic sources of contamination and alternatives to burying animal material.

It is a statement of claim and contains allegations that have not been tested in court.

Environment Southland has laid seven charges against Zhi relating to the operation between August 1 and September 26, 2025.

Six concern alleged discharges of blood, leachate or contaminants to land where they could enter water; the seventh alleges failure to comply with abatement notices.

The district council has also laid charges against Zhi and NZAgri Development.

On September 9, Environment Southland announced further interim orders requiring Zhi and his company to stop receiving and processing carcasses, cease unlawful discharges and remove carcasses, containers of minced animal material and contaminated liquid.

Both councils declined to comment because the matters remain before the Environment Court.

Zhi’s response has been anything but quiet, with his campaign of protest veering into performance art.

Since September 11, he has taken dead animals to council offices on the back of a truck, sat across a carpark entrance while removing his clothing and appeared in white overalls covered in red.

Before his Facebook account was suspended this week, Zhi was a regular poster in Southland community groups, using them to document his dispute with the councils and share graphic images from inside the Tuturau operation.

Facebook said the account had breached its standards on account integrity and Zhi had 180 days to appeal.

Zhi says he is exercising his democratic right to protest and trying to defend his workers and business.

Environment Southland eventually trespassed him from its offices.

The next major step is an Environment Court hearing in Invercargill on October 7, where Environment Southland is seeking further enforcement orders and Southland District Council is seeking to revoke the slink-skin factory’s resource consent.

The outcome could determine whether Zhi’s operation can continue.

Ben Tomsett is a multimedia journalist based in Dunedin. He joined the Herald in 2023.
