The bold ideas to future-proof Melbourne’s sporting heartland

Sydney Morning Herald October 05, 2026

A fan-friendly revamp of the MCG and better links to Melbourne and Olympic Parks would turn sporting events into festivals and cement Melbourne’s sports capital status.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Cricket Victoria chief executive Nick Cummins still remembers the excitement when he first sat in the MCG’s brand-new 45,000-capacity Great Southern Stand just over 30 years ago.

“At the time, it was like a spaceship,” he said. “It was amazing that you could have such a big stand with so much seating and great sight lines … compared to somewhere like Victoria Park, where you had to stand on two cans so you could see over the tall person in front of you.”

Since renamed in honour of Victoria’s legendary spin bowler, the Shane Warne Stand still holds a special place in Melburnians’ hearts.

But in terms of consumer experience, in the age where anyone can watch almost any sport live from the comfort of their own home, Cummins said the MCG was at risk of falling behind.

As LA Rams president Kevin Demoff said last month, when comparing their shiny home ground, SoFi Stadium, with the Melbourne venue that hosted the first NFL match Down Under: “We play in the world’s greatest modern stadium … the MCG can be the greatest old stadium.”

Cummins said the MCG was catering predominantly for die-hard “sit down, sit still, watch the game” fans and failing to deliver for those who viewed sport more as a social experience – a segment of the market that is increasingly important for full-day events, such as Test cricket, to remain relevant and engaging.

So, how do Melbourne’s major sporting arenas compare with those around the country, and what do they need to change to remain competitive in the future? And how can Melbourne retain its much-cited status as the sports – and arts – capital of Australia?

Over the coming days, we are taking an in-depth look at Melbourne’s sport and the arts. The theme is one of the key pillars of Melbourne Assembly, a civic forum The Age is hosting later this month, bringing together industry leaders, key decision-makers and the community to shape the city’s future.

Cummins cites interstate and American sports venues as examples of how the MCG could evolve.

“A lot of American stadiums now have these open patios where you can have almost like a barbecue deck or party deck,” the Cricket Victoria boss said. “At the AT&T Stadium where the Dallas Cowboys play, there’s a bar just below ground level ... and the players actually run through the bar to go onto the ground, and people will pay a lot of money just to be part of that.

“[In Australia] other states are building bigger venues … [with] superior facilities, including corporate hospitality, so although they might not hold as many people, the sports can make more money because they can get a more corporate return.

“We assume as Victorians that we’re entitled to these major sporting events … But other state governments are getting quite bullish in terms of challenging Victoria for that content.”

The MCG, the jewel in Melbourne’s crown, has evolved significantly over its 173 years, and its future is inextricably linked to the city’s reputation as Australia’s sporting capital. Alongside a highly competitive financial bid, the stadium was a key reason the NFL chose Victoria to host its Australian debut.

But while it retains the title of the largest stadium in the southern hemisphere, sports venues in other states have leapfrogged it in terms of consumer experience.

Perth’s Optus Stadium, which opened in 2018, is widely regarded as Australia’s most forward-leaning stadium. Among the first fully LED stadiums in the world, it features two 340-square-metre “super screens”, a light-up halo roof, adaptable seating configurations, and several open-air, pitch-facing terraces.

Other venues are on the horizon in Hobart and Brisbane, as well as major upgrades to the Queensland capital’s Suncorp Stadium, which will include Australia’s first 360-degree wrap-around LED ribbon screen, a “halo board” suspended from the stadium roof.

According to Melbourne-based venue-technology and intelligence firm PMY Group – one of the companies consulting on an MCG redevelopment business case, co-funded by the state government and the Melbourne Cricket Club – this is just the tip of the iceberg.

Chief executive Paul Yeomans said several stadiums overseas were completely rethinking the fan experience. At Intuit Dome in Los Angeles, a new NBA stadium where PMY led the technology design, fans can earn spendable loyalty points and prizes by cheering louder for the LA Clippers, with technology able to measure decibels down to a single seat.

“Going to sports games in the future will be a completely personalised, frictionless experience. Physical gates may be a thing of the past and queuing hopefully will be long gone. Venues will be able to remember who are you, where you like to sit, what you like to eat, and how you like to experience the action, and will customise their value proposition accordingly,” he said.

“They will also all be multi-use, with more collaboration between sports codes, music and entertainment to bring holistic ‘sportainment’ to life. The goal is really to sweat these infrastructure assets to maximise return on investment, so working out how to use them 365 days a year.”

How the MCG can be redeveloped to include “the contemporary facilities that athletes and spectators require” will be assessed as part of the business case, according to Development Victoria, a government planning agency. It is due to be finalised next year, with any eventual works – including to the Shane Warne Stand – expected to take at least a decade.

In the future, Yeomans said stadiums would be less like “colosseums” and more integrated with the surrounding area and businesses. He said the new stadium being built in Brisbane’s Victoria Park for the 2032 Olympics was a good example of this approach, as the parkland provided a natural precinct to spread out events.

Across the train tracks from the MCG, Yeomans said a number of these ideas were also being embraced. He said Melbourne Park was leading the way in its use of data to optimise the fan experience by better understanding the different demographics moving through the precinct, and tailoring its experience, food and beverage offerings, activations and advertising accordingly – a bit like a real-life version of social media algorithms.

The precinct, which has been redeveloped with a $1 billion state funding injection since 2010, is best known as the home of the Australian Open, and is packed with tennis fans throughout January.

Melbourne Park chief executive John Harnden has been tasked with planning how to make the most of the space the other 11 months of the year. While Tennis Australia has long pushed for a more permanent footprint, Harnden – a panellist at Melbourne Assembly, of which Melbourne Park is a major partner – said he did not want the precinct to be “a one-trick pony”, and all venues had been designed to accommodate a range of uses and fans.

But the precinct has its own challenges. While it might have the modern edge on the MCG, and be only a stone’s throw away, the rail infrastructure between them have left it isolated, with minimal natural foot traffic. It also does not share the same historic or cultural weight of the ’G, that brings tourists to its gates for tours and photo opportunities almost every day of the year.

As Harnden pointed out, it is, for the most part, a nighttime venue. Full to bursting on evenings when major events are in town, it is notably empty on an average weekday – an odd sight in an era of a growing population and squeezed inner-city space.

According to Melbourne sports magnate Eddie McGuire, the answer to both sports precincts’ future relevance lies right between their noses.

Of McGuire’s many ideas for the city’s future, building a sports and entertainment precinct over the rail tracks between the MCG and Melbourne Park is among his most enduring. He said it would lead to more foot traffic through Melbourne Park, and allow its modern facilities to be put to use during major events hosted at the MCG, such as the AFL grand final.

“We’ve got all of this magnificent infrastructure that the government has built … Centrepoint is just one of the best places, Rod Laver, Margaret Court, John Cain, all there. Collingwood’s ground is across the road. Punt Road’s there,” he said. “It costs you a fortune every time you put a marquee up [outside the MCG] … portable toilets. This is all there [at Melbourne Park]. Beautiful, air-conditioned, plumbed, magnificent.”

McGuire said covering the rail tracks would enable major events to expand their fan offerings outside the grounds, with big screens, stages, pop-up pubs and restaurants – a concept recently proven by the NFL’s takeover of Yarra Park to mirror popular tailgating parties outside games in the US. It would also limit the need to rely on temporary facilities in the parkland, which has frustrated some local residents.

“For major football games, cricket games, rugby league games, NFL games … we could get 100,000 in the ground and 200,000 around it, and turn it into a complete festival,” he said.

“You can then buy tickets to come into the precinct, but the outer precinct you can make free for kids and have jumping castles and AusKick over at Gosch’s Paddock, and turn the whole place into something great … You’ve got to remember why you’re doing it, and that’s why you’re doing it. It’s not just for the bloke with the super box, it’s for the kid who’s coming in, and maybe even for the kid who can’t get in.”

McGuire said he understood the idea would be explored as part of the MCG redevelopment business case. He said the main question still to be answered was how much it would cost and who would fund it, adding private equity could play a role. Harnden has also thrown his support behind the idea.

“From Melbourne Park’s perspective, stronger connections with the MCG would make it easier for people to experience everything this extraordinary precinct has to offer. We would welcome the opportunity to help shape any future proposal so it works well for visitors, events and the precinct as a whole,” he said.

Victorian Tourism Industry Council chief executive Lisa Patroni said she also viewed it as a natural next step.

“As competition between global destinations intensifies, we must continue to think ambitiously about the infrastructure, experiences and connections that will position Melbourne as a leading global destination for generations to come,” she said.

“Connecting two of Melbourne’s iconic sporting destinations [the MCG and Melbourne Park] presents an exciting opportunity to shape the future of Melbourne as Australia’s premier events and sporting capital … [and] would unlock new opportunities to experience, stay, explore and spend more time in our city. It represents the next evolution of a truly world-class events precinct and strengthens Melbourne’s ability to attract and host major sporting, cultural and business events well into the future.”

The state government did not respond to a request for comment.

McGuire said that once the rail area was covered, the precinct could be further expanded to connect other key areas of the city.

“I’ve always felt that the difference between Melbourne and particularly Sydney is [that] Sydney is a whole series of villages around this magnificent harbour. Melbourne has always had football grounds, racecourses, everything that was open to the public … so it’s just about connecting all that up,” he said.

Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website.

Jonathan Taylor’s double earns Colts win against Commanders in London

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 18:28:29 GMT

Indianapolis 30-13 Washington

Treylon Burks scores 47-yard TD for Washington

“Welcome to the NFL’s home away from home,” was the rallying cry from former running back and current in-stadium hype man Ronde Barber before the league’s 19th year holidaying in the UK began. And welcome Washington’s injury bug which must have stowed away on the flight to London. The mighty Commanders defense that overwhelmed the Colts at times could not overcome having another quarterback knocked out of commission. Indianapolis capitalised on the misfortune with crafty running back Jonathan Taylor carrying them to a 30-13 victory.

The Commanders were already missing starting quarterback Jayden Daniels with an elbow injury and their pesky interloper wasn’t satisfied that Washington had endured enough torment. The game-defining moment came early as a knee injury forced backup passer Marcus Mariota out of the contest after a strong start. Rookie third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis replaced him and though he delivered the play of the game with an incredible showcase of vision and accuracy on a 47-yard touchdown throw, it was too much, too soon for the 23-year-old.

Washington’s brutal defense, fresh from toppling the Super Bowl champions last week, burst out of the traps as defensive tackle Odafe Oweh drove his opposite number Bernhard Raimann straight into Colts quarterback Daniel Jones. The stunned signal caller fell backwards while coughing the ball up to the Commanders who had a turnover after two plays and three points after a 31-yard field goal from Drew Stevens.

From then on it mattered little that Jones continued to struggle in the face of Washington’s ferocious front seven. The Colts passer would finish with 19 completions from 34 attempts for 143 yards, no touchdowns and an interception. Lucky for Indianapolis that they have the capable legs of Taylor who picked up the quarterback’s slack with 95 yards on the ground and a pair of touchdowns either side of half-time. His game-winning efforts sandwiched a 48-yard Spencer Shrader boot that put the Colts 17-6 up at the break and out of sight.

Meanwhile Kaliakmanis was dealing with the pressure of being thrust into his first professional game. The crowd noticeably quietened at defeat looming far too early as veteran running back Austin Ekeler edged the Commanders to midfield. Those in burgundy and gold had accepted their fate after the unknown QB had started the second half with an ominous interception that set up Taylor’s second score.

The backup’s backup quickly restored some faith though with a breathtaking throw. Kaliakmanis saw Treylon Burks breaking down the left sideline and drove the arcing pass just ahead of the sprinting receiver’s path. Burks made the grab in stride for the touchdown. The crowd could not believe it. Neither could Kaliakmanis as he grinned from ear to ear after giving his team a fleeting spark to sit 17-13 behind.

The rookie continued to receive help from his impressive defense as Indianapolis favoured conservative play calling to avoid any more costly turnovers as they added a field goal from Shrader. Alarm bells from the early fumble and interception had been silenced with Taylor taking care of the ball.

Then for a few seconds it looked as if Kaliakmanis could be delivering a quarterback debut for the history books as his receiver Antonio Williams raced 80 yards for another touchdown that would have levelled the scores. To the crowd’s deafening ire it was not to be due to an illegal shift penalty.

As the final quarter began it was the reliable Taylor again at the controls. Two 12-yard rushes moved the Colts to the goalline. A faked handoff to their linchpin then allowed Jones to tuck and run for a score to add some much-needed positivity after his arm wilted under Washington pressure.

Indianapolis will be glad to escape London with a 2-2 record and realistic ambitions of making the playoffs after the rockiest of starts. Washington will lick their wounds hoping Daniels is back soon to revive their season.

Evans ends Britain’s wait for world rally title after Solberg crashes two corners from glory

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 18:14:26 GMT

Elfyn Evans becomes first British winner since 2001

Oliver Solberg’s hopes shattered by tumble down bank

⁠Elfyn Evans ended years of heartache, and a quarter-of-a-century wait for Britain, by winning the World Rally Championship title with Toyota after a dramatic season ⁠finale in Sardinia on Sunday.

The ⁠Welshman had been ​championship runner-up five times in the last six years but emerged triumphant after a final Powerstage duel with teammate Oliver Solberg ended with the charging Swede crashing ⁠out two corners from the finish while on course to take the crown.

Solberg, 25, ran wide and careered down a bank before getting the car back on the road. ⁠He still won the rally but lost the crucial bonus points on offer for the top five in the ​final stage.

Evans, with co-driver Scott Martin at his side, ‌became the first British world ‌rally champion since Englishman Richard Burns in 2001 and only the third since Scottish driver Colin McRae became ‌the first in 1995.

Sweden’s Solberg, son of Norway’s 2003 champion Petter, ended the season as runner-up. The final standings left Evans on 243 points, Solberg on 238 and Sami Pajari on 237 in what was also the end of an era for the sport with new regulations in force next year.

Evans said: “It hasn’t sunk in. I was sure it was over. I didn’t drive the best ‌stage but threw everything at it but it wasn’t clean. I feel for Oliver. He had an incredible weekend.” The Welshman completed his final run first and had to ​watch and wait to see whether he had done enough to take the title.

“I don’t really know what my reaction is, it’s surreal with how it happened. It’s a relief. It wouldn’t be my proudest way of winning it, but it’s job done,” added the 37-year-old, who finished fifth in the gravel rally.

Evans had started the rally – the ⁠final round after Saudi Arabia’s finale was cancelled due to conflict in the region – ​17 points clear of Finland’s Pajari, ​also in a Toyota, and 21 clear ​of Solberg.

The Reluctant Vampire review – Lenny Rush’s absolute joy of a comedy is perfectly cast

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 18:10:34 GMT

This gag-packed adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s children’s books – by the writing team behind Alan Partridge – is full of stunning comic talent. Bill Bailey, Ross Noble, Tom Davies, Sian Clifford and Asim Chaudhry are all brilliant

Oh my goodness; how long has it been since we all had a lovely teatime treat? Too long, that’s how long! But now joy is at hand, courtesy of Neil and Rob Gibbons (the pair behind the most recent incarnations of Alan Partridge) and The Reluctant Vampire. It is their adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s 1982 children’s book of the same name and its 1983 sequel, The Vampire’s Revenge. They have kept the books’ warmth and daftness and added their own talents to the six-part series for youngsters. There are jokes for parents in there too, but the brothers have wisely kept the exquisite cruelty with which they craft Alan’s misadventures safely stowed away.

Here is the tale of an undead royal-ish family (temporarily usurped a few generations back when the paterfamilias choked on a scab), living a traditional vampiric life in their traditionally gothic castle. There is proud patriarch Victor (Tom Davis), who revels in the hunting and draining of the humans he despises (“I see,” he says, looking round the overdecorated bedroom of his latest about-to-be-victim, “you have a keen eye for tat”). He is married to Valeeta (Sian Clifford) – they share a hot-to-trot vibe with Gomez and Morticia of The Addams Family films – and they have two children. Vernon (an absolutely wonderful turn from Gabriel Nagy in his first major screen role) is a chip off the old block, loving the vampire life and able to identify blood vintages with a single sip (“Poor circulation … lavender … the neck of a Flemish merchant?”).

But he is the second son and so the spare to the heir, Valentine (Lenny Rush, who counts as a veteran actor by experience but is still only 17 and whose age only highlights his astonishing talents). And Valentine, alas, is not a very good vampire. His fangs still haven’t come in, he’s not a fan of blood and he can’t fly or turn into a bat. A very late developer, his family all sigh and agree. Eventually, however, Valeeta is forced to admit the truth to her boy – that he is not a vampire at all, but a human baby she rescued from a fire while Victor was away in Carpathia and raised as her own. “You were going to eat me, weren’t you?” sighs Valentine. “Maybe a little bit, at first,” she agrees. But then she fell in love with him and thought he would pick up their vampire ways. But alas, he has not. Possibly because, as Val notes: “It’s not conversational French.”

Soon a series of misunderstandings lead Victor to believe Val is at last ready for his initiation ceremony and the struggle to conceal the truth from him and an increasingly suspicious Vernon is on. Underneath runs a gently developing friendship and maybe more between Val and Gertie (Dodger’s Ellie-May Sheridan, in another great performance), whom he meets while on the run from a horde of villagers – led by a man who turns out to be her father (Charlie Cooper), which adds another complication to life.

Around the family is gathered a perfectly cast collection of supporting characters. There is Bill Bailey and Ross Noble as gargoyles Guy and Gary, not just siphons for rainwater (“A common misconception”) but effectively the castle’s CCTV cameras, if CCTV cameras were easily distracted and no use at surveillance at all. There is Asim Chaudhry as Igon (he wears an eyepatch over the missing one because when Eric Morecambe writes that joke, it stays in the act), and there is Joe Wilkinson as Wilf the werewolf, a perfect send-up of a certain type of man, as he leans heavily over an anxious-looking maid telling her that he “totally gets the female experience, because in a way I have a monthly cycle too”. He is keen that people shouldn’t let the monster define the man. “No one ever talks about the yeti’s love of literature or his wonderful baritone!” he cries. And Jekyll, he says, “in the daytime, is a bloody good GP”. The Reluctant Vampire is full of these little flourishes as well as the more straightforward gags coming thick and fast. And I really must insist that you stick around until at least the second episode in order to catch the ham-sandwich-based homage to Morecambe’s finest hour (courtesy of the late, great Eddie Braben, of course).

The Reluctant Vampire has a stacked cast, a gag-packed script and the ineffable air of a labour of love – of Eric, of the tradition he worked in, of comedy itself as something for all and not just for snarky adults – with nobody phoning anything in. Fang-tastic.

The Reluctant Vampire aired on BBC One and is available on BBC iPlayer

Shaw seals thrilling win over Arsenal to extend Manchester City’s 100% WSL start

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 18:07:47 GMT

Arsenal’s under-pressure head coach Renée Slegers still believes they will turn their form around, despite falling 10 points behind Manchester City with Sunday’s defeat in an absorbing six-goal thriller against the defending champions.

Arsenal were last season’s runners-up in the Women’s Super League and had high hopes of mounting a strong challenge this term but their chances of lifting a first WSL title since 2019 now appear to be hanging by a thread after five rounds of fixtures, while City maintained their 100% start by coming from behind twice to beat Slegers’ struggling side.

The 37-year-old Dutchwoman, who in January signed a new contract until the summer of 2029, said on Friday that she felt the full support of the club. Asked, after this pivotal 4-2 defeat, whether she would be the one in charge after this month’s international break, she replied: “All I know so far is that the last couple of days we’ve been together as a club, as a team, with support, aligning on the direction. Of course, this result is disappointing, but I’m here, I’m full of energy and I care a lot for the club.”

Slegers added she feels the international break will come at a good time to change environments and that there will be a “big review of our season so far” during the break. She continued: “We see solutions and we see the closeness. It’s not that we’re totally off it. It’s been consistently about margins – when we get them on our side, I think we’re going to be really good.”

The match was the first to be played at the Etihad Stadium since the Premier League published the guilty verdict against Manchester City and there was something of a subdued atmosphere outside the stadium in the buildup to kick-off. That quickly changed once the game started, and was wholly different in the second half as the hosts began to take control and their supporters were thoroughly enjoying themselves.

City had frequently insisted their women’s team were treating this as “business as usual” before their draw with Real Madrid on Thursday. There were very few references to the ongoing saga here on Sunday, aside from some Arsenal fans chanting “same old City, always cheating” during the first half, and one City fan – sitting just in front of the media seats – who defiantly shouted about which part of the anatomy people could “stick your 115 charges”, but nobody else joined in. Matters on the pitch were more interesting.

City will have felt aggrieved about the nature of Arsenal’s opener, as replays showed that Lisa Baum appeared to be offside when Lotte Wubben-Moy headed goalwards. Baum was the quickest to get to the rebound after Ayaka Yamashita’s save and poked home. The visitors could not hold on until the break, however, as Lauren Hemp’s deflected strike found its way into the far corner.

Arsenal went back in front shortly after half-time when Yui Hasegawa lost the ball inside her own area and Alessia Russo pounced, curling a terrific finish into the far corner. It was her first league goal of the campaign. Arsenal appeared to be in control until a triple substitution from Andrée Jeglertz, including the introduction of Kerstin Casparij, changed things.

The 26-year-old, playing as an inverted full-back, latched on to a loose ball and curled in a delightful strike to equalise and soon afterwards Hemp tucked a tidy finish through Anneke Borbe’s legs to make it 3-2. Suddenly Arsenal’s body language changed and City were on top. They added a clinical fourth when Shaw latched on to Aoba Fujino’s excellent through-ball and her low finish was superb.

Nearly all women arriving on small boats have been raped, says Shabana Mahmood

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 18:00:34 GMT

Home secretary warns people traffickers will exploit asylum seekers because they decide who comes to the UK

Nearly all women who try to reach the UK in small boats from northern France have been raped on their journey, Shabana Mahmood has claimed.

In an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast, the home secretary said far-right, balaclava-wearing activists would “kill” or “kick me out of my own country” if they took power.

Speaking to the former Tory minister Rory Stewart and Tony Blair’s former close adviser Alastair Campbell, she said sexual abusers would exploit most asylum seekers as long as traffickers continued to decide who came to the UK.

She said: “We’re not in control of this border. The sifting of the people that end up in the north of France and are about to get on a dinghy is done by criminal gangs who are also, by the way, people traffickers.

“You can almost guarantee that every woman that’s in the north of France has probably been raped along the journey. Some of the men too, they’ve certainly been abused and threatened. That is not the model that should decide whether somebody gets to come to the UK, make this their place of sanctuary and ultimately become one of us.”

Asked by Campbell about balaclava-wearing protesters shutting down ports and praising her policies, she said they should “sod off”.

She added: “They’re just troublemakers. You know, they’d kill me in a minute if they could, and they’d definitely kick me out of my own country. So let’s just be really clear about who and what they are. They don’t think I’m a true Brit and they hate the fact that I’m a Muslim.”

Mahmood also said she considered herself “part of the pro-Palestinian cause” and felt “very uncomfortable” over the arrests of activists opposing the ban imposed on Palestine Action.

Merseyside police arrested 82 people on Monday at the Labour party conference on suspicion of wearing or carrying articles supporting a proscribed organisation.

In a protest organised by Defend Our Juries, scores of people sat outside the conference centre in Liverpool, many holding handmade banners saying they supported Palestine Action.

Mahmood said: “For those of us who have been in the pro-Palestinian cause all of our lives, these are people – sometimes you’ll know who they are, you know, you’ve been on the marches with them – it feels very uncomfortable to see them falling foul of section 13 of the Terrorism Act.”

However, she defended enforcing the ban, regardless of her views: “You’ve got to be able to apply your principles, even when it’s uncomfortable for you, because you’re going to really want to apply them when it’s something you, you know, with your whole heart, are feeling very passionately about.”

Authorities were preparing on Sunday for the arrival of a migrant dinghy heading for the south coast. The boat was being shadowed by French coastguard and rescue vessels and moving toward the Channel boundary line, according to ship tracking data.

It appeared to have set off from near the Utah Beach area of Normandy on Sunday morning.

Caroline Dinenage, the Conservative MP for Gosport in Hampshire, said there was “nothing to suggest” the boat would land on the county’s coast but police were “making preparations should that situation change”.

A government spokesperson said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border. It is vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival.”

Imran Hussain, a director at the Refugee Council, welcomed the home secretary’s acknowledgment of widespread sexual violence, but questioned why the government had closed safe and legal routes which could help asylum seekers avoid falling into the hands of predators.

“We know from our services that women and girls fleeing war and persecution face sexual violence both in the conflicts they have escaped and on the journeys they are forced to make in search of safety,” he said.

“That is why in welcoming the government’s announcement last week of new safe routes we called for them not to be limited to a few hundred people. Last year the government closed family reunion, the safe route for refugees which overwhelmingly benefits women and children.

“It is entirely right to talk about the dangers women face on these journeys but we should not be closing the safe routes that could keep them out of harm’s way. Protecting women means more safe routes, not fewer.”

Tuchel says Alex Scott’s emergence gives England – and Rice – ‘high level’ competition

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 18:00:34 GMT

Tuchel praises Scott’s all-round display in Croatia win

‘We will not survive on two midfielders. More the better’

Thomas Tuchel warned that there is competition for Declan Rice’s place in England’s midfield after Alex Scott marked his first international start with an outstanding display during the 7-0 away win against Croatia.

Rice, who struggled with neural pain in his upper hamstring during the World Cup, withdrew from the camp because of load management and the vice-captain’s absence at the start of the side’s Nations League campaign has allowed Tuchel to broaden his options alongside Elliot Anderson in midfield.

England’s head coach has added youth to the squad and enjoyed the competition between Myles Lewis-Skelly and Scott during the past fortnight. Lewis-Skelly did well after starting the 3-2 defeat by Spain and the 2-0 win against Czechia but the Arsenal midfielder was outshone by Scott, who partnered Anderson in Croatia and delivered a performance full of energy, speed and quality on and off the ball.

It was Scott’s second cap – he also impressed after coming on against Czechia in Prague – and the 23-year-old’s excellence was one of many positives on an important night for Tuchel. The manager can feel a new England emerging after the pain of their World Cup defeat by Argentina. The squad has been refreshed and it was interesting that Tuchel used a question about Jordan Pickford’s spot as the No 1 goalkeeper last Friday to suggest, unprompted, that Rice does not necessarily have a guaranteed place in the team.

The bigger picture is that Rice, who has helped England reach two major finals, remains part of Tuchel’s best XI. However, Tuchel delivered another pointed response when asked if the Arsenal midfielder will feel his place is under threat after seeing Scott’s performance in Rijeka.

“Of course, and he does, we need performances like this,” the German said. “This is just the nature of it. We will not survive on two central midfielders. The more the better – and it’s always about the guys who are in camp.

“Declan knows about his importance, and he’s one of the very best midfielders in Europe. Nothing will change that. But it’s exactly what we need. We need more, more, more, more variety. We need more, more, more options. Then it’s always about the guys who are in camp. Alex was in the highest level.”

Anderson and Scott dominated against the experienced pairing of Luka Modric and Mateo Kovacic. The England youngsters built on playing together when Lee Carsley’s under-21 side won the European Championship last year.

“I guess it helps,” Tuchel said. “Not only as players but even in their character. They’re a good mix and match. Alex had a fantastic match, and we need to be strong in the middle of the pitch. I’m very happy with the level that Alex trained at.”

Scott explained his partnership with Anderson. “We work really well together,” he said. “We saw that last year at the Euros and we’ve been speaking about it ever since, playing this midfield together.

“I love playing with Elliot. He makes life so easy for me. He’s one of the best midfielders in the world. We bounce off each other very well. We like getting on the ball, aggressive off the ball, we suit each other. Playing next to him is great and I know he enjoys it as well.”

It is easy to see why Bournemouth were determined not to lose Scott last summer. Arsenal asked about the former Bristol City player’s availability, Manchester United were interested and Chelsea had multiple bids rejected.

Tuchel sees Scott as one of the best midfielders in England. That assessment adds to the sense that not taking him to the World Cup was a mistake. Tuchel gave no minutes to Kobbie Mainoo and lost Jordan Henderson when the 36-year-old broke a wrist during the celebrations after the last-16 win against Mexico.

But Scott, who may well have ended Henderson’s hopes of a recall, refused to sulk. He used his World Cup disappointment as motivation and has started the season well.

“It gave me more hunger but there’s so many top players for this country,” Scott said. “There was no bad feelings about not going to the World Cup. I went to the prep camp, I wanted to learn as much as I can and it helped me coming into this camp.”

England’s triumph in Croatia keeps them in second place in their Nations League group, three points behind Spain and well placed to reach the quarter-finals in March. They close this extended international break at home against Czechia Harry Kane will expect to equal Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps and is playing brilliantly with Jude Bellingham.

“They were good in the World Cup,” Tuchel said. “They get better and better. They love playing with each other. They understand each other better.”

Green party votes to adopt policy that equates Zionism with racism

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 17:40:39 GMT

Motion calling for single Palestinian state, which is opposed by most Green MPs and expected to be challenged, passes by 1,022 votes to 813

The Greens have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state, a move opposed by the bulk of the party’s MPs and which is expected to face legal challenge.

Zack Polanski, who heads the Greens in England and Wales and missed the vote at the party’s conference in Brighton to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, has faced criticism for a perceived lack of leadership on a hugely divisive issue.

There have also been concerns that the policy change was pushed largely by newcomers who have little interest in the rest of the party’s platform.

Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the motion. Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns said they were “deeply saddened” while Siân Berry and Carla Denyer said they would support any Jewish members who believed they were being targeted as a result of the policy change.

The binding policy motion, passed by 1,022 votes to 813, says Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism”. It calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”.

While opinion among Jewish Green members is split, some have expressed worry that this will mean they could face disciplinary action for belonging to Jewish organisations that officially support Zionism, even synagogues.

After the vote, one backer of the motion, Salma Yaqoob, a former member of George Galloway’s Respect party who is now a Green, insisted this would not happen, saying: “Nobody will be removed, challenged, disciplined, suspended because they put forward or articulate their belief in Zionism.”

However, an amendment put forward saying the motion should not be used to “pressure, proscribe or discipline members based on affiliation with Jewish community institutions” was voted down.

It is understood that some Green members are consulting lawyers over whether the policy could be challenged for breaching equalities legislation.

Adam Wagner KC, the barrister who led a case that concluded Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour broke equalities laws over antisemitism, said such a case would have a good chance of success.

“I think there is a strong risk that the motion as passed contravenes the Equality Act 2010, which applies to political parties, as it will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally,” he added.

Zionism when defined in the broad sense of supporting a Jewish nation state “is likely to be a protected belief” under the act, he said.

The motion argues that Zionism is necessarily racist as it “privileges one ethnic group on the basis of the subjugation of others”. It adds: “This motion is aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism, as defined, and not at the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists. Not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews …

“Zionism, as defined above, will be treated as any other form of racism, and this motion will be implemented by the anti-racism policy working group as appropriate and in accordance with its ordinary practice.”

According to the Institute for Jewish Policy Research, about two-thirds of British Jews consider themselves Zionists.

after newsletter promotion

During the lengthy debate, which was for members only, Chowns and Caroline Lucas, the former leader who was the Greens’ first MP, argued against the plan.

The motion had been pushed by a group called Greens for Palestine, which encouraged non-party members to sign up to the party to make sure the policy was debated and adopted. After it was passed, supporters came to the front of the hall to hug and cheer.

One member who opposed the motion said: “There are now two Green parties – the everyday members, and those who have joined for just one reason, Palestine, and who have no interest in anything else.”

There is considerable disquiet among some senior Greens who feel that Polanski, who is Jewish, could have taken a stronger stance on the issue. The party leader has justified the motion’s broad argument by pointing to the death toll in Gaza during Israel’s assault on the territory.

Asked on Saturday if he believed Zionism was racist, Polanski told the BBC: “Well, in the motion, it is defined as the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people. I think that is clearly racism.”

After the vote, the party’s five MPs, plus Polanski and his two co-deputy leaders, released a joint statement saying the party “will never tolerate any form of discrimination or harassment”, adding: “We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.”

However, Ramsay, Chowns, Berry and Denyer all posted this on social media with messages noting their opposition to the motion.

The Movement for Progressive Judaism, one of the main Jewish denominations in the UK, condemned the vote, saying: “The motion is antisemitic in its formulation and intention. By adopting it, the Green party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party.

“Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews. The Green party has chosen to brand Jews who hold this belief as racists and make their equal participation in the party conditional on renouncing it.”

Adam Langleben, who coordinated complaints from the Jewish Labour Movement to the Equality and Human Rights Commission, said: “This is without doubt the most antisemitic and racist motion brought before a mainstream political party in my lifetime. It is Corbynism on steroids, and would seem even more open to legal challenge.”

For Kemi, being the Nasty party is not toxic but a badge of honour

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 17:13:49 GMT

The Tory leader says the party’s plans to cut people’s benefits are no more than ‘common sense’

It’s a thought. A bold one. Possibly a career-ending one. But a thought nonetheless. When Theresa May told the Tory conference in 2002 that under Iain Duncan Smith the Conservatives had become “the Nasty party”, many members took that to mean they had become undesirable. Within a few years, David Cameron had moved the Tories closer to the “hug a husky” centre and by 2010 he was prime minister.

Kemi Badenoch takes a rather different view. For her, being the Nasty party is a badge of honour. An aspiration. People had had it far too good with austerity, Brexit, Covid and the Liz Truss mini-budget. The country needed a reality check; a return to old-fashioned unpleasantness. A taste of genuine hardship. People had got far too used to getting something for nothing. Especially the physically and mentally ill. What they needed was a short sharp shock of intense labour from 8am to 8pm. That would make them feel better. And anyone found skiving would be banged up for a short time in prison. Say 10 years.

And take a bow, her cheerleader-in-chief. The man whose sycophancy consistently goes above and beyond the call of duty. We’re talking, of course, of the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp. He had chosen to mark the beginning of Tory conference with an interview to the Sun in which he had identified himself as a one-man vigilante force. For the next four days, he had personally guaranteed that Birmingham would be a crime-free zone. The Philpster would be on guard night and day to arrest all shoplifters and to check up on people who hadn’t paid their TV licence. From now on he would be a superhero. BatTwat.

For Kemi, the beginning of conference was marked with the traditional BBC interview with Laura Kuenssberg. One where she would try to be the cosiest version of herself. The nasty leader with the heart of gold. A woman who could say in all honesty that “this was hurting her more than it was hurting you” as she removed someone’s benefits. This was Kemi returning in triumph. A year ago, her position as leader had looked ropey. Now the Tories have had a long, hard look around and concluded there actually isn’t anyone better.

“Is this a return to the nasty party?” asked Kuenssberg. Kemi was trying not to phrase it in precisely those terms. Nasty was only a word to be implied. Rather, she would prefer it if we could use the words “commonsense” party. Common sense, as in it was plain to everyone that something had to be done. And that something was to pick on the poorest and most vulnerable people in society. For years now, these parasites had been lounging around and getting fat on benefits. Asking themselves not what they could do for the Tory party but what the Tory party could do for them.

To illustrate her point, Kemi proudly drew Laura’s attention to her rather desperate pamphlet The Right Way, which the Tories have published as their new credo. Six principles of Conservatism to get them through the bad times. To remind them they are right even when the country thinks they are unelectable. Kemi’s Kemistry, as she hopes we will call it. The first rule is that Kemi never makes mistakes. Asked to name anything she has changed her mind about, she comes up with nothing. The laws of physics will change long before Kemi. She wants us to think of The Right Way as her foundational document that will be spoken of in hushed tones for decades to come. It will be lucky to survive until tomorrow.

We then moved on to Kemi’s latest big idea: to give everyone who makes more than £100,000 a year unlimited free childcare. The case was unarguable, said Kemi. Free childcare was totally wasted on people on the minimum wage because they couldn’t be trusted to spend the money wisely. It would probably all be wasted on Happy Meals at McDonald’s or a Sky subscription. Let’s face it, it was just chucking good money after bad. Most working-class kids were bound to end up on benefits anyway, so why encourage them from the moment they were born? It’s time they learned to be self-sufficient. What a contrast with the top 5% of the country. They could at least spend their benefits on something worthwhile. Like baby yoga.

Kemi was also keen to keep pensioners happy. We will retain the triple lock, she said. Even though half the shadow cabinet know it’s completely unaffordable. Old people definitely had to be kept sweet, as they were about the last section of the country who actually voted Tory. Not that this was any factor in shaping current policy. Because Kemi had just published The Right Way, in which she had declared that her principles were whatever she wanted them to be on the day. And, by the way, this would all be paid for by cutting benefits for the 10 million scroungers who were cheating the system. Could you verify that figure? Laura asked. Kemi shook her head. It was just a well-known fact that she had made up. So no need.

After going on to say she would be building 50,000 more prison spaces for all the criminals BatTwat arrested in the next four days, the interview meandered to a close. In the studio, Penny Mordaunt declared it to be the best interview a Tory leader had ever given. Penny is beside herself with joy at having passed the test to be admitted to the MPs’ candidate list. Answering yes to questions such as: “Are you mad?” and “Are you happy to trash the Good Friday agreement?” It was Penny’s performance in the Sky reality show The War Game that swung it. As defence secretary she couldn’t wait to start a nuclear apocalypse. Come friendly bombs.

Over in the conference centre, the complex was strangely quiet. Maybe the news that everything is going swimmingly for the Tories hasn’t yet filtered down to MPs and members. Even the main hall wasn’t full, and there was nothing going on elsewhere. But those who were there seemed happy enough. Perhaps they are genuinely delighted that things aren’t going even worse. That they are still only four points in the polls off their disastrous 2024 election result. That it doesn’t matter that the so-called Keminaissance exists largely in their imaginations.

But on we go. A party the country still regards as toxic is determined to double down on its toxicity. Desperate to track ever further to the right and abandon its centre right to Labour and the Lib Dems. It feels like madness. But this conference is all about Kult Kemi. There is even an AI slop, sub-Beano reproduction of the Bayeux tapestry. A series of tableaux leading to the moment Kemi saves the world. She looks on beatifically as several easily identified journalists take dictation. Curiously, I’m not one of them.

Good palliative care and assisted dying can go hand in hand

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 17:06:32 GMT

Readers respond to an article on the urgent need for palliative care reform

Jane Turner is right that end-of‑life care needs fixing (MPs, you told us clearly that end-of-life care in the UK is broken. So now we need you to fix it, 28 September), and I argue that it needs fixing on two fronts at once. My husband, John, died in March aged 43 after nearly six years of bowel cancer treatment. He endured more than 70 rounds of chemotherapy, determined to watch our children grow up. He spent his last three months in a hospice, receiving the best palliative care on offer. Even so, he suffered terribly.

Some pain cannot be controlled quickly, and some suffering cannot be treated at all. One evening he screamed in agony while stranded in a bath, unable to move, for nearly an hour before relief took effect. As the cancer swelled his torso, he slowly suffocated – and no drug could prevent it. He was fully aware throughout, and told me repeatedly that he could not go on. In his last hours, I wore earplugs to bear the sound of his gasping.

Most hospices are charities that receive very little state funding – that must change. Better palliative care will spare many people needless suffering. But it cannot spare everyone, and no amount of funding would have given John what he wanted: the chance to face the inevitable on his own terms.

Improving palliative care and legalising assisted dying are not rivals. Doing both would also free hospice beds for those who want them; John occupied one for three months.

John was always going to die from his cancer, but the trauma of his final months, for him and for our children, was preventable. MPs should not choose between fixing care and offering choice. They must do both. Liz WilsonCoventry

Jane Turner is absolutely right that we need to invest in palliative and end-of life care. She is also correct that the greatest unmet needs are seen in NHS hospitals, and that it is here where investment is most urgent. That all sounds very expensive, but if we look at the headline financial figures, we see that actually it might cost very little in terms of new money. The Nuffield Trust tells us that the UK spends £6.6bn on emergency hospital care in the last year of life. This contrasts with only £1.1bn to run all 204 UK hospices, including the 24 NHS hospices.

I was a consultant physician at one of these units for 20 years, and I am told that it now costs around £5m annually to provide a comprehensive specialist palliative care service to a population of 250,000, delivered across all settings, including hospital wards. This implies a total cost of around £1.4bn to provide this NHS service across the UK population of 70 million people. The NHS has complete access to the patient activity and financial figures of these 24 units, so these figures can easily be confirmed.

One of the strengths of specialist palliative care services is that they always try to help patients and their families to plan for the future: when you get more poorly, where would you want to be cared for? If this planning enabled us to avert only 10% of emergency admissions in the last year of life, the money saved would more than fill the funding gap. If emergency admissions fell by more than 10%, it would, overall, save the nation money. Stephen KirkhamLytchett Minster, Dorset

Jane Turner is absolutely right that palliative and end-of-life care must be properly funded and available to everyone who needs it. Those of us who campaigned for assisted dying have never argued otherwise. Better palliative care and greater choice at the end of life should not be competing ambitions.

But there is an important question that cannot be lost now the parliamentary vote is over: what happens to the people whose suffering even excellent palliative care cannot adequately relieve?

I am living with incurable secondary breast cancer. I love my life and want to be here for my daughter for as long as possible. But I also know from painful personal experience that I am allergic to opioid painkillers. After the birth of my daughter, when I needed multiple operations, my pain could not be properly controlled. It was frightening. So when I am told that better palliative care will remove the need for assisted dying, I have a very simple question: what if it cannot?

Jane is right that even with the best quality care, some deaths can still be difficult. Those people matter too. Since the fall of the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill, terminally ill people have not suddenly become less frightened about what lies ahead. Our diagnoses have not changed, and neither have the limits of medicine.

So yes: fix palliative care. End the postcode lottery. Make sure nobody reaches the end of their life without the support, expertise and compassion they deserve. But we should be able to hold two thoughts at once. Excellent palliative care can transform many deaths. It cannot guarantee that every dying person’s suffering can be relieved.

The question for those who opposed assisted dying therefore remains: what is the answer for those people?Sophie BlakeHove, East Sussex

Let’s build a better future for female scaffolders

Adrian Chiles is right: scaffolding is hard work (Britain’s scaffolding should be a source of national pride – instead we’re struggling to recruit workers, 1 October). It demands physical resilience, skill, judgment and proper training. That will naturally mean it is not a job for everyone – men or women.

Which is why the conversation about the skills shortage should be less about who traditionally became a scaffolder, and more about who is willing and able to learn the trade and meet the same standards.

As the industry is already facing the significant shortfall that Chiles describes, we need to widen the pool of people who can see scaffolding as a genuine career.

That includes women, but the bigger issue is attracting capable people into the trade, training them properly and keeping standards high. That is part of what the Women in Scaffolding Association (WiSA) is trying to do.

We support women already working on the tools, make them visible and connected, and show women and girls that scaffolding is a genuine skilled career. We also work to bring more people into construction generally.

Nobody is suggesting lowering the bar. Scaffolding requires strength, but also technique, teamwork, training and considerable skill. The standards should remain the standards.

Chiles also makes an important point about AI. Scaffolding is practical, skilled work that cannot simply be automated away. Britain still needs people who can build, solve problems and work safely with their hands. If scaffolders are becoming a dying breed, perhaps the answer is to look more widely for the next generation. Some of them will be women. Emma ClaassenFounder, WiSA

Parental alienation and the pain of custody battles in the the family courts

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 17:06:15 GMT

Readers respond to an article about a mother who feels let down by the family courts

Hannah Summers’ article raises disturbing concerns about the misuse of parental alienation allegations in family courts (‘Just like that, I lost my girls’: the mother who feels betrayed by the family courts, 29 September). However, I believe that it would benefit from a clearer distinction between the discredited theory of “parental alienation syndrome” (PAS) and genuine, demonstrable alienating behaviour.

PAS proposed that a child’s unjustified rejection of a parent could be identified as a distinct syndrome. It is no longer an accepted clinical diagnosis, since a child’s rejection of a parent cannot itself establish manipulation, therefore treating it as diagnostic risks overlooking abuse or other legitimate reasons for the child’s feelings.

However, rejecting PAS as a clinical diagnosis should not obscure the reality that one parent can manipulate a child into rejecting the other. Persistent denigration, emotional pressure and demands for loyalty can leave a child feeling that loving one parent means betraying the other. No child should have to carry that burden.

The Children and Family Court Advisory and Support Service (Cafcass) deliberately uses the term “alienating behaviours”, recognising that these can damage children’s identity, self-worth and wider family relationships, and that manipulation or coercion may amount to emotional abuse. The Family Justice Council similarly distinguishes the unsupported syndrome from behaviour whose existence and consequences courts must determine as matters of fact.

For a child, being made to feel that loving one parent betrays the other is an intolerable burden. For the rejected parent, losing a relationship with a living child can bring devastating grief. These experiences deserve recognition alongside the suffering caused to both the child and rejected parent.

Children must be heard, domestic abuse taken seriously and allegations carefully examined. Rejecting an unsupported diagnosis should strengthen that scrutiny, without obscuring the reality of harmful parental manipulation.

Balanced reporting should acknowledge both the danger of unfounded allegations and the anguish caused by proven manipulation. These are not competing concerns. Both demand our attention if children and families are to be protected. Name and address supplied

Reading this article was painfully familiar. I lost custody of my daughters in 2013 after initially applying for shared, 50/50 care.

My experience was complicated by the fact that my barrister argued that it was my ex-husband who was alienating the children from me. My daughters, now adults, have since told me that their father and his family coached them on how to answer Children and Family Court Advisory and Support Service (Cafcass) questions and encouraged them to believe that I was mentally ill and did not want to care for them.

At the time, Fathers4Justice and fathers’ rights were receiving considerable media attention. The judge in my case was approaching retirement, and my barrister told me she believed his decision to award my ex-husband full custody was intended to make a wider statement. I cannot know whether she was right.

Central to the judgment was the claim that I was mentally unstable. After my ex-husband abruptly removed the children from school and obtained an ex parte order preventing me from seeing them, I was distraught and called the Samaritans. My ex subsequently obtained my phone records and used that call as evidence. The judge treated calling the Samaritans as evidence that I might be suicidal and therefore unsafe to care for my children.

At my barrister’s suggestion, I obtained an independent psychiatric/psychological assessment. It found no reason why I could not care for my daughters. As I remember it, that report was simply ignored.

So I struggle with the suggestion that parental alienation is not “real”. The label may be problematic, but parents can manipulate and coach children against another parent. My daughters have since confirmed to me that this happened to them. Name and address supplied

Your report on Sarah’s case raises concerns about reliance on flawed psychological assessment. My experience in Zurich highlights the consequences of failing to obtain any such assessment.

I am a father living in England, whose son lives with his mother in Switzerland. Despite joint legal custody, court orders providing for contact and repeated enforcement proceedings, I have not seen him since July 2023.

Zurich court decisions recognised his mother’s interference with contact. Two sets of social workers, involved at different times, recommended psychological assessments of the parents to assess parenting capacity. Yet the authorities never acted on those recommendations. Without those assessments, my son has remained with the parent whose behaviour I regard as emotionally manipulative, while his relationship with me has been allowed to disappear.

Reliable psychological assessment can help authorities understand family relationships; its absence can leave damaging behaviour unexamined. The answer to poor expert evidence should be rigorous assessment where warranted, alongside careful examination of the facts.

A child’s expressed wishes matter, but so does understanding how they developed. Refusal of contact may reflect harmful experiences, pressure, divided loyalties or several factors together.

We should therefore resist drawing general conclusions from individual cases. Misusing allegations of alienation to dismiss genuine abuse is an injustice. Ignoring deliberate obstruction and denigration can also deprive a child of a loving parent. Rejecting a disputed diagnostic label does not establish that the underlying behaviours never occur.

Neither mothers nor fathers have a monopoly on suffering or causing harm. My case cannot establish what happened in Sarah’s family, any more than hers settles mine. Both call for competent investigation, timely intervention and scrutiny of outcomes. Years lost to a parent and child cannot be restored by a later acknowledgment that the system failed them. Name and address supplied

UK politics live – latest updates

Alex Norris has been unable to say how many prisoners freed early from jail this week have been tagged, despite previous reassurances from the justice department.

In an interview on Sunday, the justice secretary said it was “too soon” to say how many of the roughly 700 male prisoners let out on Thursday had been fitted with monitoring devices.

The government has introduced a “presumption of electronic tagging” for offenders released early from prisons in England and Wales to help manage severe overcrowding.

The first wave of releases began on Thursday, with nearly 5,000 prisoners due to be freed in stages over the next year as the Sentencing Act 2026 comes into force.

Asked how many of those released so far had been tagged, Norris told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “I don’t have that figure today, it only happened on Thursday. You know, there can be a bit of a lag.

“We don’t have that number. But you know, we’re very candid about who’s leaving prison and when they do.”

Asked if he knew if released domestic abusers have been tagged or not, he said: “It would be too soon to know that, as it was only on Thursday. We’ve been talking to every victim to offer them the chance to say what controls they’d like to see over that individual.

“I’m well aware of the past in tagging. Over the last year, performance has increased significantly.”

Several prisoners released last week told the Guardian that they had not been tagged.

Michael Bogle, a former bus driver who left HMP Wandsworth on Thursday having served 78 days in prison after breaching a 32-week suspended sentence for shoplifting, said he had no idea when he was going to be tagged. “I have an appointment with probation officers on Thursday, but as far I know it could take months before I actually get given a tag,” he said.

Bogle, who is taking anti-psychotic drugs and has more than 100 convictions including for common assault and drug possession, was told in prison that he would be housed in a bail hostel and had been promised a place in south-east London. However, he said he had instead been housed in a bed and breakfast facility in north-west London.

“I am running out of money, and if I have to shoplift a sandwich to stop being hungry, I will just have to do it,” he said. “I won’t have a choice. But I really do not want to go back to prison – it is a pigeon-infested, rat-infested place and people are dying in the conditions there.”

Prisoners thanked the prime minister as they celebrated walking free from jail on Thursday. One told the press as he left HMP Durham: “Justice system, what justice system? Thank you, Andy Burnham.”

A prisoner released from HMP Cardiff after being jailed for burglary said he would “probably be back in the next month or two”.

Ministers intervened to exclude rapists and the most serious child sexual offenders from early release, after criticism of the policy over the summer.

The rules will also not apply to those guilty of manslaughter, such as the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019.

Almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders’ movements are not fitted on time, with significant delays putting victims in England and Wales at risk, a report found last month. HM Inspectorate of Probation said some criminals waited up to five months to be fitted with a tag, leading to repeated breaches of court and prison orders.

To compound Sarries’ pain, their England duo of Theo Dan and Elliot Daly departed prematurely in the second half while Alfie Barbeary lasted only 40 minutes. A nicely worked try scored by Charlie Bracken following a compelling surge from his brother Jack, did narrow the gap to 21-17 entering the closing stages but Sale, motivated and physical, had enough in reserve physically to silence a home crowd previously encouraged by last week’s win at Leicester.

Unfortunately Venter – or ‘Brendan Vintner’ as he has been dubbed – now goes by the less snappy title of ‘head of culture and technical director’ with corkscrews no longer required. Speaking to the written media, regardless, is not top of his priority list, with head coach Joe Shaw again wheeled out for post-match duties instead.

The ‘wine’ analogy arose from a pre-season theme about the importance of finding the right blend.

The Guardian view on trapped leaseholders: Labour must keep its promise to set them free

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 16:30:32 GMT

The government pledged to end an unfair system. Ministers must give homeowners power over costs, rather than another place to complain

“To the millions of leaseholders across the country, you have my word. The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,” Andy Burnham told the Labour party conference. Only a few hours earlier, his housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had announced that the government would legislate for a new independent regulator and launch a consultation to cap “rip off” administrative fees. While these are undoubtedly steps in the right direction, they are miles away from Labour’s manifesto promise to “finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end”.

In its modern form, leasehold in England and Wales turns homes into income streams for freeholders. It should be abolished. There are powerful vested interests – billionaires, aristocrats and big businesses – that would oppose this move. But the system of service charges is crippling the housing market because its exorbitant cost puts off prospective buyers. The average annual service charge for a flat in England and Wales is now £2,405, up 32.6% since 2020 and 55.6% over a decade. Owners of flats in high-rise blocks in London are paying service charges of more than £7,000 a year. Little wonder that first-time buyers are increasingly bypassing flats.

The current system sees homeowners enter into long-term leases in which they must pay sums annually to freeholders. These can rise quickly to very high levels. The government proposes a £250 annual cap on ground rents for existing residential leases and limits on fees for requests such as keeping a pet. Ministers are consulting over whether residents could pay less to buy out freeholds. But there is no sign of action on annual service charges for maintenance costs determined by distant firms. Last year, 37% of flats across England and Wales had a service charge that exceeded 1% of their value – making them hard to mortgage and sell. Surely homeowners should not have to buy their freedom at an outrageous price while being charged for years by a management system they cannot realistically change?

The issue of leasehold has become a campaign flashpoint in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Six out of seven homes sold in the constituency last year were sold as leasehold. The Green leader, Zack Polanski, who is standing to be the MP, has made the issue a concrete test of Labour’s credibility. The Greens have paired leasehold abolition with rent controls and affordable housing as part of their claim to end “rip-off Britain”, accusing Labour of favouring developers. Labour denies this, but ministers know that housing is a political powder keg that has already exploded in Berlin and across Spain.

It is remarkable that while legislation banning new leasehold properties is expected before the next election, it is unlikely to come into force until after it. Ministers are said to be afraid of being taken to court by freeholders. But government has already won against them in the courts when defending Michael Gove’s housing bill. The question for the government is whether the proposed reforms give the owners of the existing 5m leasehold homes a credible route out of their dependency – or just regulate their continued subservience. Ministers must show how a leaseholder trapped today will in the future take back control – by obtaining the right to manage property, being able to buy the freehold or converting to commonhold. If ministers offer just another complaints mechanism, they will have broken their promise to end an injustice.

The Guardian view on nurseries: some things are going right for under-fives

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 16:25:32 GMT

England’s strong results in an early learning study are a Sure Start legacy that ministers must build on

Recognition of the importance of babyhood and early childhood continues to grow. It is widely understood by many ordinary people, as well as experts, that what happens to us when we are very small, and our brains are at their most malleable, has lasting effects. As the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) put it in a study of early years education, “the first five years of a child’s life represent a window of opportunity, but also of vulnerability”.

New Labour’s grasp of this underpinned its pioneering Sure Start programme. Much of this was dismantled under the Tory-Liberal Democrat austerity programme. But despite that loss, England’s results in this year’s OECD Early Learning and Child Well‑being Study were strong. This study does not have the high profile of the programme for international student assessment (Pisa) comparing the academic performance of 15-year-olds. It is newer and relies on a far smaller sample size. But while its findings should not be treated as gospel, it is heartening that England’s five-year‑olds were found to be thriving. On a social-emotional development measure, they came out on top.

Concerns about school readiness, with a rising number of children in England arriving in reception classes without basic skills such as climbing stairs, must continue to be taken seriously. So must the attainment gap between economically disadvantaged children and those from wealthier backgrounds. The recent announcement by the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, that the Healthy Babies programme will be extended to more family hubs should be warmly welcomed as one means of tackling these problems.

But as well as addressing the inequalities that restrict children’s chances, ministers should focus on the early years sector’s strengths – which are a legacy of Sure Start and all the investment that went in. While less often discussed than the national curriculum, England’s early years framework is admired internationally.

Early years funding has expanded massively, with eligible working parents entitled to 30 hours’ childcare weekly for children from nine months until school age. The Tories now propose removing the £100,000 earnings ceiling: a £700m policy that rewards richer families. The model sees public money follows working parental demand rather than building universal provision. Families without working parents remain less well supported, while private providers gravitate towards wealthier areas, where extra hours and charges are more affordable.

The Competition and Markets Authority found that private providers were making excess profits in the children’s social care market. A study into their role as childcare providers requested by the former education secretary Bridget Phillipson should establish whether something similar is going on in nurseries, and assist ministers in finding ways to target low-income areas. Alan Milburn’s review of young people and work is expected to highlight the role of early years in getting toddlers on track for school.

The OECD was right to acknowledge the vulnerability, as well as the potential, of the youngest children. The horrific abuse of toddlers by Vincent Chan at a nursery in London was a grim reminder of what can go wrong. Safeguarding must continue to be strengthened; the switch to more frequent inspections by Ofsted was a good move. But as well as facing up to failures, ministers should embrace past successes – and work out how they can be built on.

Russia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine.

Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Two people were injured in the strike, said Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.

The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine, as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined.

Kyiv has come under near-constant attack from Russia’s new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, as an intensifying strike campaign increasingly disrupts everyday life in the capital and threatens to leave the city without power this winter.

On his visit, Merz announced that Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production.

“This will quickly and tangibly strengthen Ukraine’s air defence,” he said. “And this strengthening is urgently needed.”

The German leader got a taste of the new reality of daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Air-raid sirens sounded repeatedly during his visit, including as Volodymyr Zelenskyy showed him the badly damaged National Academy of Sciences building, where a Russian drone strike killed two people last week.

The Ukrainian president told Merz that people in Kyiv were suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”.

“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” said Merz, adding as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”. “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.

Russia had already damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly struck its Southern Bridge. Although the crossings remain standing, repeated attacks and the threat of further strikes have prompted the city’s authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, causing temporary closures and large traffic jams.

If Moscow succeeds in seriously damaging Kyiv’s bridges, it could create a logistical nightmare for the city of 3 million people, whose crossings over the Dnipro were last destroyed on a large scale as Nazi German forces retreated in 1943. More than a third of residents live on the left bank while much of the city’s employment and infrastructure is concentrated on the right.

The attacks form part of a broader Russian campaign against civilian and industrial infrastructure inside Ukraine. In recent weeks, strikes have hit logistics hubs, railway lines, datacentres, medical storage facilities and steel plants, alongside a sustained assault on the country’s energy system that is expected to intensify over the winter.

“He [Putin] is counting on constant escalation. He wants this very much,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference alongside Merz. “This is an answer to everyone – to those who believe that all you have to do is simply ask Putin and he will end the war for real. It won’t happen, simply.”

Russia’s foreign ministry on Saturday warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against remaining in or travelling to Ukraine. “Responsibility for any possible adverse consequences lies entirely with those who choose to disregard this warning,” the ministry said.

A number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv.

“The EU delegation is staying,” the European Union ambassador, Katarína Mathernová, wrote on X on Sunday. “Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters.”

In Moscow, some pro-war commenters noted with glee that the Russian strikes had continued despite Merz’s arrival. “Russia used to pause strikes on Kyiv during visits by European politicians. Not any more,” wrote Sergei Markov, a prominent pro-war commentator.

The trip is Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been among Kyiv’s most outspoken supporters in Europe and a leading voice warning about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other nations.

Last month, Germany formally accused Moscow of being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport, a key logistics hub for western military aid to Ukraine. But Merz is also facing growing discontent at home over his support for Ukraine, as his approval ratings fall.

Germany’s far left and far right are sceptical of support for Ukraine and want Berlin to scale back aid. The pressure has intensified as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made big electoral gains.

Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, wrote in a social media post: “Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis.”
