Wakefield’s wondrous Super League fairytale a victory for loyalty and logic

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 15:51:55 GMT

Owner has put in £10m but seven victorious players at Old Trafford were in the Championship two years ago and stayed at Trinity

It may seem quite obvious to suggest there is plenty Super League can learn from its newest champions but as Wakefield Trinity’s dreams came true after beating Warrington 23-10 at Old Trafford on Saturday evening, it was easy to ponder just how transformational a moment this is for not only them, but so many others, too.

This fairytale has captured the national attention and punctured the mainstream unlike few other Super League stories in recent times. A second-tier club just two years ago, Wakefield are now champions of England and have a possible showdown with the NRL champions, Sydney Roosters, to contemplate early next year in the World Club Challenge.

A city which has languished in the rugby league pecking order for generations has now been awoken in vivid Technicolor, epitomised by the scenes in Wakefield on Sunday as tens of thousands of supporters lined the streets to welcome home their heroes. Trinity, champions of Super League: it is a statement that still defies belief.

But there are lessons in here for everyone. This is all happening at an intriguing time, with a Super League-NRL partnership set to be signed off in the coming weeks and potentially opening the door for more opportunity for growth for the English game, in a year when more than two million supporters attended matches for the first time.

Wakefield’s rise from cellar-dwelling afterthought to champions of Super League is inspirational to so many, but it is how they have done it which warrants further attention. Firstly, the loyalty they have shown to their players. The headlines have all been about owner Matt Ellis’s investment and how that has been the catalyst for this remarkable turnaround.

That, of course, is true. But the fact that seven of the 17 who lifted the trophy at Old Trafford were playing for Wakefield in the Championship two years ago is proof loyalty matters, and some can tell this story with first-hand experience.

Max Jowitt has spent his entire career with Wakefield, and remembers the days where Trinity were training at amateur-standard facilities, playing in a crumbling Belle Vue, pre-Ellis, and fighting for survival on an annual basis. He still recalls sitting on the pitch at Leigh in 2023 in front of a couple of hundred supporters when Wakefield were relegated.

On Sunday afternoon he was sitting down again: this time on an open-top bus that ran through the city centre with the Super League trophy for company. “I’ve seen it at its lowest low and now its highest high,” the full-back, who will end a career-long association with the club to join York in 2027, says.

“It’s an unbelievable story for the game. To be part of the worst time in Wakefield’s history being relegated and then the best, winning the title, within three years is beyond my wildest dreams. What a ride.” A fine lesson in loyalty paying off.

There is another lesson for clubs now chasing Wakefield too; sensible, logical recruitment. Trinity’s rise to the top has been underpinned by a “moneyball” strategy of plucking players from Australia’s lower grades and making them stars. The likes of Caleb Hamlin-Uele and Caius Faatili, now Wakefield legends, moved to England on a pittance: less than the average man on the street.

They just wanted an opportunity to shine, and Hamlin-Uele would have been in England’s World Cup squad on Monday had he not opted to correct a knee issue. While others have splurged big money on big names, Wakefield have been meticulous. “It’s unbelievable, I can’t put into words what a dream come true this is. I owe Wakefield everything,” Hamlin-Uele said.

Then, of course, there is Ellis. Ridiculed in 2023 when he said Wakefield would win a trophy within five years just as they were heading for the Championship and he had purchased a club on its knees on and off the pitch, his only inaccuracy was that it took just three, not five. This third and final lesson from this story is one which stretches beyond Wakefield Trinity, though.

Ellis estimates it has cost him £10m to make this dream, one he harboured since he stood on the Belle Vue terraces as a boy, come true. That includes renovating the stadium and putting together the squad that has just won the league title for the first time since 1968.

With NRL investment coming over the hill, you wonder if there are others considering purchasing Super League clubs who feel they could make a similar vision a reality. In comparison to the money spent in other sports, £10m is small change to reach the very pinnacle; Ellis and Wakefield have shown dreams can become a reality if you go about it the right way.

Wakefield Trinity made their supporters believe again for the first time in generations. If they can do it, why can’t everyone else?

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen won in Sepang but only after F1 suffered the embarrassment of a host of cars barely able to complete two ­formation laps in the wet as they were making their way to the grid.

“It was insane,” said the championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes. “At some point we were five-wide in the straight, because we couldn’t understand what was going on.”

Lewis Hamilton was one of the field who ground to a halt. “I had to stop on-track, stop the car, the engine, and restart it. I’ve never done that before,” he said, while Verstappen reiterated his previous criticism of the engine regulations. “What can you say? It’s not what you want for the sport. I hope there is a lesson learned,” he said.

The issue was caused by software designed to control the engine but which had been insufficiently tested in low-grip, wet conditions which led to what the sport’s governing body the FIA called “an unintended loss of power”.

The start had to be aborted and the field returned to the pit lane to have the software updated in a delay that lasted 53 minutes, leading to a ­chorus of disapproval from the drivers who were already dissatisfied with the current engine formula.

The defending world champion, Lando Norris, who finished ninth for McLaren and is one of many who have been critical of the engine regulations, described it as “just ­horrible” and noted once more that it demonstrated the sport had taken a wrong turn, adding: “We shouldn’t have any of that stuff, the electronic side.”

The formula, an almost 50-50 split between electronic and combustion power, will not be changed this ­season with a minor adjustment next year and more serious change in 2028, but the issue had once more raised the question of how the sport reached this point.

“[F1] needs to have a hard look at themselves and see how we ended up in this situation,” said Williams’ Carlos Sainz. “It is clear the regs are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the power units, for the manufacturers. It is too complicated. Again, my only question mark is who five years ago decided that this was the direction to go?”

Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 15:04:34 GMT

Reform UK leader was interviewed for half an hour last month over money from crypto billionaire

Nigel Farage has been interviewed by the standards commissioner for an investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

The Reform UK leader spent about half an hour being questioned over the money, the Sunday Times reported. Farage maintains the gift was for his personal security.

The interview conducted last month is a sign the process is nearing a conclusion, although Reform UK is not believed to have been informed that the report is finished.

An MP under investigation is usually notified before the conclusion of the process. If the commissioner finds that there has been a serious breach of the rules, the matter is passed to the standards committee of MPs and lay members, which can ask for further evidence.

The committee can recommend a sanction or override the report.

If it suggests more than a 10-day suspension from the Commons – and parliament agrees – the Reform UK leader could find himself facing a recall petition and second byelection in his Clacton constituency.

Farage has been under investigation over the gift since shortly after the Guardian revealed in May that Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024.

The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.

After a slide in the polls over the summer, Reform is about to embark on a major reorganisation at its headquarters to try to revive its fortunes.

Insiders said it would involve a big shake-up of staffing, in addition to the suspensions of James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, Farage’s close aide. The pair are facing an internal investigation into whether they encouraged illegal foreign donations during an undercover investigation by reporters from Verbatim.

The inquiry is being carried out by lawyers who are expected to reach their conclusions soon. The matter is also the subject of a police inquiry.

The party is working out how to spend £72m in donations from Harborne and another crypto billionaire, Ben Delo. The huge sums have prompted calls from political rivals for a donation cap.

A possible use of the money is the relaunch of a TV channel that produces Reform-related video coverage and a show fronted by Farage.

It is not clear whether the donations fall within the rules because the government is putting forward legislation to ban overseas donors from giving more than £100,000 in a calendar year – backdated to March this year.

Harborne joined the UK electoral register only this summer and Delo has been largely based in Hong Kong, although on the register for some years.

If the donations are ruled impermissible, Reform could have to hand them back, a prospect that is likely to lead to court action.

Thousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and Wales

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 15:00:31 GMT

Exclusive: Average of nearly five sexual crimes a day against under-13s were reported to police between 2021 and 2025

From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schools

Lawyers and campaigners have condemned the “horrifying” scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools after a Guardian investigation revealed thousands of sexual offences against under-13s, including multiple rapes, are reported to police every year.

Close to five sexual crimes against children aged 12 and younger were recorded on average by police every day in primary and secondary schools in England and Wales, according to Guardian analysis of police data for 2021-25.

The figures include reports of almost 2,000 rapes and attempted rapes, which is equivalent to an average of one allegation of rape at a school received by the police every single day. More than a third of the rape victims were children under 13.

The new data showed at least 8,500 sexual offences against under-13s were recorded by police as having occurred on school premises or nearby between 2021 and 2025 – equivalent to 4.7 offences reported each day.

While most of the police reports did not specify the age of the alleged perpetrator, they are likely to be fellow pupils, and in at least 1,890 of the offences reported as being committed against under-13s the offender was described as under 18.

Girls are more likely to be victims of sexual offences than boys, according to the analysis, which found that close to two-thirds of reported crimes affecting under-13s where the sex of the victim was documented had involved female victims.

Responding to the figures, the children’s commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, described peer-on-peer abuse in schools as “widespread, normalised and too often brushed under the carpet”.

“We have taken important steps in the last few years,” she said. “But as these figures show we have a long way to go. This is not simply a school or college issue, it is a societal one.”

The data, obtained via freedom of information requests, also includes reports of a further 6,140 crimes involving the possession, taking, making or distribution of indecent or prohibited images of children under 18.

This has become a significant problem in schools, particularly with the introduction of AI and deepfakes, but headteachers are hoping phone bans and social media restrictions will help to turn the tide.

Andrew Lord, a partner with Leigh Day solicitors who represents survivors of sexual abuse, said: “This new dataset evidences clearly the horrifying true scale of sexual abuse of children within schools.

“Those in authority can no longer claim that they were not aware of how prevalent an issue this is. Parents deserve to know that their children are safe while undertaking their education, and anything short of concrete action to tackle this problem is simply not good enough.”

The data also detailed reports of at least 2,300 sexual crimes against children aged 13 to 16 and a further 9,100 sexual crimes against those aged 13 or over recorded by police as having happened in or in the vicinity of schools between 2021 and 2025. Three-quarters of these involved a female victim.

The true figure is likely to be significantly higher, since the analysis is based on data provided by 33 police forces that replied to FoI requests, out of a total of 43 in England and Wales. There may also be variation in the ways forces collect data.

Janaya Walker, interim director of the End Violence Against Women (EVAW) campaign, said: “This data is shocking but sadly not surprising, and underlines the urgent need to protect children from sexual violence at school.

“We’ve long raised the alarm about this national crisis in schools. However, despite what should have been numerous watershed moments, young people continue to be harmed en masse.”

Excluding 2021, when schools were closed between January and March due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the rate of sexual offences increased by 4% outside London, with 26.6 offences per 100,000 children under 13 in 2022, rising to 27.6 in 2025.

A government spokesperson described the figures as appalling. “No child should be unsafe at school, and no child should have to carry this alone. That is why schools’ duty to respond to sexual violence and harassment is now statutory, and why staff are trained to spot concerns early and support victims.

“As part of our strategy to halve violence against women and girls, we have pledged to make sure all young people are taught about healthy relationships and consent from an early age – and we’ve forced tech companies to tackle harmful content and protect young people online through the Online Safety Act.”

Acting chief constable Becky Riggs, who leads on child protection and abuse investigation for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, said the number of sexual offences reported in school settings was “deeply concerning”, but might also reflect growing awareness and greater confidence among child victims to come forward and report what has happened to them.

“These findings underline the urgent need for a stronger focus on prevention through age-appropriate education, digital resilience, effective safeguarding measures and greater support for parents, schools and professionals to identify concerns early and intervene before harm occurs,” she said.

“Tackling child sexual abuse requires a whole-system response, with policing, education, social care, health services, technology companies and communities working together to prevent harm, protect children and hold offenders to account.”

Soma Sara is the chief executive and founder of the Everyone’s Invited campaign, which has played a key role in highlighting sexual violence in schools. She now runs education programmes for young people. “When we first launched [in 2020], people refused to even refer to rape culture,” she said.

“It is now accepted as an issue both in wider society and within our schools. But we cannot expect schools to tackle it alone, particularly when the online world is changing so rapidly.

“The proliferation of violent pornography and the increasing harms young people are exposed to online are creating challenges that are incredibly difficult for teachers to keep pace with.”

Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “The prevalence of these incidents is simply appalling and a source of great concern for everyone working in education.

“We hope measures being taken by the government to better protect children online will improve matters but ministers must be prepared to go further in regulating online platforms.”

Figures from some forces were taken from keyword searches of police summary notes, so may include cases that mentioned schools but happened outside school premises. Some other forces recorded schools as a location for crimes both on and nearby school premises.

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 15:00:30 GMT

From ‘Sharon London Sex’ to ‘Trashy Anne’, the names saved in our phones are tiny records of how relationships began. Why erase the evidence?

At first glance, it’s such a simple, reasonable ask. A Threads user went vaguely viral last week, with a post announcing: “In other news, my wife of 11 years is respectfully requesting that I take ‘(hinge)’ out of her contact name on my phone.” A lively discussion then followed, which included the pertinent note that Rob in the Channel 4 comedy Catastrophe “has the mother of his children in his phone as ‘Sharon London Sex’”. Somebody else reported a husband of more than a decade saved as “Feyonce”, but this makes perfect sense, because if you thought of a pun that good, of course you’d be reluctant to let it go.

Personally, I’ve never got over noticing – on their reality show rather than while lunching – that Kim Kardashian has her mother saved as Kris Jenner instead of, say, Mom. It felt like an extremely revealing detail from the queen of the genre.

The Threads debate raised an interesting question, though: should your contact list be amended and updated, or preserved as a historical artefact? Perhaps the poster is underestimating the warm glow to the heart and soul he subconsciously receives whenever his wife’s name pops up and he’s transported back to the beginning of their unlikely love story. Living app-ily ever after is rare, after all.

Other replies echoed the notion that contacts provoke memories. “I’m coming up on the 10th anniversary of ‘Trashy Anne’ … who I got to know volunteering as bin collectors at a local festival,” said one. Another confided: “My best friend and I met through a mutual friend almost 15 years ago. I’m still ‘Ayannah (Gabby’s friend)’.” The comfort we get from a reminder of these origin stories may be more important than it seems.

There are exceptions, though, particularly when you edit in haste. As this repenter-at-leisure explained: “When I was still dating my husband, I got mad and I changed his contact to ‘dumbass’. It was like that for about seven years, lol.”

It’s never been so easy to find answers. But sitting with uncertainty can ultimately bring wisdom

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 14:00:30 GMT

Even the greatest prophets had questions but they learned to wait to see the full picture

We live in an age that has become profoundly uncomfortable with not knowing.

A delayed email reply becomes a source of anxiety. A medical symptom is immediately searched online. We refresh news feeds, ask AI for instant explanations, and expect the answers to life’s biggest questions to arrive at the same speed as food deliveries.

Modernity has conditioned us to believe that uncertainty is a dilemma to be solved.

Perhaps that is why one of the Qur’an’s most remarkable stories, involving Prophet Moses and al-Khidr, feels so unexpectedly relevant today.

In the story, Prophet Moses embarks on a journey to learn from a mysterious servant of God known as al-Khidr, otherwise known as the “Green One” or “Green Man” . Before the journey even begins, al-Khidr warns him: “You will never be able to remain patient with me.” It is a curious statement. Moses is one of the greatest prophets, a man of extraordinary faith and wisdom. If anyone should possess patience, surely it is him.

But the lesson is not about Moses’s character. It is about the limits of human understanding. As they travel together, Moses witnesses some deeply troubling events. Among them, al-Khidr deliberately damages a boat belonging to poor fishers. He repairs a crumbling wall for a town whose people had refused them hospitality, without asking for any payment.

Each time, Moses objects. Each time, he judges what he sees according to justice, compassion and reason. Each time, he is gently reminded that he does not yet possess understanding of the whole story.

Only at the end of this story are the hidden reasons revealed. The damaged boat was saved from confiscation by a tyrannical king. The wall protected an inheritance belonging to orphaned children.

The story is not asking us to suspend thinking or rational inquiry. Rather, the narrative exposes something far more subtle: our tendency to mistake partial knowledge for complete understanding.

That tendency feels particularly familiar today.

Our lives are increasingly shaped by technologies that promise certainty. Artificial intelligence summarises complex subjects instantly. We have become accustomed to immediate explanations, immediate diagnoses and immediate conclusions.

The great paradox of our age is that although information has become ubiquitous, our tolerance for uncertainty has never been lower. We increasingly expect life itself to function like a search engine with immediate output in response to our input.

The Quranic story of Prophet Moses and al-Khidr gently suggests that reality does not work that way.

One of the most overlooked aspects of this story is that understanding arrives only after patience. The explanations are deliberately delayed. Had al-Khidr explained each event before it occurred, there would have been no lesson at all. The transformation lies precisely in learning to remain faithful before understanding appears.

This challenges one of modernity’s deepest assumptions, that peace comes from having all the answers.

The Islamic spiritual tradition proposes something different. Peace is not born from eliminating uncertainty but from learning how to inhabit it without despair.

This is not an invitation to passive resignation or to explain away suffering. What the story offers is humility about the limits of our own knowledge and perspective.

Most of us are living somewhere in the middle of our own stories. We judge our lives from chapter three without knowing chapter 20. We interpret delays as failures and endings as defeats. We rarely consider that we may simply lack the vantage point from which the full picture can be seen.

That is why the story continues to resonate across centuries. It reminds us that there is a profound difference between something that is meaningless and something whose meaning has not yet become apparent.

In a culture that rewards instant opinions and relentless certainty, perhaps one of the most radical spiritual practices is learning to say “I do not yet understand.”

Not because reason has failed. But because wisdom sometimes arrives more slowly than information.

And perhaps faith begins, not when every question has been answered, but when we discover the courage to keep walking before the explanation arrives.

Muhammad Abdulsater holds a PhD from the school of law and business at the University of Notre Dame Australia where he is a sessional academic. He is also a student of Islamic sciences at the E-Hawza international school of Islamic theology

Brazil goes to polls in decisive election for future of Latin America

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 13:52:33 GMT

Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro face off in battle between leftwing incumbent and far-right son of jailed ex-president

Brazilians are going to the polls in the first round of a highly polarised and high-stakes presidential election that could change not only the direction of Latin America’s largest country but that of the entire region.

The election on Sunday pits the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump and the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election attempt.

Brazil is one of the few Latin American countries that still has a leftwing government after a wave of rightwing and far-right electoral victories across the region and the US takeover of Venezuela after the capture of Nicolás Maduro.

The 80-year-old Lula has positioned himself as one of the last regional leaders still willing to say no to Trump, and has recently accused the US president of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.

Like his father, who was Brazil’s president during Trump’s first term, Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, frequently praises the US president and has pledged to join the US-led anti-drug-cartel coalition that has killed dozens of people in airstrikes and carried out military operations across the region.

Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable. In recent days, both have focused on persuading undecided voters in hopes of reaching 50% plus one vote; if neither does, there will be a runoff on 25 October.

Voting on Sunday morning in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, Lula said: “People will have to choose between strengthening democracy and barbarism.” The incumbent played down polls released on Saturday that showed the race was wide open – they suggested either candidate could finish ahead and force a runoff, or even win outright on Sunday. “The poll that matters will be carried out today,” he said.

Flávio Bolsonaro, who voted in Rio de Janeiro’s north zone, urged supporters of other rightwing candidates to switch to him in a “protest vote”. “Our internal polls show people who would have voted for other candidates, who are also against Lula, already voting for Flávio Bolsonaro … I hope it’s enough to give us victory in the first round,” he said.

Claudinei Ferreira Viana, 45, a workshop manager in Pinhais in Paraná state, is one of the senator’s supporters. “My first choice would be Jair Bolsonaro but, since he is under house arrest and there is no other rightwing candidate strong enough to take on the current president, I’m going with Flávio,” he said.

At the beginning of the year, polls suggested Bolsonaro voters would have preferred a ticket led by the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, or the former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro. But the former president chose his eldest son.

The campaign was also marked by a scandal in which the senator was caught on tape asking a banker accused of corruption for $26.8m (£20m) to fund a film about his father, as well as speculation that Bolsonaro might strip the country’s widely cherished patron saint of her status, but he has nevertheless remained highly competitive.

For many analysts, that reflects a combination of a straightforward transfer of his father’s voter base – Jair Bolsonaro lost to Lula by less than two percentage points in 2022 – and an anti-Lula vote, with the president still facing high rejection rates despite strong social and economic indicators.

The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, as well as a scandal involving supreme court justices, which, despite having no connection to Lula, is seen as fuelling an “anti-system” vote and by extension an anti-incumbent one.

Brazilians will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal congress members and 54 of the country’s 81 senators in Sunday’s vote.

AMC, 40, who asked to be identified only by her initials because she fears reprisals from the local conservative government where she works in the interior of Amazonas state, will vote for Lula on Sunday “because of the many programmes he created to support the most vulnerable groups”.

“Jair Bolsonaro weakened protections for Indigenous peoples, and everything Lula has done over the past four years to strengthen those protections and protect the Amazon would be seriously threatened if his son came to power,” she said.

Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for?

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 13:00:29 GMT

Their careers are peaking, they’re rich in money and time – and young people think they’re cool. But maybe it’s not as simple as that

‘Stop sleeping on gen X.” I heard this on TikTok recently. I misinterpreted it, with a guilty start, as: “Stop sleeping, gen X,” because I am 51 (peak X), so always tired; while not sleeping at the time, I may have been resting my eyes. In fact, Joel Marlinarson, a marketing guru, was suggesting my generation have become a powerful, if underrated, force online.

Aged between 46 and 61, gen Xers with proper jobs are peaking, career-wise (although it’s a different story for those out of work, as a report last month on the struggles of over-50s jobseekers made plain). We’re more likely to own homes than the following generations; we’re emerging from the trenches of childrearing and, the argument goes, ready to indulge in some me-time. “If gen X were a country, it would be the world’s second-largest consumer market,” the World Economic Forum reported last year, with gen X women in particular influencing 70% to 80% of all consumer spending.

That makes us great customers – witness the tidal wave of menopause-washed wellness guff (Which? reported last month that many pricey supplements were no better than a cheap multivitamin) and beauty brands for people suddenly horrified by their necks. But does it give us content-creating clout? We’re supposed to be (or at least meme lore presents us as) the forgotten generation, low-key, countercultural slackers on the sidelines in the grudge match between millennials and boomers; aspiration and self-promotion aren’t really part of our brand.

Sure, kids are scrambling for Oasis tickets and rediscovering zines; US Vogue called us “the cool ones” and the New York Times went further with “the greatest generation”. I get the argument that it’s our time to shine. But real gen Xers have a lot on their plate and it doesn’t necessarily lend itself to fun, aspirational content.

Being peak career means peak responsibility: our parents are faltering (I’m writing this as my mother-in-law is moving into sheltered accommodation) and our kids are facing awful geopolitical and economic prospects that undermine their mental health and chances of independence. We’re falling apart physically: for women, the sorting hat of perimenopause doles out a set of grim symptoms, while men are wondering what will fell them next – heart, stomach, back or knees? Who wants to hear about that? And who can be arsed to make perky TikToks?

I’ll tell you who: Kathryn Turner. I was introduced to Turner, M&S Food’s director of product development, by Marlinarson, for whom she is evidence that over-50s employees are “the next biggest influencers”. Turner, a cheery woman in smart trousers who exudes quiet competence, has worked for M&S since 1995. She launched her account in May, but her TikToks already garner up to 2m views and her nearly 250,000 fans are devoted: “Would follow that woman into war,” commented one. “Why did we give Andy Burnham the job over her,” asked another. “I love you Kathryn turner [sic],” wrote an account claiming to be the Heartstopper actor Joe Locke. I love her, too: Turner’s calm sunniness, as she talks viewers through innovations in the picky bits space, is a balm in a fractious world.

Turner isn’t Kate Moss, Miranda July or any of the other impossibly glamorous gen X figureheads – she seems like a normal, middle-aged woman who knows her stuff and does it well. I love that she’s popping up on TikTok and I get it – I’m projecting, but I bet Turner’s great in a crisis, her desk drawer and handbag well stocked with protein-rich treats, blister plasters and ibuprofen.

Maybe this is our online USP. Could watching grownups quietly bossing their busy, complex lives be the next ASMR? Because, mostly, gen X aren’t the “cool ones”: they’re the knackered ones, dealing with life, death, work and frozen shoulders. I don’t know any Mosses or Chloë Sevignys, but I know lots of Turners and I, too, would follow them into war, or at least get a dopamine hit from watching them be extremely competent in short-form videos. No one would want to watch me staring at a screen then breaking to fold some pants, obviously, but I’d love to see more of my capable peers ditch the self-deprecation (very gen X) and shine online.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 13:00:29 GMT

Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption

There’s a common fear among people who work in Silicon Valley: snag one of the fast-growing, high-paying jobs in artificial intelligence, or get trapped in the “permanent underclass”, a phrase describing the fate of those who won’t have upward mobility in the age of AI.

The phrase usually describes a future in which AI automates human jobs. But for women in tech, it’s starting to look like the present.

“A lot of people say: ‘Oh, AI is lowering barriers, it’s equalizing the playing field for women,’” said Urvashi Batra, co-founder and CEO of Prioriwise, an AI platform for IT service providers. “I actually think it’s the opposite.”

Batra said people take her less seriously as the founder of an AI company than her male co-founder. When pitching investors, she and her co-founder have learned that they are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching.

Women made up only about a quarter of new hires in AI roles in the last year, compared to 50% of new hires in non-AI roles, according to a recent report from LinkedIn. In executive roles, that number drops to just 13%. At the same time, LinkedIn’s research shows that women are more likely to work in roles with high exposure to AI disruption, like customer service, meaning they are also at higher risk for job loss due to AI.

AI jobs, whose postings have doubled since 2023, come with a salary premium, on average paying more than twice as much as roles that don’t involve working with AI, according to LinkedIn’s research. But women who do have jobs in AI are disproportionately concentrated in low-paying roles, like data annotators, said Sarah Steinberg, the head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn. Across all AI occupations, men have $45,000 higher median pay than women, partly due to the types of jobs they are likelier to have.

“AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying and most consequential jobs in the global economy,” said Steinberg. “Women are just strikingly underrepresented.”

The ongoing trend could produce the greatest gender pay gap in generations and leave women out of building a technology that shaped the economy, advocates for women in tech said.

“What we’re witnessing is a sort of backsliding,” said Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president of AnitaB. org, a non-profit devoted to advancing women in tech jobs.

Initiatives to promote women in the tech industry have been ongoing for years, with mixed results. Women now hold about one-third of tech jobs in the US. But research has found that women leave the tech industry at a much higher rate than their male counterparts, citing factors like non-inclusive cultures and barriers to advancement.

Women working in AI may face even greater challenges. “AI moves extremely fast, and the pressure to keep up is immense,” said Jayeeta Putatunda, an AI engineering lead at investment firm Turing. “I have seen throughout my career so many amazing women I know kind of fall through the cracks.”

Putatunda said it’s not uncommon to be the only female engineer on a team, and that when women are outnumbered, they have to speak up louder to make their ideas known. Mentorship in the AI field, especially by other women, can be hard to come by. And the breakneck pace of AI advancements means anyone working in the field should expect to put in long hours in order to keep up.

“If you have very ambitious career goals in this field, there will be seasons when you work beyond normal hours,” she said, noting that a culture of working 12-hour days to keep up was not uncommon. “I don’t think there is always a neat shortcut around that than to put in the hours.”

Those kinds of work expectations can make it impossible for everyone to stay in the field. “I went on maternity leave for four months, and by the time I came back, there were completely different frameworks and levels of models,” Putatunda said. Getting caught back up was overwhelming. She said it was only possible with the help of supportive co-workers and a husband who equitably split childcare.

“That is one way women get pushed out of AI,” she said. “They don’t lack the interest or ability to keep up. They may lack the infrastructure that makes keeping up possible.”

The AI industry is so new and fast-moving that it should in theory be more meritocratic. No one has a decade of experience working with a model developed one year ago, which should mean everyone has a level playing field. But instead the field has indexed more on personal networks and other loose signals, according to some women who work in AI.

“Companies are hiring at a breakneck speed, but they’re finding people through the same networks, the same referrals, the same filters that they’ve always used,” Wilkerson said. “Generally, that’s not given women the same sort of exposure they should have.”

When people have tried to address these tech industry problems in the past, the solutions have largely come down to giving women more mentorship and implementing diversity programs with goals around representation. But in recent years, companies have aggressively scaled back their diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, largely in response to a political climate that discourages them. That has left fewer companies with institutional programs to hire and promote women.

The political climate has made it more challenging to get AI companies to support initiatives focused on women, said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. Newhouse, a product marketer who has worked in technology companies for two decades, points to the Department of Justice targeting corporations with DEI programs, claiming the initiatives violate anti-discrimination laws. Companies like Accenture, Deloitte, IBM and PayPal have all agreed to pay multimillion-dollar settlements under this enforcement.

“It is getting harder to go into companies being called AI Powered Women,” Newhouse said. “And our advocates inside those companies are also struggling with having women-focused initiatives.”

Still, she said the risk that women are left behind in the AI workforce was something that kept her up at night. “We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” she said. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.”

I was disorganised and overwhelmed. Could a daily to-do list turn my life around?

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 13:00:28 GMT

Whenever I thought about getting a handle on life – decluttering, sorting my finances, improving my health and productivity – I felt defeated. So I tried this month-long experiment to feel more in control

Alvin and the Chipmunks was my wake-up call. A Blu-ray copy of the film had stared down from my bookshelf for years, accumulating dust, when one day a shard of sunlight landed on it, as if directed by a higher power. This prompted some uncomfortable questions. Had I watched it? No. Did I intend to? No. So why had I let it linger there untouched for such a long time? The answer is simple: I’m a disorganised mess.

Zooming out, things weren’t much better. I had a mountain of clothes that needed to be hung up or put away, cupboards stuffed with God knows what, plates and mugs that I had never used … The thought of sorting everything out was overwhelming.

My mind wandered to other areas of my life that could do with some scrubbing up: my finances, health and general productivity. There are 24 hours in a day but, more often than not, they flitter away and I’ve hardly achieved anything.

I am not the only person who struggles with the constant demands of modern life. Hence the boom in admin nights, where strangers gather in cafes and bars to blast through their backlog of unpaid bills, unanswered texts or unneeded subscriptions.

My first step, though, was to pick up a notepad and pen and do something I hadn’t done in a long time. I made a list, and immediately felt a little better about myself. As Vicky Reynal, a London-based psychotherapist, puts it: “We all have something in our minds about the kind of person we want to be, whether that’s ‘adulting’ while taking more responsibility, or looking after ourselves to the best of our ability, and sometimes a to-do list can help us move a step closer.” So began what I hoped would be a month-long journey of self-improvement.

“Sort out clothes.” This is the first item on my to-do list. And what a mammoth task I’ve set myself. My clothing rail has two dozen smart-looking white wooden hangers to give my setup a sleek, curated look. But this is undermined not only by the shabby old garments hanging off them, in a sight to make Miranda Priestly gag, but also by the heap of clothing that sits in a compartment above. The lower layers are neatly folded but the T-shirts, trousers and shorts near the top are scrunched and rolled up, slotted into random gaps to maintain the structural integrity of my fabric Jenga tower.

The first step is to dismantle this heap, which, I’m ashamed to say, is almost three feet high. “Oh, I was looking for that” and “I’d wondered where that was,” I mutter intermittently as I sort through it.

My word, there is a lot of hideous stuff. For years, I have bought clothes only if they are in the sale and, aside from a few gems, I’ve amassed a wardrobe full of one-hit misfires, worn once before being tossed on the pile or shoved on to a hanger. Among them is a multicoloured denim Tommy Hilfiger jacket that Andrew Lloyd Webber would probably consider a bit much even for his Joseph.

I am about halfway through, with two bin bags full of clothes for the charity shop, when I realise I have taken on too much for one day. This is where I learn my first lesson: break down each task. “A good to-do list is achievable, realistic and has concrete objectives,” says Reynal. “When you break down tasks into small steps, they become more manageable and less frightening.”

Starting my day with a to-do list is not only becoming part of my morning routine – it is helping me form one again. Instead of jumping straight into work emails, I put my phone and laptop aside and, notebook in hand, think: what do I need to do today? This is much easier without the constant barrage of notifications.

I squiggle down the basics: make coffee and eat breakfast. It may sound silly, but as I tick off every task, no matter how insignificant, it gives me a push to keep going. I then write up a list of my work tasks, including a few I would normally leave until they became urgent, and feel calmer for it. It is the most productive working day I’ve had in ages. I also jot down some other things I’d like to achieve today: spend an hour reading, go to the gym and buy some more bin bags for my clear-out.

I finish sorting out my clothes after work. A gym session follows and, just before going to sleep, I fit in an hour of reading. I tick this final item off my list and get another hit of dopamine.

Today is my first big test. I’m in Barcelona for a weekend trip, and surely a holiday is a time to unwind and leave the pressures of normal life behind? But I don’t want to fall back into bad habits, so I’m pressing ahead with my daily to-do list.

As I lie on my hotel bed, however, I realise filling it with tasks is a bit of a struggle. “Read for an hour” is the only substantial one. The rest are things my mum would tell me to do: put on sunscreen, eat dinner, get souvenirs.

I place the notebook in my backpack in case something else pops into my head, but I get carried away with having fun instead.

Before I know it, it’s 2am and I’m in a nightclub. Out of nowhere, a pang of guilt hits me. I haven’t opened my notebook for hours and most of my tasks remain undone. I consider whipping out my copy of The Grapes of Wrath to fit in the reading, but reconsider and press on with the night.

I’ve been ill ever since I made a noisy exit from the nightclub at 4am, and an angry local doused me with cold water. For the past two days, my notebook has been untouched. I know I have a valid excuse but I can’t help feeling bad. Reynal had warned me that to-do lists can be destructive, especially if they are too ambitious or you “beat yourself up over what you didn’t achieve that day”. Even so, I can’t help thinking of all the tasks mounting up.

I’m much better now, and excited about tackling my backlog, which includes finishing sorting out my home and getting on top of work emails. As an experiment, I’ve also ditched my notebook in favour of an app called Todoist.

In the morning, I log my tasks on my phone but notice that I am wandering towards other apps, my focus on the day at hand beginning to dwindle. Nevertheless, I crack on with tackling my bookshelf, which has more than 100 books plus 50 DVDs, video games and that damned Alvin and the Chipmunks Blu-ray. It’s the first thing tossed into a bin bag. Among the other tat I’ve accumulated are three copies of The Day of the Triffids, none of which I’ve read, stacks of magazines, some of which date back at least five years, and a few 1,000-page doorstoppers that I’m never going to read.

Some things are hard to let go of and I feel a conflict between the person I thought I might one day become (an incredibly well-read master of the zeitgeist), the reality (I crack the spines of about a dozen books a year) and who the lists are making me (ruthlessly organised and productivity-driven). I take a step back and return some of the more ambitious titles to my bookshelf. Although I want to be more productive, it’s not at the cost of believing that I’ll get around to War and Peace one day.

My digital to-do list isn’t really hitting. Starting my day off in the virtual realm allows my thoughts to sway and old impulses to take over: namely succumbing to notifications and doomscrolling. So I’ve reverted to my notepad, and oh, how I’ve missed it. The quaint squiggle of a pen focuses my thoughts once more. Reynal says it’s a matter of “personal preference … Some clients tell me of the satisfaction they feel from physically crossing something off a list. But these days apps can throw confetti at you and help you feel equally in touch with the emotional feeling that comes when you achieve something.”

I spend longer than usual collating my list and use today as a bit of a reset. To help me along, I invite some friends over for our very own admin night. According to one study with which Reynal was involved, attending one of these a month could save you £2,400 a year, especially if you use the time to focus on budgeting or find cheaper utility providers.

Two friends show up at about 6pm and we get ready to knuckle down. I even throw some picky bits in the air fryer and put on some ambient music. But I soon realise that my small studio flat isn’t really set up for this, as we all squeeze on to my sofa, computers on our laps.

I plan to get a handle on my finances: cancel subscriptions, study my outgoings and see how much I can save if I cut out all my frivolous spending. I make a good start, filling in a few columns of my spreadsheet but the close quarters setup soon becomes stifling. This, combined with the music, makes me feel as if I’m stuck in a cramped lift with no way out.

Things are firmly back on track. My notebook is getting well used and today is all about meal prep. Usually when I go shopping, I don’t have a list and grab whatever catches my eye. This results in some very haphazard meals that rarely hit the spot. No more, I say today, and go to the supermarket with a thought-out list accounting for protein, cost and taste. When I return home, I whip up an extra-meaty chilli, some spicy chicken noodles and, with my remaining mince, beef kofte and some bulgur.

Would I have done this without my to-do (and shopping) list? No. Balanced nutrition is one of the last things I usually think about while trying to keep up with everything.

Today doesn’t get off to a great start: I rush out of the door without jotting down my tasks. To be fair, I’m covering the Clacton byelection and expecting a hectic day once I arrive in Essex. So when I have a moment, I do something that might sound pointless: I write down the tasks I’ve already done today – pack bag, buy train ticket, email XYZ – to take stock of everything I’ve accomplished so far. Reynal says some of her clients do the same: “You’re trying to tap a little bit further into that feeling of achievement.”

The day drags on, and then the night. The result isn’t declared until about 5am. The lack of sleep must be making me hallucinate: an intergalactic bin came in second.

A lot of the big tasks on my list are getting crossed out. My flat is getting decluttered, I’ve zoomed through a big pile of non-urgent work emails, and my financial and physical health has improved. A few hard tasks remain, though Reynal says ticking off the easiest things can “spark a virtuous cycle. It gives you a sense of confidence that you can achieve something.”

But she advises against leaving the toughest stuff until the end, “when you’re depleted and your energy is at its lowest”. Her warning is ringing in my ears as I tackle two big cupboards I haven’t dug through properly in years. Aside from a few surprise items, including a pink minifridge, the expectation turns out to be worse than the reality. The bulk of the rubbish is empty appliance boxes. I speed through the clear-out, and proudly tick off this once daunting task.

It’s the final day of my to-do list experiment. Has it changed my life? In some ways, yes. Not necessarily because of what I have thrown away, or replied to, or tidied up, but because of the sense of control it has given me. I had long assumed there was nothing I could do to battle my feeling of being overwhelmed. We are always accessible through our phones, subscriptions are king if you want to keep up with the cultural zeitgeist, and with contactless taps and takeaway apps the norm nowadays, it’s no wonder our finances and health can spin out of control.

“As life becomes more chaotic and complex, it becomes increasingly difficult to hold everything in our minds. Our mental load is growing and, with it, so is the stress of holding it all together,” says Reynal. “Any tools that can help us hold it all in place are helpful and to-do lists are one of those tools.”

Hear, hear. That gets a tick from me.

Oat of this world: cooks descend on Scotland for ultimate porridge making contest

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 13:00:28 GMT

Technical mishaps and plenty of whisky as competitors from as far afield as US and Australia vie for Golden Spurtle

There are many varieties of spurtle. The traditional Scottish cooking implement, designed for stirring porridge without forming lumps, comes in a range of sizes, can be formed from cherry wood, beech, or maple, and might be topped with a decorative finial or smoothed out at its end for a more modern finish. But on Saturday in Carrbridge, in the Scottish Highlands, only one spurtle mattered: the Golden Spurtle, awarded annually to the winner of the World Porridge Making championship, which have been hosted here since 1994.

The sun shone on the picturesque village as almost 40 competitors lined up in the village hall for six heats across the day. Tasked with producing a traditional porridge – made only from untreated oatmeal, water and salt – and a speciality dish where additional ingredients and flourishes were permitted, entrants had travelled from across Scotland and as far afield as Australia and the US for a shot at the Golden Spurtle.

As the first heat kicked off, technical difficulties beset some contestants when the provided induction hobs, new this year after a long tradition of gas, failed to heat. But the reigning champion, Norway’s Sven Seljom, was unaffected, serenely stirring Norwegian mutton into oats and filtered water he had brought with him especially for the competition. He had planned to bring Norwegian cheese, too, he said, but import rules meant he had to make do with something more local. A sizeable entourage watched on in traditional Scandinavian dress as he measured, stirred and tasted, boisterous chants of “SVEN, SVEN, SVEN” breaking out at each mention of his name.

The first of the day’s many whisky breaks came 10 minutes into proceedings at 10.40am, with shots of a lowland malt distributed throughout the exuberant crowd as competitors did well to retain their focus. The drams’ effects meant nobody seemed to mind too much when the crucial timer was accidentally reset just moments from the heat’s tense final countdown.

Any initial teething problems were quickly ironed out as the day settled into a well-oiled rhythm. In a separate “judging chamber”, a trio of judges from Scotland’s culinary scene blind-tasted each batch, assessing primarily for taste, texture and colour. Among the speciality porridges on offer throughout the day were a “Granola Espanola”, a porridge cannoli from the Australian national champion, Robert Reid, and a recipe featuring soft-boiled quail eggs.

“The first thing I did was burn my oats,” lamented Switzerland’s Jeremy McTeague after a heat that didn’t quite go to plan. But he remained upbeat: “It gave them a distinctive toastiness – maybe the judges will like it.”

Hundreds of spectators showed up for the day’s spectacle, from Carrbridge residents who turn out each year to support the community-powered event, to tourists such as Joe, 43, and Tina, 39, who were visiting from England and had overheard a conversation about the championship in a local pub the previous night.

“We looked it up and decided straight away we’d be here,” said Joe. “It’s Scotland, it’s porridge, someone said there would be whisky … it was a no-brainer.” The pair said they were making a beeline for the tasting room to sample the produce left over from judging.

The event proved so popular that the village hall had to operate a one-in, one-out policy. Those who couldn’t fit inside were decanted into a merch tent bursting with oats, spurtles and “always stir clockwise” tote bags, while local cafes and tourist centres screened a live stream of the competition. There was plenty of action to be found around the village, from competitors spotted calming their nerves with pints in the local hotel, to an American visitor who accidentally caused controversy by dressing as a box of Scott’s Porage Oats – rolled oats of the kind not allowed in competition, and a rival to the event’s sponsors, Hamlyns.

By the afternoon, the hall was full of cooking aromas and the crowd full of whisky and porridge as they took their seats once more to see who would walk away victorious. There was a minor upset when the reigning champion, Seljom, missed out on the final, but a surprise win for McTeague saw him through to the cook-off despite his earlier woes.

Once the top six had taken to the hob one last time, though, it was the Netherlands national champion, Gina Saarberg, who emerged victorious in the traditional competition, with the speciality prize going to Reid for his cannoli.

“I’m at a loss for words,” Saarberg said as she clutched her Golden Spurtle. “To be here was already such a win in the first place. This is a beautiful community, so of course I’m very happy I won, but it’s also just a pleasure to be here.”

The demands of Welsh devolution are simple: just give us what Scotland has

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 12:21:16 GMT

Andy Burnham is a Westminster leader whom Welsh nationalists could finally work with - but only if he stands up to the devo-sceptics in UK Labour

As I sat in the first Plaid Cymru conference since the party won the Welsh election and started leading the Welsh government, I heard things I had never heard before. I have been to a lot of Plaid conferences and not once have I heard people being really positive about a UK Labour leader. But there was no mistaking it: the Welsh nationalist party feels that Andy Burnham is a man it can work with.

When I interviewed Welsh first minister Rhun ap Iorwerth, he indicated he was hopeful – in a way he never was under Keir Starmer – that there was a prime minister who had a genuine desire to give Wales meaningful concessions when it comes to additional powers.

In his speech in Llandudno, the first minister said that the prime minister had “looked me in the eyes and promised he would not [bypass the Senedd]”. He said he had written to Burnham with a “formal ask” for “a new deal for Wales”.

There were five demands from the Welsh government to Westminster: powers over policing and justice, powers over rail infrastructure, control over the crown estate, “fiscal fairness” and control of welfare. Seems like a pretty long shopping list, right? Well, it can actually be summarised in just five words: “Give us what Scotland has.”

The Scots have control of the crown estate, a better funding settlement, with more money through the Barnett formula, heavy rail is devolved, and the Scottish government controls policing and justice, as well as having partial control of welfare spending.

When you look at it from that perspective, it’s not as if the Welsh government is asking for something unprecedented. The UK government only has to look north to see the precedent.

You don’t have to be a Welsh nationalist to think it’s unfair that Wales’s government is equipped with fewer tools than its Scottish counterparts to meaningfully tackle Wales’s challenges. Wales has less borrowing capacity than a local council and, as mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham had more power over policing in his area than the first minister of Wales does.

The stars are aligning for Wales to get more parity with Scotland. If Burnham follows his own devolution logic – that decisions should be taken closer to the people they impact –then how could he defend a region of England getting more autonomy than a nation?

Though figures within Plaid clearly believe that Burnham is genuinely open to giving Wales more powers, they have real concerns that the more devo-sceptic figures within both the UK Labour party and the civil service will hinder their attempts. These fears are not unfounded. A leaked memo from Starmer revealed that he warned his cabinet against being “overly deferential” to devolved governments. In December 2025, 11 Labour Senedd members wrote to the then PM accusing him of “rolling back” devolution.

This fear led to one of the better lines in ap Iorwerth’s speech, where he said that if Burnham fails to give Cymru concessions: “Wales will know again that our best interests will never be served by Westminster, and that it matters little whether who lives in No 10 Downing Street is an Evertonian or an Old Etonian.”

With all the talk of “the Burnham bounce”, one thing that I think is being missed in the wider media is the total collapse of Labour’s status in Wales. Before the Senedd election in May, Welsh Labour was the most successful democratic party in history, having been the largest party in Wales at every general and Senedd election since 1922.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

When Labour was struggling in England and Scotland against the Tories, led by both David Cameron and Boris Johnson, Welsh Labour was winning election after election. But now Labour’s dominance in Wales is over. In a 96-seat Welsh parliament, Labour now has just nine seats.

At Labour conference in Liverpool, speaking to people on both the Welsh and UK sides of the party, it was clear to me that they were facing very different trajectories. UK Labour members were full of hope, optimism and excitement for what is to come: the conference was like an engagement party, to celebrate a union with their new partner.

Meanwhile, Welsh Labour members had just broken up with their partner of 27 years and were totally cut up about the divorce. They were at the engagement party, trying to keep a stiff upper lip while nursing a can of strong lager and wondering how they were going to afford to furnish their new one-bed flat.

But this is a very bad time for Welsh Labour to have an identity crisis. All of the demands made by Plaid to Burnham are longstanding Welsh Labour policies. For so long, Welsh Labour and devolution were synonymous with each other, but now the mood music is very different. Welsh Labour’s new leader, Ken Skates, has actively criticised Plaid for pursuing the very policies Labour previously sought around more devolution.

There is a chance for the people of Wales to get more direct tools to improve their own prosperity, but to do so they need all their representatives to understand the value of devolution and be united in their fight for it, regardless of the party they represent.

Will Hayward is a Guardian columnist. He publishes a regular newsletter on Welsh politics

The perfect everyday coffee machine: De’Longhi Magnifica Start review

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 12:00:27 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

This automatic bean-to-cup machine will be ideal for many: a single button press serves up espresso, black coffee and cappuccinos – and it’s affordable, too

The best coffee machines for every home

You don’t need to spend big money to get a good coffee machine. Strictly speaking, you don’t need a coffee machine at all – a nice cafetière will do just fine. If you do crave a lower-effort solution that doesn’t cost a fortune, then a fully automatic bean-to-cup machine, such as the De’Longhi Magnifica Start ECAM220.60, is a good place to, um, start.

It makes espresso. It makes black coffee. It makes cappuccino. It produces hot water on demand. Fill the hopper with good coffee beans, top up the water and fill the little milk carafe (if you want milk, that is), and all you need to do is plonk a cup on the drip tray and prod the corresponding button. Whirr, hum, splutter. Your cup is now full of coffee. Nice coffee, too.

As with every coffee machine I test, I put the Magnifica Start ECAM220.60 through its paces in my home for several weeks. I used the full range of its drink settings and assessed how easy it was to set up, use and maintain.

I’ve tested more than 30 coffee machines for the Filter, so not only do I know a good cup of Joe when I taste one, but I also have a sense of where this machine sits in an overwhelmingly crowded market.

The Magnifica Start is one of De’Longhi’s most affordable fully automatic models. It’s simple to use, well designed and if you time it right you can sometimes find it on sale from about £300. At this price you can expect to forgo features such as touchscreens or LCD panels, but many people will find the Start’s fuss-free controls more user-friendly.

Before you rush out and buy one, be aware that – as with many of De’Longhi’s machines – the Magnifica Start comes in an array of models – four on the brand’s website, and a few retailer-specific options. Cheaper ones swap the milk carafe for a simple wand, which you can use to steam and froth milk manually. They share the same grinder, brew group and general design, though, so will make an equally pleasant espresso or longer black coffee. They’ll still make a decent milk-based coffee, but you’ll need to hone your barista skills to manually steam milk using the steam wand. If you develop a knack for it, this can help with the lack of adjustability you’ll find with fully automatic models, but there’s a learning curve. If you like the sound of manual milk steaming, look for a model with a lower number at the end of its part code, such as ECAM220.22. These are usually cheaper.

If you prefer your bean-to-cup machines to be fully automated – and I think most people do – then make sure you’re buying a Magnifica Start with a 6 in its part code, such as the ECAM220.60 I have here. This will create frothy coffees poured into a cup at the touch of a button.

Type: assisted espresso machine Dimensions: 24 x 44 x 35cm (WDH) Water tank: 1.8l removable Replaceable water filter: yes Accessories supplied: water hardness test strip, measuring scoop, milk carafe, descaler, water filter Time to heat up: 40 seconds Grinder included: yes, 13 settings Noise: grind 75dB, brew 55dB, steam 60dB Weight: 8.8kg Warranty: two years

Despite all the fancy – and pricier – coffee machines at my disposal, the Magnifica Start has kept its place in my kitchen over the past few months. That’s because it makes a decent coffee at the touch of a button, and it’s simple to use. All the buttons are easily accessible on the front panel, meaning choosing drinks and adjusting the strength of each is straightforward. The buttons are touch-sensitive rather than old-school clicky ones, but I had no trouble with accidental presses or prods not registering.

The drinks menu is small, but it’ll suffice for most people. You can choose between espresso, long black coffee, cappuccino or hot water. I found the default amounts on the small side – 45ml espresso, 150ml cappuccino and 200ml of black coffee. Thankfully, it’s easy to adjust each drink if you want a longer coffee. For cappuccino, you can adjust the volume of coffee and milk individually to get the strength and consistency you want – and that means you make it more of a flat white, or a latte, depending on what settings you choose. Just hold the corresponding drinks button for a few seconds, then tap it once you’re happy with the amounts of coffee or milk in your cup.

The Start’s milk carafe is smaller than on pricier models, but it clips on and off easily and opens the door to one-touch cappuccinos. It does a cracking job of producing a reasonably fine, creamy foam, too. It’s not as silky as the best bean-to-cup machines, but it’s not a million miles away.

There’s no ability to adjust the amount of froth, however: if you want hot, unfrothed milk, then you’ll need to either make it yourself in the microwave or on the hob, or upgrade to one of De’Longhi’s machines with more adjustability, such as the rather excellent Rivelia, which starts at £599.

Black coffee and tea drinkers can press the quick-release button on the carafe’s side, slot the water spout into place, and the little LED light under the hot water button illuminates. This allows you to top up a black coffee or turn an espresso into an americano. Or even just make a cup of tea if you don’t want to boil the kettle, although puritans should be warned that the water is hot, not boiling.

The rest of the design is similarly sensible. Lift off the plastic lid on top of the machine, and you can fill the bean hopper with up to 250g of coffee beans. A dial in the middle gives you 13 steps of grind adjustment, which is plenty enough to suit most coffee beans. In its centre, a flap hides the ground coffee chute – if you run out of beans or you want to switch to decaf, you can add a dose of preground coffee with the supplied plastic scoop.

The 1.8-litre water tank slots in on the right-hand side and is made from clear plastic so you can see how much is remaining. A water filter comes in the box, and this lasts for about two months under normal usage. Replacements cost about £15 at full price from De’Longhi, but if you shop around you can get the price down to about £7.

The drip tray has a decent capacity, so it doesn’t need emptying too often. Slide it out, and you’ll discover that it’s attached to the grounds bin, which is large enough to contain at least a few days of coffee grounds, depending on your dose settings and caffeine consumption. The various parts separate for easy cleaning – and are dishwasher safe aside from the grounds bin – but normally a quick rinse and wipe down to remove coffee and milk residue and clean coffee grounds out of the bin is all that’s required.

Once the water tank is out, you can quickly pull out the coffee infuser, also known as the brewing head, where the ground coffee sits during brewing. This is very welcome. These kinds of machines can get mucky inside, so being able to pull out the infuser and give it a thorough rinse is definitely a good thing.

One minor irk is that, at 75dB, the Start’s grinder is noisier than any coffee machine I’ve tested. That’s 12dB louder than the otherwise comparable Philips LatteGo 5500. This is mostly because the thin plastic lid doesn’t have a tight seal, so it doesn’t muffle the noise as much as other designs.

My main complaint, though, is that the milk carafe could – and should – be bigger. Its 220ml capacity is much smaller than on De’Longhi’s pricier models – such as the Rivelia, which is more than double the size. You’ll get a couple of small, default-sized cappuccinos out of it, but if you increase the preset volume of milk, you’ll need to refill the carafe after every drink.

Also, unlike De’Longhi’s pricier machines, there’s no dial to adjust the milk froth – you get a fixed amount, and that’s it. Yes, it produces a fine, creamy foam without too many big bubbles, but it’s a shame you can’t adjust it to your preference, especially if you’re a fan of a flat white, which tends to have less frothy milk than a cappuccino.

That said, my review model did occasionally produce barely frothed hot milk. It turned out, however, that this wasn’t a hidden setting. It was because I hadn’t cleaned one crucial part of the carafe. The button on the side of the carafe doesn’t just allow you to remove it from the machine, it also releases the light-coloured plastic connector for cleaning. Fail to rinse this regularly, and even small amounts of residue will block the air hole and prevent optimal frothing. Lesson learned.

Although not exclusive to the Magnifica Start ECAM220.60, a downside of any coffee machine with a removable milk carafe is that you need to be diligent when it comes to cleaning – forget, and the milk residue may mature overnight. Milk has a tendency to taint plastics when it goes off, so once it’s got into the rubber tubes and plastic parts, you’ll need to buy milk cleaning tablets to soak it off – or potentially replace them. Washing-up liquid does not suffice. My advice is to dismantle and clean it after every use, either by hand or in the dishwasher if you’re feeling lazy. And if there is milk left in it, then pop the carafe in the fridge overnight to prevent the milk from spoiling. Some users may find this fiddly – if you’re at risk of forgetting to clean the frother, you might want to consider a manual steam wand instead.

And if all this talk of spoiled milk hasn’t put you off your babyccino, then you’ll be disappointed to hear that there is no dedicated hot milk button with the Magnifica Start. To get the Start to froth milk without making a coffee, it’s necessary to use a trick: namely, to select the cappuccino option and set the strength setting to use ground coffee. Do this without adding any ground coffee to the chute, and the Start will froth hot milk into your cup. Once it detects that there’s no coffee, it abandons the brewing cycle. I’d prefer a button, but as workarounds go, it’s not hard.

The only other criticism is one I could level at most bean-to-cup machines that come through my door: the coffee preset – the long black – tends to taste bitter. This is because the machine uses the same dosage and grind size of coffee as it does for an espresso, but pulls more water through the grounds to brew a longer drink. This is drinkable at default settings, but noticeably more bitter than espresso. Adjust it to pour a longer coffee, however, and bitterness overwhelms.

This can be fixed. One option is to grind coarser, but then you’ll find that your espresso will become weak, watery and under-extracted. My advice with this – and most bean-to-cup machines – is to make an americano instead. Get the espresso tasting good by adjusting the grind size (normally a little finer than default) and reducing the volume slightly. Then simply top this up with hot water to make an americano. You can add milk if you like. Yes, it’s a bit more of a faff, but it tastes way better.

after newsletter promotion

You get a standard two-year warranty from De’Longhi, covering the usual faults, and the brand will attempt free repairs in that period. If not, you’ll get a replacement, which may be new or a refurbished model – at De’Longhi’s discretion.

Once you’re out of warranty, De’Longhi still offers servicing for a flat fee. With its £99 Essential Service, De’Longhi will pick up the machine from your home, identify any show-stopping or potential issues, descale the machine, change seals and advise of any repairs. If there are issues to be fixed, you can either upgrade to the £150 Comprehensive Service, or else pay that fee upfront if you’re specifically sending it to repair a problem. Bear in mind, though, that parts will cost extra – depending on the scope of the repairs required, it may cost significantly more.

An alternative is to use an independent coffee repair engineer. I spoke to our go-to coffee whisperer, Radu Bria, and his experience with these machines is that repairs are viable. Replacement parts can be sourced from approved parts resellers such as 4DeLonghi. If you’re a dab hand at fixing things yourself, you can always buy the replacement parts direct and give it a go, although bear in mind that you’re very likely to void your warranty in the process.

If you’re concerned that you should be spending more than this machine costs, then don’t be. When it comes to fully automatic machines, the differences in coffee quality between a really good £400 model and a £1,000 rival aren’t that pronounced. The upgrades are more drink choices, bigger milk carafes and more adjustability to suit a wider range of coffee beans.

So, if you’re looking for an affordable fully automatic bean-to-cup coffee machine, then the Magnifica Start lives up to its name. It’s simple to use, sensibly designed and makes good coffee with little faff. For everyday coffee drinkers, it’s a great buy.

Wondering what a more upmarket bean-to-cup machine can offer? There are several reasons to upgrade to De’Longhi’s Rivelia. The key one is better coffee; another is choice.

The Rivelia offers a wide menu of coffee drinks – 16 one-touch drinks for starters – and each recipe can be saved to one of the four user profiles, with adjustments for strength, drink size and temperature. The amount of milk foam is adjustable, too, and there are two interchangeable bean hoppers in the box, so you can swap to decaf or different beans without having to empty the hopper.

The Rivelia’s Bean Adapt technology is the standout feature, though. This helps you fine-tune the brewing process to eke out the most refined flavours from light, medium or dark roast coffee beans. The touchscreen runs you through the process, and after a few test shots, uses your feedback to change the brew settings and dial in the perfect grind size. It really works, too.

Sometimes, even an automatic bean-to-cup machine can be too much faff – and this is where a capsule machine may be a better choice. For instance, because De’Longhi manufactures a number of Nespresso machines under licence, the Nespresso Vertuo Lattissima upgrades one of the brand’s standard Vertuo machines with the same De’Longhi LatteCrema technology found on the Magnifica Start. The result? A relatively compact machine that brews pretty much everything from espresso to long black coffees through to cappuccinos and indulgently long, creamy latte macchiatos at the touch of a button.

The library of Vertuo capsules is vast, and all are tailored to a specific length of drink. These capsules can brew anything from 25ml to 80ml shots of espresso, through to 150ml to 355ml black coffees – or even a 535ml jug. Opt for a milk-based coffee, however, and the machine will automatically tailor the recipe to create the tastiest drink possible. All that’s left is for you to slot in a capsule, fill up the milk carafe, and find a suitably giant cup.

Espresso is the bedrock of great coffee. All the machines here will create a tasty shot, but none can compete with an attentively brewed cup from a manual espresso machine. This is where the Stilosa saunters in: if you’re willing to grind your own beans, steam every jug of milk by hand and perfect your own brews, this budget manual machine will leave its automatic brethren in the dust.

For good results, it’s essential to budget for a small set of scales and a grinder, but with about £300 in your pocket – or even a little less – you can put together a capable package. For instance, buy a Kingrinder K6 hand grinder, and you’ve got a pairing that, with a little elbow grease, can soon see you rivalling your local coffee shops. And if you prefer an electric grinder, something such as the Baratza Encore ESP is a great pick. The kicker? You can spend the money you’ve saved on great coffee beans and start practising.

Sasha Muller is a tech and consumer journalist, avid coffee drinker and craft beer enthusiast with more than two decades of experience in testing products and avoiding deadlines.
