Manhattan ‘mole’ mystery: rumors of lost gold spur clandestine excursions into New York sewers

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 12:00:26 GMT

A recent arrest suggests that underground invaders of city’s sewer system are lured by the promise of lost valuables

There’s been one thing in particular that has been intriguing New Yorkers this summer: the existence, and whereabouts, of so-called “mole people” – a mysterious group of individuals who spend at least some of their time wading about in the city’s sewers.

New Yorkers learned a bit more about the phenomenon this week, when two men were caught red – or perhaps another color – handed, after allegedly emerging from a tunnel in Manhattan. Their arrests have shed some light on a slew of instances where people have been witnessed lifting manhole covers and clambering underground.

Samuel Reveron and Kevin Rodriguez were apprehended in Queens after police tracked them down through video footage. The pair were allegedly spotted entering the sewers with four other people, who have yet to be identified.

Both were charged with criminal trespassing, but it is the reason the men gave for their adventure that has proved particularly fascinating.

“We go into the sewer and look for valuables that get stuck in the storm drains and sewers, gold, anything of value,” Reveron, 25, reportedly told police after his arrest.

The gang’s quest fits an apparently misguided pattern of people thinking New York’s sewers are paved with gold. Last year, three men were arrested after they were allegedly seen emerging from a sewer in Brooklyn, one of them telling police: “The reason we went down there is that people lose their gold down there. We got to get it and sell it to make money.”

Despite that vaulting ambition, there is little evidence that sewer foraging is a lucrative trade. Steve Duncan, a former urban explorer who has spent a lot of time in New York’s sewers and subway tunnels, told the New York Times that in more than 100 sewer trips, the most valuable thing he found was an expired credit card.

Still, the penchant for sewer exploration continues. In May this year there were three separate reported incidents of people climbing down into sewers, two of which were captured on video. In footage of the first incident, three people, wearing dungaree-style hip waders and carrying flashlights, walk into the middle of the road in Astoria, Queens. They haul a circular man cover aside, and descend into the darkness of the sewer.

“Three random guys walking around in a strange suit. Open the sewer, go in like the Ninja Turtles,” eyewitness Aki Jakupovic told NBC New York at the time.

Jakupovic isn’t the first to make the comparison to the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a fictional group of human-turtle hybrids who, across a comic book, cartoon TV show and feature film, are depicted as living in the sewers. Per canon, the turtles mutated into humanoids after being exposed to a toxic green goo. They are subsequently trained in martial arts by a large rat.

The turtles, who are brothers, fight crime, frequently crossing paths with a man called Shredder and his accomplices Bebop, who is a mutant warthog, and Rocksteady, who is a sort of rhino. They also encounter Krang, an alien blob-thing who lives in a robot.

While there appears to have been an increase in sewer incidents this year, this isn’t a new phenomenon. In 2015, a trainee at the New York department of environmental protection was arrested after being caught in the sewers, and last year three men were arrested after entering the sewer system in Brooklyn, allegedly in an attempt to find gold.

“God knows what they were looking for. I know for damn sure I wouldn’t be crawling through the sewers of New York, but these three were evidently looking for something,” the then New York police commissioner, Bill Bratton, told journalists at the time.

after newsletter promotion

Reveron and Rodriguez’s September sojourn might have been written off as a bit of a hoot, but police were seemingly extra interested because it coincided with world leaders gathering at the UN, some of them staying at swanky hotels close to where the two men went underground.

Brian Kennedy, an attorney for Reveron, dismissed those concerns when he spoke to NBC News.

“It seems like not much of a case,” Kennedy told NBC News. “I understand that it is strange that it’s alleged he went [into the sewer]. But there’s no connection to the UN or the appearance of Netanyahu or any other kind of nefarious scheme.”

It’s both strange and dangerous, Rob Wolejsza, a spokesperson for New York’s department of environmental protection, previously told the Guardian. Wolejsza said it was “both illegal and extremely dangerous” to go into the sewers, adding: “Sewers can contain numerous hazards, including noxious and potentially deadly gases, unstable surfaces, flooding risks and confined spaces. For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole or outfall.”

Whether people will listen remains to be seen. On the same day Reveron and Rodriguez were arrested, another three men were spotted climbing out of a sewer at 4.30am in Bensonhurst, south Brooklyn.

ABC7NY reported that police found a shovel in the sewer, but the men got away.

Can teaching schoolchildren about Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade remain optional?

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 11:00:27 GMT

Mounting evidence about how slavery shaped Britain shows that teaching about its history cannot be a matter of choice

I often think back to my years as a secondary school history teacher, and to what I was and wasn’t able to teach. History is a foundational subject in England, taught to children from the age of five to 14 to build critical thinking, weigh evidence and help pupils understand the world they’ve inherited.

The key stage 3 national curriculum, covering ages 11 to 14, states that pupils should understand how “Britain has influenced and been influenced by the wider world”, including a historically grounded understanding of empire.

That standard was on my mind as I trawled through the recently published Register of British Slave Traders, read the names commemorated in the Great Hall atBarts hospital, and followed our series Enslaving Nation as it traced connections to enslavement across the church, the monarchy and the banking system.

Soon after, the Former British Colonies Enslavement Registers made the records of 4 million enslaved people across 20 former colonies searchable to the public for the first time, a searing record of how enslavement irreversibly altered lives across the former empire.

Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of Africans and much of its imperial history sits as non-statutory content in the current national curriculum, included to preserve choice. But the evidence keeps mounting that enslavement was so embedded in British society that choice is the wrong framework. In my experience, non-statutory becomes optional within a term, and optional is quickly recoded as sacrifice-worthy. Teachers end up teaching the history they can defend, not the history that matters.

In November 2025, the government’s curriculum and assessment review was published. It recommended clarifying what counts as statutory and non-statutory, so teachers understand exactly how much optionality they’re working with, before a new national curriculum due next spring. The government’s response promises to “strengthen” the teaching of the country’s history, and to let teachers reflect Britain’s Black history within it.

Take, for example, Elizabeth I’s resistance to the Spanish Armada in 1588, a mainstay of English history. Two decades earlier, the same monarch had funded John Hawkins’s voyages along the west African coast, among the earliest English expeditions into the slave trade. Teach the armada without Hawkins and you keep the crown’s ambition, but you lose where a bulk of its money came from.

A teacher trying to build a class of intellectually curious students who are keen to learn about enslavement and its legacies has to find the lesson time, build the resources, and defend every hour spent on it. The government’s own response concedes the pressure, citing curriculum overload as grounds to loosen what’s compulsory. The Holocaust remains the only topic children in England must study between the ages of 11 and 14. In Wales, by contrast, learning about Black, Asian and minority ethnic histories has been mandatory since the current curriculum was introduced in 2022.

Black History Month in some settings exists precisely because of this gap, an annual fix for a curriculum that doesn’t otherwise make room. The Black Curriculum, founded in 2019 to get British Black history taught year-round, provided a wake-up call regarding the knowledge gaps around the lives of Black people on these isles.

Those initiatives have not always been popular in political circles. In 2021, the then schools minister Nick Gibb defended the government’s decision not to make lessons on empire and the slavery compulsory, triggering criticism. The leader of the Conservative party, Kemi Badenoch, continues to say Britain ultimately led the fight to end the slave trade and that’s where the focus should be. A month, or a bolt-on curriculum, however well meant, risks treating this history as an addition to the national story rather than part of it. The fix for optionality can’t itself be optional.

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

The history survives in today’s context where an individual teacher is stubborn enough to protect it. I read scheme after scheme of work marking whole periods “optional” or “if time allows”. If you hail or have heritage from a Commonwealth country, you have probably encountered scholarship that adequately contextualises and foregrounds how imperial history is central to British history – that cannot be omitted. The Guyanese historian Walter Rodney argued that Europe didn’t simply fail to develop Africa, it drained it. Howard W French, the US journalist and author, argues that Africa and its people were central to the making of the modern world, not marginal to it. And in addition to these foundations, undeniable feats of research are adding intellectual weight to arguments around what should be covered.

None of it changes the basic fact: enslavement is a load-bearing wall in Britain’s story. Remove it and the country becomes unexplainable – the wealth of its ports, the reach of its empire, the shape of its economy. To make that history elective is to make the explanation itself optional.

No wonder critics would rather toast the abolitionists than audit the traders who came before them. I rarely got to choose. The curriculum did that for me.

A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 11:00:26 GMT

After Turkish police found drugs on board the Phoenician M, the ship’s chief mate, Ali Albokhari, was sentenced to 30 years in prison. His wife is still fighting to free him

In the early hours of 6 October 2023, Elena Albokhari was woken by a text message from her husband. Ali Albokhari, 42, a Finnish-Syrian with dark hair and cherubic features, was chief mate on a cargo ship named the Phoenician M and had been at sea since June. The 180-metre bulk carrier had docked at Ereğli in the Turkish Black Sea a few days earlier and Ali was due to return home to Helsinki soon, but instead of feeling excitement, Elena was growing increasingly worried about his welfare.

She’d had a similar feeling of unease a month earlier, when the ship had arrived at Barranquilla, Colombia. Ali had called in a panic to report that drugs had been found; Armada Nacional officers had marched onboard and uncovered holdalls stuffed with 137kg cocaine. Labels on the packages – the crest of Turkish football club Kayserispor – hinted at their destination: Turkey was the next port of call. “I never want to work as a seaman again,” Ali told Elena. “We are having big problems.”

For two days, the ship was held at the port. Elena, 39, a tour guide from Russia, was so anxious, she could barely sleep. Then she received a photo from Ali of the crew happily drinking beer in a restaurant – the drugs had been removed and, after a meeting with the harbourmaster, the ship cleared to depart. “So will you go on working as a seaman?” Elena asked. “Yeah,” Ali said. “Sometimes it happens … so it’s OK.”

Yet when the Phoenician M arrived at Ereğli on 2 October, loaded with coal, it was targeted by Turkish narcotics officers. The ship’s captain, Marko Bekavac, 63, a steely Croatian with three decades’ experience as a seafarer, had already informed the ship’s management company about the incident in Colombia, and when Turkish authorities boarded, he immediately declared that drugs had previously been found on the ship. Despite this, officers delivered a statement: should anything be found onboard, he would be accountable.

The 20 crew members, including citizens of Russia, Ukraine, Poland and the Philippines, were ordered to remain in the ship’s mess room as the police continued to investigate. Nothing was found in an initial search but days later, as the coal was unloaded, suspicious bags were reportedly found buried in the cargo hold. They were packed with more cocaine. The captain and other crew were escorted from the ship.

Ali, who was second in command, remained onboard as unloading continued. He had managed to keep hold of his phone and was sending Elena updates. These had done little to allay her fears. Now, in the middle of the night, a text message confirmed the worst: “They are going to arrest us.”

Unless we are related to a seafarer, or live near a major port, most of us don’t encounter the people who work in shipping. Yet without them our lives would grind to a halt. Oceanic trade routes are the thread that weaves the world together. Merchant shipping – often described as the “lifeblood of the global economy” – is responsible for the movement of 90% of trade; every year, 11bn tonnes of goods, from coffee to fuel to fashion, are transported by ship. The scale of the maritime infrastructure is staggering, but the 2.57 million seafarers who operate within it remain largely invisible, as do many of the challenges they face.

Elena never thought of Ali’s work as inherently risky, and the life of a merchant seaman can seem mundane. Cargo ships travel at around 15 knots (17mph). A boat like the Phoenician M can take more than two weeks to traverse the Atlantic. The routine involves inspections, maintenance checks, paperwork and long stretches at sea. But seafarers have become vulnerable to rapidly shifting conflicts – from the Russian invasion of Ukraine to the battle around the strait of Hormuz – as well as poor regulatory oversight, abandonment by shipowners and abuse by port authorities. Seafarers’ rights are frequently neglected and they are too easily scapegoated for events outside their control. When an incident occurs, it is often far easier for authorities to pursue crew members than the shipping companies that employ them, who have an incentive to let the blame fall on individuals, and the P&I (protection and indemnity) clubs that insure them are there to serve the company, not individual crew members. The very nature of the job means voyaging to far-flung destinations, so if things do go wrong, seafarers can be forced to navigate unfamiliar judicial systems, with discretionary legal support, and face long periods of detention in a foreign country. Data on the scale of the problem is limited, but one 2018 survey by Nautilus International, the maritime professionals’ union, found that 90% of seafarers feared criminalisation above anything else. A recent survey by InterManager, the ship management association, has compiled 118 known cases over the past three decades, with a peak of 23 cases in 2023. Senior officers are most at risk; in 63% of cases, the captain was imprisoned.

Cases of seafarer criminalisation range from fuel smuggling allegations to collisions, but of particular concern is the global drug trade. Much like any other commodity, the vast majority of cocaine is transported by sea. Ports in Colombia are key export hubs. Cargo ships are up to 400 metres long and usually have just a couple of dozen crew; it’s not hard to find a place to hide something on them. In 2019, Capt Andrzej Lasota, a Polish seafarer, spent two years in prison in Mexico after 240kg of cocaine – planted on the ship at Barranquilla – was uncovered during unloading at Altamira. He was charged with “negligence” for failing to be aware of the drugs buried under coal in the cargo hold.

The case was widely condemned, and resonates with that of the Phoenician M. Ali is now the only crew member who remains imprisoned, three years after his arrest. The International Maritime Organization has said the case “demonstrates how vulnerable seafarers are when they fall victim to organised international crime”. The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF), a union that represents seafarers, described it as a “gross abuse” of human rights.

As a seafarer’s wife, Elena was used to spending time apart from her husband. But now Ali – whom she would speak to by phone or message almost daily – was no longer contactable, she felt truly alone. When she called the German crewing agency, Team Ship, desperate for answers, it was still unaware of the incident. A number she had for the company responsible for the crew and the ship, Iskenderun Ship Management, a Turkish operator, went unanswered. She waited for a call from some sort of official body, explaining what was going on, but none came.

Elena frantically tried to make contact with anyone who might know what had happened. After she posted on online chat groups for seafarers, she was messaged by the wife of a crew member who had not been among those taken by the police. Only after calling him was she able to piece together what was happening. Ali, along with Bekavac and eight other crew members, had been arrested on suspicion of drug smuggling.

Another week or so passed. Elena had another call with the crewing agency, which said lawyers would be provided by Iskenderun at no cost. “Don’t worry, they are in the police station, they are being questioned, then they will be released,” Elena recalls an agent telling her. “You just need to wait.” So she waited. But instead, the men were detained and charged. During those first days, Elena says, the crew had no legal representation.

When shipping incidents occur, a lawyer is usually appointed by a local P&I club “correspondent”, an independent adviser who can act on behalf of the shipowner and the club. When a lawyer was appointed, the crew said they were encouraged to accept the charges and sign what they described as arrest warrants, written in Turkish. “So we did,” one told Human Rights at Sea International, an NGO. “We were detained.” UK P&I, the club that provided insurance for the Phoenician M, said all appointments in this case, “including legal representation and the P&I correspondent”, were made by the shipowner, not them. They added that while they were not bound to do so, they provided support for the crew’s “significant” defence costs.

Days turned to weeks, then months. The men were moved from a local detention centre to a maximum security prison. Ali was one of many now isolated from their families, terrified about what would happen next. “Every day I was crying inside of that cell,” one Filipino crew member told me, adding that for a long time he didn’t know why he was being held. As for Elena, six months passed before she was finally able to speak with her husband. He put on a brave face, telling her he was OK, but asked her to send money: “If nobody sends you money in prison, you can’t buy food, you can’t buy anything.” Elena sent money and clothes, and waited for the men to stand trial. Another six months passed.

Finally, on 16 September 2024, following a number of hearings at Karadeniz Ereğli high criminal court, a verdict was due. Elena was sure Ali would be released. While he sat in the courtroom, she spent the day at home, anxiously awaiting the outcome. Then she received a brief message from the Finnish embassy. “I’m so sorry ... ” it said. While the eight other crew members had been acquitted, Ali and Bekavac had been found guilty on the basis of “command responsibility” and sentenced to 30 years’ imprisonment. Elena was stunned. Eventually she replied, “What should I do now?”

Ali and Elena’s home is a one-bedroom flat in a modern housing estate not far from Helsinki’s airport. When I visit in September, Elena, true to her profession as a tour guide, has laid out a spread of local treats: pancakes, blueberry juice, grilled cheese with cloudberry jam. Ali’s suitcase, which she was able to retrieve after his sentence, is still slumped near the balcony door. She tries to remain optimistic for his return. Every week, she buys fresh flowers. On the wall above it she has pinned a banner: “Welcome Home”.

If the maritime industry is emblematic of the power of globalisation, Ali and Elena’s relationship is a story of what it means to live on its faultlines. Ali was born in Damascus, Syria. His mother raised him and his three siblings, together with his stepfather, who ran a shoe business. When Ali reached college age, his options for further education were limited – as were the countries he could travel to – so his family decided he should attend the maritime university in St Petersburg, Russia, which was the most affordable option. He graduated in 2011, just as Syria descended into civil war, meaning he could neither remain in Russia nor safely return home. He applied for asylum in Finland and was accepted, continuing his studies at the Novia University in Turku. In 2017, Ali was granted full citizenship.

Elena was born in Moscow. Her mother was a language teacher, her father an electrician. As she got older, she, too, was eager to build a life beyond her homeland and spent time as a student in Spain. She met Ali on a dating app in 2021. At the time, Elena, who had been working as a Spanish-language interpreter and tour guide in Russia, was hoping to continue her studies in Finland. If she managed to get accepted to a Finnish-language programme, the education would be free, and she was eager to practise with native speakers. When Ali struck up a conversation, she was intrigued by this Middle Eastern man who spoke her native Russian. He was at sea at the time, but they began speaking regularly over phone and video call. When Elena travelled to Finland to take her Finnish-language test, he met her at the airport. She passed her test and they married in January 2022. A month later, Russia invaded Ukraine.

They had all these plans, Elena says, but Ali struggled to find a job. For the past decade he had primarily worked on Russian ships; now Russia was at war and he struggled to find work with Finnish companies, which Elena believes was due to his Syrian heritage. Ali eventually secured a nine-month contract with a Russian shipping company, and Elena returned to Moscow to visit her mother. She was able to meet him briefly, when his ship stopped at Murmansk, but when Ali returned to Finland at the end of his contract, Elena became stranded in Russia for a further three months while she awaited the paperwork needed to leave. It was December 2022 when they finally reunited in Helsinki. For the first year of their marriage, they were like ships in the night.

It took months for Ali to secure his next contract: not just a job but a promotion, too. “I remember when he received the call,” Elena says. “He was so happy.” In May 2023 he was packing his bags, preparing to head to London to join the existing crew as they finished their rotation. The ship he was heading for was the Clipper Palma. In June, under the new management of Iskenderun, it was renamed: the Phoenician M.

Looking back, there were things about the job that seemed a bit off to Elena. Ali, who was appointed as the ship’s security officer, described the vessel as very old. He was also critical of the attitude of Iskenderun. When the crew made requests they would be unresponsive; some of these requests would prove critical to the case. When Bekavac noted Barranquilla was on the list of destinations, he requested additional security personnel, as well as cameras and locks for doors and hatches, due to the high risk of interference from drug cartels. Iskenderun did not respond. Elena says the lawyer appointed to Ali by Iskenderun visited him in prison rarely and did not seem to be prioritising his interests. “They were saying, ‘Don’t say a single word about the company … otherwise he will spend a long time there.’”

Since Ali was sentenced, Elena has been lobbying for his release while trying to keep her own life afloat. When he was arrested, she was still a relative newcomer to Finland, with no support network and no job, as she was still studying. Sanctions on Russia meant their credit cards did not work: “I was left without money, without help.” Elena was dismayed by the lack of support from the Finnish government. While its consular service has visited Ali in prison a number of times since late 2024, statements on the case have been scarce, and it is notably absent from Finnish media. One reason may be that Finland and Turkey have not had the easiest relations in recent years. Ankara put up resistance to Finland’s application to join Nato in 2022; since then it has made a growing number of extradition requests for political dissidents, which Finland has largely rejected.

For Elena, the apparent indifference to Ali’s plight has been underlined by Bekavac’s experience. The Croatian prime minister and foreign minister spoke out against the verdict, and his then wife, Katja, received support to arrange prison visits without delay. When Elena went to Ankara, she attended the Palace of Justice with her lawyer and without consular assistance. It took all day to navigate the bureaucracy of the building and, after submitting documents and photos, she had to wait a further two weeks before a prison visit was approved. Katja, Elena says, was able to meet the captain without a barrier between them, but when she finally made it through the prison gates, after the humiliation of a strip-­search, she had to speak with Ali through a glass pane. “Psychologically, it was very difficult,” she says.

after newsletter promotion

During that first meeting, Elena was shocked by how much he had changed. “I have never seen my husband sad,” she says. “He’s always laughing, singing, dancing, but this time I didn’t recognise him. He was very thin, depressed and with grey hair.” The hardest thing was to contain her emotions: “When I’m alone here I can cry, I can tell my friends everything is very bad … but I can’t say such things to him. I have to support him.” She told him they had a new lawyer. That his mother was well. That they would be waiting for him. That they’d fight for him. After 40 minutes, their time was up.

As Elena continued to battle for diplomatic support, travelling to Turkey to visit Ali every month, she became aware the Croatian authorities were working behind the scenes. In August 2025, Ali watched from his cell as Bekavac was collected from the prison by a Croatian diplomat and flown home. In Croatia, there has been speculation that his release was negotiated as part of a prisoner swap with Mustafa Yiğit Zeren, a Turkish billionaire and close friend of President Erdoğan who was wanted by the Russians over alleged embezzlement of €600m. When Elena heard the news she felt hopeful for Ali, but soon this turned to dismay. “I was absolutely sure that after that Finland would change their attitude … but nothing. Every time they say, ‘We don’t know what happened, we do not know why the captain was released.’” It was as if her husband did not exist.

When I spoke to Jussi Tanner, Finland’s director general for consular services, he told me he cannot comment on the details of the case but described it as “concerning and troubling”. Finland, he says, continues to engage with the Turkish authorities and, particularly since Bekavac’s release, has been seeking clarification regarding Ali’s prolonged detention. “Everything I know about the case seems to indicate that it makes no sense that he’s still in custody,” Tanner says.

Elena says she spends all her spare time investigating the case herself, poring over the details as she grows increasingly suspicious of the motivations of all the parties involved. She pulls out a black folder of documents relating to Ali’s employment records. She also shows me her diary, a white book with a gold heart on the cover filled with neat handwriting. Its pages are full of memories, but from October 2023 they are blank.

As the case of Phoenician M has lingered on, it has drawn attention to the protections afforded to seafarers and the need for these to be reaffirmed. There are numerous international agreements designed to protect their rights, such as the International Labour Organisation Guidelines on Fair Treatment of Seafarers and the Maritime Labour Convention – often described as the “seafarers’ bill of rights” – but in practice they are at the beck and call of whichever jurisdiction they happen to sail into. “It’s aspirational, but not very concrete,” is how James Turner KC, who specialises in shipping law, summarises it to me.

Maritime organisations have also expressed growing concern at the extent to which supply chains are being exploited by organised crime. In 2019, MSC, the world’s largest ocean carrier, came under intense scrutiny after 20 tonnes of cocaine with a value of $1bn was discovered by US authorities on the MSC Gayane at Philadelphia. Large cocaine shipments were also found on three other MSC ships that year. An investigation by Bloomberg alleged the company had been infiltrated by members of a Balkan cartel. Eight Gayane crew members pleaded guilty of involvement in the drug-smuggling operation.

Criminal actors clearly do exist in the industry, but innocent seafarers are also being caught in the net. Keith Svendsen, an executive at Danish group Maersk, told the Financial Times shipping companies were now dealing with “some of the most dangerous people in the world” and cited crew members coerced into helping smuggling gangs. Fabrizio Barcellona, a coordinator at the ITF, says the issue is not with countries taking a strong stance against drug trafficking, but that seafarers are being scapegoated. “It’s not good enough just to put them in jail without clear evidence,” he says.

Over the past decade, Turkey has become a significant hub for the importation of cocaine to Europe, and there is growing pressure to address the issue. Erdoğan’s government has been accused of allowing organised crime to proliferate, and high-ranking political figures have been accused of involvement in drug trafficking. Imdat Öner, a former Turkish diplomat turned public policy analyst, told me that instead of effectively pursuing organised crime networks, the authorities are focusing on low-volume trafficking of the sort found on the Phoenician M. “It allows the government, the police, to save face internationally,” he says.

David Hammond, a former military seafarer, qualified barrister and founder of Human Rights at Sea International, has published a review of Ali’s case which calls it a “grave miscarriage of justice” and questions the prosecution’s integrity and motivations. Court papers state that the investigation was triggered by intelligence from Kayseri province police narcotics department, and the conviction based on evidence gathered following the seizure. But according to Hammond, Turkish police failed to request documentation relating to the Colombian incident, key witnesses were not interviewed, and no forensic evidence linking crew members to the drugs was presented. It is unclear why, of 20 crew onboard, only 10 were arrested. The prosecution seems to have rested solely on the rank and responsibilities of the crew. The conviction, as Ali’s lawyer argued, “rests on speculation rather than proof”.

There appears to be some awareness of these weaknesses within the Turkish judiciary. In April 2025, the chief public prosecutor referred the case to the supreme court of appeal, which in March 2026 upheld Ali’s conviction by a 3-2 majority. However, the opinions of the two dissenting judges pointed to many of the issues raised by Ali’s defence. They agreed the investigation was incomplete, there was not proper communication with the Colombian authorities, and police did not pursue an investigation in regard to the source intelligence that led them to the drugs on the ship in the first place. In July, Ali and Bekavac (who remains convicted as far as Turkish law is concerned) had their sentences increased to 33 years, due to a failure to pay a £3,000 fine that was part of their original sentence.

Bekavac may now be at home with his family, but he remains incensed about the case and is outraged at the suggestion that he could have been involved in a drug-smuggling operation. He told me he was made aware of the destination list for the Phoenician M only three days before it arrived in Barranquilla and the responsibility for loading cargo fell on the stevedores working at the port. The cocaine reportedly found in Turkey was buried 5 metres deep within the coal, he adds, so could only have been concealed while the ship was being loaded in Barranquilla, not during the journey, as alleged by the prosecution. Bekavac, like the other crew, believed that, having been cleared by the Colombian harbourmaster, they would have no further issues.

The captain also told me he documented his email correspondence relating to the incident on a USB drive. This was confiscated by Turkish police and not presented as evidence in the case. When it was returned to him, the drive had been wiped (he was later able to recover the data). In an interview with Slobodna Dalmacija, a Croatian newspaper, Bekavac said the lawyer provided to him by the company told him not to mention the stamps on the packages or talk about the company.

As Hammond sees it, there is evidence that gestures to serious organised crime – as well as the possible knowledge of state authorities – yet Turkish police appear not to have pursued lines of inquiry that might shed light on this. The cargo’s recipient, for example, does not seem to have been scrutinised, nor were any representatives from Iskenderun called as witnesses. If the crew can be held liable due to “command responsibility”, then the shipping company should, at the very least, have to answer as to whether it did all it could to address the risk of drug trafficking on its vessel.

Hammond believes the case should be a wake-up call for everyone who has a moral duty to the welfare of seafarers – from P&I clubs to shipping companies to unions – and is appalled that a sector responsible for trillions of dollars of trade cannot guarantee the protection of its workers. Seafarers, he tells me, are simply treated as “disposable assets”.

Iskenderun did not respond to requests for comment. However, the company appears to now be operating as Phoenician Shipping & Crewing, which has the same office address and is listed as the owner of the Phoenician M. Emails to Phoenician Shipping bounced, and the telephone number dialled to Orontes Shipping, another Turkish company established in 2024, which also lists the ship in its fleet. Emails and calls to this company also went unanswered. The Turkish Ministry of Justice did not respond to requests for comment.

In January, Elena returned to Ankara to visit Ali. He always has presents for her, she says, holding up an intricately beaded cushion by way of illustration, but this time he told her there was a box waiting for her to take home. “The guards will give it to you,” he said. When she left, she collected it. Inside were two budgerigars. One boy, one girl. “A couple.”

Ali has always loved birds, Elena says. There were budgies and parrots in the prison, and Ali began breeding them. Dozens of his fellow prisoners have a bird now and Ali wanted her to have some, too. Transferring them to Finland was not straightforward, though compared with the other challenges in her life, it was, at least, achievable. Panjo and Lucy now live in a cage above the kitchen counter, chirping loudly. Elena opens the cage and they flutter around the room before landing happily on her outstretched finger. Along with the cat, Koko, they join the list of those waiting for Ali to return home.

Ali’s lawyer has petitioned the chief public prosecutor – who appears to believe there are questions over Ali’s conviction – to file an objection to the supreme court of appeal’s decision, which would prompt a further review of the case. While Elena awaited further news, she was distraught to receive a call from Ali telling her he was being moved to a unit for prisoners whose convictions are considered final. Then, in August, the prosecutor agreed to submit the objection to the court.

No date for a decision has been set, so again Elena waits. She says Ali is coming under intense pressure from the Turkish authorities to accept a transfer to Finland, but to do so could disrupt attempts to overturn his conviction – and risk him remaining in prison on his return. For now, both their lives remain suspended. Elena takes care of the cat and birds, and continues to make a living as a guide in Helsinki. She avoids talking too much about herself to holidaymakers. To do so would probably tarnish the theme of the tour: “The happiest country in the world.”

Trump wants control of South America. If Bolsonaro Jr wins in Brazil, that could become a reality

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 11:00:25 GMT

The US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddling

Donald Trump has enjoyed very few foreign policy victories since returning to power. From failed wars to failed peace processes, his second term in office has been marked by one costly blunder on the world stage after another. In Latin America, though, the US president has a different story to tell.

His administration’s national security strategy outlined how the US wanted to “restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere”. It was a brazen document, laying out how his government would interfere in the political life of countries it considered part of its sphere of influence, rewarding governments and movements that are “broadly aligned with our principles and strategy”.

To this end, Trump bailed out Argentina to the tune of $40bn and threatened to withdraw the funding if President Javier Milei’s party lost the midterm elections. In Colombia, he repeatedly bullied and threatened the leftwing president, Gustavo Petro, hitting him with personal sanctions and accusing him of being an “illegal drug leader”. And most dramatically, he invaded Venezuela and kidnapped its president. The day after Nicolás Maduro was brought to the US, the state department posted a picture of Trump above the slogan “This is OUR hemisphere”.

Over the past 18 months, seven rightwing or far-right candidates have won presidential elections across Latin America. In most of them, Trump openly backed the winning candidate. “We’re doing very well in South America,” Trump said last month. “Lots of people that I got elected.”

This weekend, he will be hoping to add the greatest prize of all: Brazil, South America’s biggest country and its largest economy. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, is neck and neck with the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. If he wins, Trump wins – and the hemisphere really will be his.

The White House has not simply been watching the election from afar. Since Trump returned to power in January 2025, administration officials and Maga-world allies have been doing what they can to damage Lula and boost the Bolsonaros. Initially, the aim of the support was to keep Jair Bolsonaro out of jail. Like Trump, he had not accepted defeat at the ballot box when he lost in the 2022 general election. Like Trump, his supporters stormed government buildings. But there were two crucial differences in Brazil – the seriousness of Bolsonaro’s attempt to hold on to power, and the determination of Brazilians that he should be held to account.

Investigators uncovered a sprawling conspiracy led by Bolsonaro and seven of his closest allies to keep him in power. It included an astonishing plot to kill Lula and his running mate, as well as a supreme court judge. A draft decree had been written that would overturn the result. The military would step in and ensure Bolosnaro returned to power. But the plot failed and Bolsonaro and allies, including his defence minister and the navy chief, were arrested and put on trial.

In response, Trump threatened in July 2025 to impose a 50% tariff on all imports from Brazil, arguing the case against Bolsonaro was a “witch hunt”. This blatant attempt at interfering in the judicial procedure of another country backfired. Lula made clear he wouldn’t bow to US pressure, the trial went ahead and Bolsonaro was found guilty and sentenced to 27 years in prison. Lula also received a bump in the polls after standing up to Trump.

In July, as the election campaign was kicking into gear, Trump tried his tariff trick again, imposing a new 25% rate on some Brazilian goods. The state department then tried to dispatch two officials to Brazil to investigate “electoral integrity” – Brazil denied them visas, accusing the officials of coming to “meddle in Brazil’s elections”.

In the final weeks of the campaign, Lula has leaned into those accusations. A recent advert accused Flávio Bolsonaro of being “Trump’s candidate” and said the US president wants “to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust”. What remains unclear is whether the White House’s strategy in Brazil is working. “Some in Brazil joke that Lula’s most effective surrogate is Trump,” Brian Winter, editor in chief of Americas Quarterly, told me.

Indeed, while Latin American countries have undoubtedly moved to the right in the past 18 months, US interference, despite Trump’s boasts, has arguably had little direct impact. In Peru and Chile, the Trump-aligned candidates were careful not to seek his endorsement for fear it would cause more trouble than it was worth. In Bolivia, the leftwing Mas government was responsible for its own downfall, winning just 3.16% in last year’s election after 20 years of increasingly chaotic rule.

The biggest reason countries have moved to the right has nothing to do with the US and everything to do with safety and security at home. Organised crime gangs, many of them linked to drug trafficking, are increasing in power. As Crisis Group put it in a report last year, while drug-related organised crime has been a problem across the continent for decades, “never has it spread so wide, and rarely has it penetrated so deeply into states and communities”. The failure of leftwing governments to deal with the problem has hurt them more than Trump’s attempts at interference.

If there is a foreign president whose policies are having an influence on Latin America, it’s El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. His authoritarian clampdown, which has involved arresting tens of thousands of people, mostly without legal process, has become a model for other rightwing leaders in countries beset by gang and drug cartel-related violence.

after newsletter promotion

Democracy has been eroded and human rights trampled upon, but Bukele claims that his strategy – best described as “security populism” – has turned one of the most violent countries in the world into one of the safest. Other rightwing populists have found success in vowing to emulate him.

In Brazil, Flávio Bolsonaro has made a crackdown on drug cartels and organised crime gangs the centrepiece of his campaign. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people,” he said at a recent campaign stop, vowing to chemically castrate rapists and reduce the age of criminal responsibility.

On this issue, Trump may have an influence. The US decision in May to designate two criminal organisations – the Red Command and First Capital Command (PCC) – as terrorist organisations has put Lula on the back foot. Bolsonaro has campaigned relentlessly on the issue, accusing Lula of weakness. Lula has talked about targeting the crime boss “who lives in a penthouse”, but has been more comfortable campaigning on improvements he wants to make in education and health. Bolsonaro Jr, should he win, will almost certainly sign Brazil up to Trump’s Shield of the Americas, a coalition of 18 rightwing Latin American and Caribbean heads of state that promises to use “lethal military force to destroy the sinister cartels and terrorist networks”.

Trump arguably paved the way for this new generation of Latin American political leader. His first victory in 2016 showed that posing as an outsider, using coarse language and embracing authoritarianism could be popular. Jair Bolsonaro was the first to emulate him, embracing the “Trump of the Tropics” tag. If Flávio Bolsonaro wins this month – either on Sunday or in the probable second round on 25 October – Trump’s ideology will dominate the continent.

It is likely to outlast the man himself. The rise of organised crime has spread fear across the continent and, at the moment, the security populists are the only ones who voters believe have the answer. As long as that remains, the right’s grip on Latin America will only get stronger, regardless of who is in the White House.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

‘The violence is off the scale’: staff and passengers at risk as assaults on trains in Great Britain soar to record high

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:00:25 GMT

Cases of abuse, spitting, head-butting and sexual harassment, have spiked as transport police numbers have dwindled

When a train was halted outside Exeter St Davids station on Monday, rail staff leapt to one conclusion: there had been a violent incident on board.

“Someone will have kicked off,” one staff member said. “It happens all the time. My boss got head-butted recently.”

On this occasion, they were wrong – but their assumption told a tale. Figures released late last month showed the number of reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways had risen by a fifth, to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year.

Staff in particular have felt increasingly under threat. While the total numbers reported by the Office of Rail and Road in 2025-26 covered threats, verbal abuse, and contact that might not have resulted in any injury, they included nearly 2,500 physical assaults on workers – an average of about seven every day.

Their unions said the numbers were horrendous, but unsurprising: the RMT and TSSA unions have campaigned for more staffed stations and policing, after the number of British Transport Police (BTP) officers fell by more than 10% between 2024 and 2026.

Many rail staff wear body cams to record and log incidents of violence. “I think it’s so sad that we have those,” said Dave*, a rail worker in south-west England. However, after 20 years in the job, he said: “The threats, the abuse, the violence we see is off the scale.”

Drink and drugs play a part, he added. “We’re also seeing a lot more people with mental health issues. If you’re out on the street you can steer clear, but if you’re on a train or a platform you can’t. Our workplaces are becoming more and more dangerous.”

Steve, a guard based in the north of England, was punched in the head by a passenger: “It was my last train of the night. I’ve had to look away to see the door controls and the next thing I know, I’m waking up on the platform.”

Every guard gets verbally abused on a daily basis, he said, with behaviour worsening since the pandemic: “Now it’s mostly bad days, and you’re searching for good days, where nothing’s said, or nothing happens. The amount of times we’re getting threatened now with physical attacks, even when you walk through the train and say, ‘Tickets, please.’”

Even those working on the infrastructure can be on the receiving end. One rail contractor, Liam, based in Somerset, said: “We’re there working on the tracks and we sometimes get sworn at and even spat at. It’s just a minority, but somehow they think we’re responsible for slow journey times, cancelled trains. We’re in bright orange so we’re easy targets.”

The railway is by no means unique: bus drivers have faced repeated abuse and threats, as the Unite union has highlighted. Transport for London staff working on roads are issued with “spit kits”, or forensic saliva collection tubes, so common is that form of assault.

Violence against women and girls is of particular concern; at the Labour conference this week, the minister for buses and local transport, Simon Lightwood, described it as a “national emergency”.

Speaking alongside him, the mayor for the north-east, Kim McGuinness, said that as well as measures such as more staffing, lighting and CCTV, a crucial point for women was “knowing that if you raise an alarm something is going to be done. It’s a choice to use public transport or not … if you’re accepting 50% of the population don’t feel safe, that’s not good.”

The rail industry and police say some of the sharp rise in recorded assaults on passengers – up 36% last year – is due to greater reporting, including using discreet text messaging to the BTP.

But while many more incidents are now reported, plenty are not.

Emily, 24, was travelling home on a late-night train between Glasgow and Edinburgh last year when a stranger made a beeline for her. “He immediately tried to start a conversation and wouldn’t give up even when I showed no interest. He was asking what I’d been up to, whether I had a boyfriend, complimenting my outfit, and then it escalated really quickly.”

The man began rubbing Emily’s upper thigh and asking her intrusive questions about her sex life. “I froze and didn’t know what to do. I looked around but everyone else was oblivious. I tried to move but I was on the inside seat and he just grabbed my leg harder and leaned in towards me,” she said.

She managed to manoeuvre out of the seat and away from the man, who “shouted aggressively and called [her] a bitch”. Other passengers looked round but did not intervene. She moved to another carriage and arrived home shaken but decided not to report the incident.

“I wanted to just move on,” Emily said. “But I never used to think twice about getting on a train by myself at night and now I’m much more nervous.”

after newsletter promotion

Edward, a trans man, was travelling home to Staffordshire with his partner, a trans woman, after a weekend in Wales. On a packed train from Aberystwyth, a man began loudly making homophobic comments and became confrontational.

“Normally in that situation I just walk on, but I physically couldn’t, we were so crammed,” Edward said. He finally yelled back, repeating: “You’re shouting homophobic abuse in front of your children.”

A railway worker eventually intervened and told the assailant and his family to move to another carriage. Edward chose not to report the incident to police, dissatisfied with the response to previous incidents. He now tries to avoid public transport: “I felt tearful, angry and scared afterwards.”

A fraction of passenger reports end up with arrest or prosecution. Last year, Sam was travelling north from London on a train packed with football supporters. As she tried to reach her reserved seat, a drunken man confronted her and pushed her backward.

She instinctively pushed him back. “Then I thought, what have you done?” she said. Other men began throwing beer cans while one held her by her rucksack. “I was being pushed and shoved … they were throwing punches as well.”

Amid the assault, one man deliberately grabbed her breasts. “I realised: ‘Oh no, I’m trapped on here with them for the next two hours’,” she said. “There’s nowhere to go. There’s nowhere to get off.”

Two BTP officers on the train got through to take a statement from Sam. The investigation was later dropped after police were unable to identify her assailant.

The experience had a big impact, leaving her “not doing a lot of things I used to do. It’s put me off trains massively. I think if faced with a train like that, I would just not board it.”

The BTP assistant chief constable Ian Drummond-Smith said: “We will never tolerate violence or abuse directed at passengers or staff on the railway, and anyone committing these crimes can expect a robust response from us.”

He noted that when staff had body-worn recording, police brought offenders to justice in about 85% of incidents. “Anyone who witnesses violence or abuse on the railway should report it to us by texting 61016, or call 999 in an emergency,” he said.

The Department for Transport said the rise in assaults was “deeply concerning and unacceptable”. It has awarded a £63m increase in BTP funding by 2028-29, allowing more than 200 additional officers to be recruited, and investments in better CCTV and body-worn video. Dozens of new BTP officers will be specialised in tackling violence and intimidation against women and girls.

* Names have been changed

The headline of this article was amended on 4 October 2026 to correctly refer to Great Britain rather than the UK.

This is how we do it: ‘My mistress has complete control over me and makes me so happy’

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 10:00:25 GMT

LD is the submissive to Lady Alice’s dominatrix – and it has been a revelation for them both

How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously

double quotation markI have cerebral palsy and live with my parents. Lady Alice is a delicious secret

I met Lady Alice on X. We aren’t lovers or friends. She is my mistress and has complete control over me. I am hers to use however she pleases and she expects nothing less than absolute obedience. I don’t pay Lady Alice a fee, though I might pay for a service she needs such as a pedicure. These payments are “tributes”, tokens of respect and devotion.

I am 43 and use a wheelchair because I have cerebral palsy. I live with my elderly parents; they cut up my food and wash me. Lady Alice is a precious secret.

I never felt in control and hated my body. I had sexual impulses, but because I have ornamental hips that I can’t thrust and erectile dysfunction, I’m not equipped for sex in the conventional sense. I had a “friend with benefits” 20 years ago. We had two – admittedly fun – meetings that unfortunately lacked any real penetration.

‘It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect’: how John Cena conquered Hollywood – and why he refuses to abandon Vince McMahon

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 09:00:24 GMT

By embracing the role of amiable lunk, the wrestler turned actor has become an unlikely, and very modern, leading man. But does his relationship with the WWE, and its controversial former owner, risk tarnishing his brand?

I must admit, I was apprehensive about meeting John Cena. The WWE wrestler turned actor has built an enviable Hollywood career playing idiots – capable idiots with real heart, but dimwits nevertheless. Still, Cena is obviously nobody’s fool; fools don’t rise from humble beginnings to become their generation’s answer to Hulk Hogan or The Rock. Would the Cena who appears on my computer screen be the real one? Or something closer to the comic-book characters he embodies so well: guileless, silly and fond of a deliberate misunderstanding?

It is immediately clear that this is no manchild. Perfectly punctual, he greets me with a lavish formality befitting a man who made his film debut as the title character in The Marine. Within a minute he has volunteered, unprompted, that “a core value of mine is respect”. Cena, 49, is speaking to me on behalf of Matchbox: The Movie, a film extension of the Mattel toy car brand for Apple TV, and for 45 minutes he is generous, funny, complimentary and elusive without ever being evasive. It’s a genuinely radical thing for a man built like a chest freezer – having only recently retired from wrestling after 26 years – to be so relaxed about being ridiculous, and in an age of such joyless online strongmen as Trump, Musk and Andrew Tate, his buff charm is welcome.

John Cena is a company man. The word “loyalty” comes up often, and about everything from his friends back home to the wrestling to the US itself. Admirable, no doubt. But Cena’s loyalty has drawn him into some uncomfortable positions, and for 20 minutes our good-natured chat about reliability, discipline and what it means to owe everything to something bigger than yourself has set us on a collision course with one of the most disgraced figures in modern entertainment.

In January 2024, Vince McMahon, the all-powerful chairman and CEO of WWE, resigned from the organisation and its parent company TKO Group Holdings following a slew of sexual assault allegations and pending lawsuits that made his position in the company he’d spent his life building untenable. The final straw was a suit filed by a former WWE employee, Janel Grant, alleging that McMahon sexually assaulted her and pressed her into sexual acts during her time at the company, sent explicit images of her with other men without her consent, and passed her to others – in one instance, the filing says, to help secure a wrestler the company hoped to sign. McMahon denies all the allegations and in June, the litigation between him, the WWE and Grant was transferred voluntarily by all parties from the federal court into confidential private arbitration.

McMahon was a mentor to Cena, and as well as sponsoring his career, provided him a second family amid the travelling circus of 00s wrestling. “I have no guilt nor shame about my friendship and my relationship with Vince McMahon,” he says, swiftly followed by “you’re obviously going to put this in [your] article”. He’s right, of course. What is strange isn’t that he foresaw this line of questioning – it’s that Cena took such an unequivocal stance in the face of something so potentially damaging. He is audibly proud of the association, revelling in the idea that he’s abiding by his principles in the face of what he calls “the storm”. “It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect,” he says.

Cena was born in West Newbury, Massachusetts, in 1977, one of five boys in a household that watched every dollar. His grandma and grandpa lived in an adjoining house. “There was a lot of ‘How are we going to pay the bills, how are we going to keep the lights on?’” Cena says. He worshipped the movie action men of the era – Schwarzenegger, Stallone, Willis – but he also loved hip-hop, which in suburban Massachusetts made him a target for bullies. Bodybuilding was the answer, and it doubles as an origin story – the boy bullied for dressing like a white rapper, growing up to become an icon for the next generation of suburban youth.

Still, when I raise it, Cena is quick to correct the emphasis: the bullying wasn’t the point; his response to it was. “I didn’t treat hostility with hostility,” he says. “I got bullied for the way that I dressed, so I dressed more outlandish.” The muscle was a visible deterrent. “I’ll just project a physical sense of: Man, I don’t want to press my luck with that guy,” he says.

After college, he drove to California in 1999 with about $500 to follow Schwarzenegger’s playbook to bodybuilding glory. He worked on the shop floor at Gold’s Gym in Venice Beach for six dollars an hour, and for a stretch, slept in the back of his 1991 Lincoln. A wrestler who worked out at Gold’s steered him towards the industry and in 2000 he made his debut in WWF (now WWE) as The Prototype, a robotic character whose deliberate speech was a clear nod to his idol Arnie. He was paid $250 a week “which meant I spiralled into debt”. To Cena’s credit he understood that the short-term loss had the potential to lead to long-term gain. “I’ve been pretty astute at understanding when luck arrives,” he says.

What followed was a 24-year stint as a WWE superstar, a period Cena describes without irony as “service”. “You can’t fake that,” he says. “If you’re in the business of bullshit, somebody’s going to see through it.” He stumbled on a character that stuck: a jersey-wearing, battle-rapping white kid from Massachusetts, who literally went by the name John Cena. Despite some distrust from fans – over his general clean-living, wholesome persona – and fellow wrestlers who initially ostracised him for not engaging in the hard-boozing that was par for the course, the gimmick worked. In fact it was so successful that it led to the slightly odd ongoing situation where Cena doesn’t own his own name.

“John Cena is who I am as a human being,” he says, “and there is a company – WWE/TKO – that has invested hundreds of millions of dollars in the intellectual property of the character John Cena. And rightfully so; they have earned their share of ownership of that.” In Cena’s words he read and understood the agreement and he thought it was fair. However, the lingering sense that a career at the top of WWE requires a deal with the devil prevails (Dwayne Johnson only got his own moniker, “The Rock”, back in 2024, and now sits on the board of TKO). But Cena explicitly rejects the idea that he has had to make sacrifices along the way. “I prefer to use the word choice … When we say yes to something, we say no to everything else.” In effect, he gave up his name for the rare chance to live his dream.

And for more than a decade he did. Cena was beloved throughout the 2000s and early 2010s primarily as an avatar for a certain brand of flag-waving, white masculinity that was firmly in tune with the climate of post-9/11 America but is maybe less so now. Donald Trump was a recurring presence in WWE during this period, memorably shaving McMahon’s head after besting him at WrestleMania and even “buying” flagship brand Raw as part of the pair’s staged rivalry. The DNA of today’s toxic masculinity can be seen in the WWE’s Attitude era: Muslim performers were painted as would-be terrorists; female wrestlers, known as “divas”, were sexualised, fighting in “bra and panties” matches; and scandals around steroid abuse and traumatic head injuries were raised in lawsuits.

The miracle of Cena’s career is that the man who spent a decade as the straight-faced embodiment of American masculinity proved to be equally good at sending it up. After a handful of underwhelming action and sports film roles, he was cast against type by Judd Apatow for the 2015 romcom Trainwreck, playing a musclebound hunk whose attempts to be threatening just sound homoerotic. Then as the pumped-up Peacemaker, first in superhero movie The Suicide Squad (2021), then in the comedy spin-off series named after the character, Cena managed to strike a balance between serious man and silly goose that would be tricky without a healthy amount of self-awareness. This quality was on full display during Cena’s small but charming turn as a merman in Barbie, a commitment to the bit that was all the more admirable given his agents tried to talk him out of the role.

Matchbox, his latest film, is a vague attempt to recapture Barbie’s magic in the more contained format of a traditional action comedy. Cena admits feeling relieved when he read the script and found the cars to be “so far down the list of things they were doing with the IP”. He plays Sean, an undercover operative whose entire life is a performance. When I wonder aloud whether the part sits close to the bone, he eagerly connects the dots himself: “How does someone who thinks they’re always being watched act in a public place? That I got a little bit of familiarity with.”

Cena’s onscreen persona is an intriguing model of masculinity: the strongman remade as softie. What’s more, his wall-to-wall presence in the childhoods of millennial men makes him a far more credible advocate of positive manhood than a Joe Rogan or a Jordan Peterson. But he is reluctant to assume the mantle. “Rather than trying to take the reins of a movement or be the poster child for something, I’m just trying to be me,” he says, before offering his own diagnosis of why so many people are in the business of selling a personal vision of masculinity. “The appetite for a certain kind of manhood is just supply and demand,” he says. To the people clamouring for it, “my advice would be: go get it”.

after newsletter promotion

Perhaps Cena’s lack of desire to be cast in the role is emblematic of why it would suit him. The system, he says, “is real fragile … if I say I’m going to be the showcase of masculinity and the supply-and-demand chain pivots in five minutes, I’m shit out of luck.” He is keen to underscore how much he “loves the United States and admires its military force that makes the vow to, under the ultimate sacrifice, protect that piece of paper that says ‘We the People’. To me, that’s extremely heroic.”

Cena’s own heroism came into question in 2021 when, while promoting Fast & Furious 9, he referred to Taiwan as “a country”. The Chinese audience took offence, and he filmed a contrite apology in Mandarin, a language he had been learning for six years in an attempt to grow the WWE’s presence in China. In the US, the grovelling video read less as an apology than a capitulation to the weight of China’s economic might. The fan backlash was so intense that he told James Gunn he’d understand if he had to be fired from Peacemaker. He takes full responsibility for the episode. “Just because you know the language doesn’t mean you know the culture,” he says, admitting, “I got way too overconfident. I thought I was the smartest guy in the room.” Part of what frightened him was the very real possibility of “the termination of employment that I love”. The same reflex to remain loyal to the brand has carried him, without complaint, to numerous events in Saudi Arabia. “WWE offers a universal language of diplomacy,” he says. “So, to your question of: ‘Hey, the thing that you’re in is sometimes criticised for the moves that it makes as an entity – is that difficult?’ Of course it is, especially when you believe in the entity.”

For a man who prides himself on saying yes, it is revealing what he has time and time again said no to. Cena does not want children, and the reasoning is entirely in keeping with his sense of discipline: they’d simply require too much of him. From 2002 to 2015 he was home “about 15 days a year and even now it’s maybe 70”, he says. “If I said yes to children, I have to say no to everything else.” His engagement to fellow wrestler Nikki Bella – his co-star on the reality show Total Bellas – collapsed in 2018, in large part over whether to have them. Cena, who’d had a vasectomy, offered to reverse it, but the relationship ended shortly after.

“I really enjoy my life,” he says. Cena has granted more than 650 Make-a-Wish wishes, more than anyone alive. He sees his ability to do so much work for the organisation as inextricably linked to being child-free. “If I have a family of my own, I don’t have those 650 moments … I’m flying with just my partner on this one.” Cena married Shay Shariatzadeh, an Iranian Canadian tech product manager, in 2020, after meeting in Vancouver while he was shooting a film. They had only been together a year but he’s said he would have proposed after three months. “I have a loving connection that people don’t see,” he says. “I don’t need the world to totally know me as a person.”

He remains on the WWE’s books as a “brand ambassador”, a reflection of his gratitude to the company, but also an unresolved transition back into civilian life. Next up, he will star in One Attempt Remaining, a comedy from Kay Cannon (director of Blockers and the writer-producer behind the Pitch Perfect series). He plays one half of a divorced couple who is forced to team up with his ex in order to track down the lost password to a crypto account worth millions. Whereas Dwayne Johnson has become a brand bigger than his wrestling fame, you get the sense Cena will never fully escape his WWE persona, his screen performances a callback to the exaggerated version of himself he’s been playing since 2002.

Perhaps that’s what it is to be a company man: not an empty suit or a servile mouthpiece but a person so thoroughly committed to the brand it is simply who he is. Present, punctual, polite and perfunctory. The job is done and it’s back to the gym.

Matchbox: The Movie premieres on Apple TV on 9 October.

Own a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google down

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 09:00:23 GMT

A deep-seated duopoly allows the tech giants to exploit the public and developers. But the regulator has powers to stop this abuse – it should use them

Chi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee

Debates around big tech and digital regulation can sometimes feel distant from the everyday concerns of voters. But the power that a small number of global tech companies hold over our lives goes far beyond what most people realise.

As chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee, I have spent years raising concerns about this: from the data they harvest and the digital “twins” they build of us, to the algorithms that decide what our children see.

But there’s a much less visible example of this imbalance of power sitting in the pocket of almost every smartphone user in Britain: the app tax. Apple and Google control the two app stores through which almost every mobile app in this country reaches its customers, and that position lets them set terms for app developers that most businesses would never accept from a supplier. Sell a subscription, game or piece of software through either app store and both companies now charge a commission of up to 30% on purchases made inside apps, regardless of what the product is or what it costs to make. With no alternative platforms, developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.

Developers are also prevented from telling users that a cheaper option exists elsewhere, known as “steering”. That restriction is enforced by Apple and Google to protect their own profits. For small British developers who might struggle to absorb the cost, that could be the difference between hiring their next engineer or not, investing in a new product or shelving it, or growing their business here or uprooting and building overseas instead.

Consumers pay the price, too. Research commissioned by the Coalition for App Fairness, as reported in the Daily Mail, indicated that British consumers pay approximately £700m per year to Apple and Google, a full £232m more than the companies paid in UK corporation tax last year combined. This is equivalent to around £55 annually for a household with four smartphone users. It is a cost built into the price of the product, invisible on any receipt, that has far more to do with market control and bolstering profits than anything the companies actually did to earn it.

My last job before coming into parliament was with Ofcom, the regulator for communications markets. I was responsible for assessing the competitiveness of markets, because it is through competition that consumers get choice. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has found that Apple and Google’s mobile platforms hold an effective duopoly, with at least 90% of UK mobile devices running on their mobile platforms. App developers have no choice but to distribute their product through the Apple App Store or the Google Play Store. If a developer happened to dislike Apple’s terms and another app store existed, they would take their app, and their customers, elsewhere, and the price would fall. But there is no alternative app store on an iPhone, and no practical route for Android users outside Google Play either. Apple and Google set the rules unchallenged.

Parliament anticipated this problem when, in 2024, it passed the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCCA) with cross-party support, giving the CMA genuine powers to force dominant platforms to change their behaviour. But, so far, the CMA has resorted to weak, voluntary commitments from Apple and Google rather than requirements it is actually obliged to enforce.

Sign up to TechScape

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

Its consultation on “steering”, which would finally let developers point users to cheaper options elsewhere, has now closed and a decision is due soon. Many are rightly nervous that this could end up with another voluntary gesture, rather than a binding rule, deemed acceptable.

But this moment also represents an opportunity. It will be one of the first serious decisions this government makes on big tech, and will likely determine the direction it takes on this issue. The prime minister has been clear, both before and since entering Downing Street, that tech sovereignty means reducing our dependence on a handful of overseas platforms. I want to see that instinct applied to decisions such as this.

This is not about being anti-technology or anti-growth. It is about whether British consumers, British developers and British regulators are able to shape the terms on which technology operates in our own market and influences our society. I urge the CMA to use the powers we gave it, and I urge my colleagues in government to back it in doing so.

Chi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee
