Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian books

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 05:00:20 GMT

A Ukrainian publishing boom sparked by the 2022 invasion is now under threat from the force and frequency of Russian attacks

On a Saturday morning in August, Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, was at his headquarters in Kharkiv – the eastern Ukrainian city that, along with Kyiv, is the centre of the country’s publishing and printing industry. Built 15 years ago on the site of a former bread factory, the footprint of the premises is about 10,000 sq metres (107,640ft). Books were stacked 12 metres high on rank after rank of shelves.

Kruglov, along with five senior colleagues, were on the warehouse floor to discuss the approaching school year. The warehouse was holding 628,000 new schoolbooks. “It was the high season of distribution,” he said, “so we were checking all our processes: how to do it more successfully, how to do it in time.”

The meeting was scheduled for 11am. But a couple of moments after it began, there came “the sound of an explosion, and almost simultaneously I saw a huge fire”, said Kruglov. The impact was about 30 metres from where the staff were gathered, and, as colleagues set about trying to put out the flames, “there came a second strike and I understood that there could be a third, and a fourth, so we started to evacuate”.

The munitions used in the attack were jet-powered Shaheds, a recent and insidious escalation of Russian drone technology, faster and harder to intercept than their predecessors. These are the weapons that have been lately terrorising Kyiv during daylight hours, ploughing into the National Academy of Sciences and a working medical clinic in the past week.

“Fifty people were on shift that day,” said Kruglov of the warehouse strike, “and I don’t know how to explain how nobody was injured.”

The combination of an explosion, jet fuel and a warehouse full of paper was catastrophic. None of the books could be salvaged and 8m were destroyed. It took firefighters a week to bring the flames under control.

Several weeks on, smoke still rose from parts of the warehouse. The roof seemed on the verge of collapse, metal beams listing alarmingly, twisted out of shape by the heat.

Shafts of sunlight slanted through the damaged roof, illuminating the catastrophe. The smell was terrible, clinging to clothes and hair. As far as the eye could see, the wreckage of books lay in mounds.

In some places, engulfed by the firefighters’ water, they had dissolved into a thick, stinking, mud-like slurry. In others, they were charred at the edges but recognisable as what they once were: children’s picturebooks illustrated with animals and flowers, geography textbooks, young-adult fiction. Others were nothing but swollen millefeuilles of blackened pages that flaked away to the touch.

A couple of editorial staff, visiting the wreckage for the first time since the attack, looked shaken as they recognised fragments of books they had written or edited. “When you see what was produced with your brain, with your hands, with your imagination, spoiled by Russia, it’s an awful feeling,” said Kruglov, a trim, bald, blue-eyed man in his early 60s.

Those 8m books represented more than 85% of Ranok’s total stock, he said. In the main branch of Ranok’s own Knyholand bookstore in Kyiv, the display still looked cheerful and dense in late September – but, predicted Kruglov, there will be shortages this autumn when the books instore run low and there is nothing to replace them.

In total, this summer, 13m Ukrainian books have been destroyed by Russian missiles or drones – a third, estimates the government, of all books printed in Ukraine this year.

Books, literature, culture and language are not peripheral to Russia’s war on Ukraine – they are bound up in it. The full-scale invasion in February 2022 was prompted, at least in part, by Vladimir Putin’s conviction that Ukraine and Russia have no true separate cultural identity.

Kruglov said he was sure his warehouse full of Ukrainian-language, Ukraine-produced books had been deliberately targeted. “It is nowhere near any military facilities and everyone knows it is a book warehouse,” he said.

Bohdana Laiuk, a Ukrainian deputy minister for culture, who works on literature and publishing, takes a slightly different view: the recent attacks on books should not be seen in isolation, but as part of the invaders’ recent campaign of attacking warehouses, depots and fulfilment centres of any kind. “They cannot occupy Kyiv,” she said. “So they target warehouses around Kyiv to take the possibility of everyday life from us – and books are part of everyday life.”

But books are also part of language, and language is part of identity and, often, nationhood. Books are, said Laiuk, certainly considered important by the Russians invaders. “When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do – and we know this from the areas that were occupied and then liberated in 2022 in the Kherson and Kharkiv regions – is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books out, and destroy them,” she said.

Until 2022, about 70% of the Ukrainian book market was Russian-language titles – most imported from Russia, some published in Ukraine.

The dominance of Russian publishing had a long history. Its seeds lay in 19th-century decrees under the tsars against publishing in Ukrainian and continued through the Soviets’ promotion of Russian as the language of aspiration, education and culture. Ukrainian writers were purged and Ukrainian literature left in the shadows, shut out from a canon that lionised the Russian novel.

After Ukraine’s independence in 1991, the idea of a commercially successful Ukrainian-language novel that tackled modern social issues was so unthinkable that publishers initially suggested to Oksana Zabuzhko that her 1996 novel Fieldwork in Ukrainian Sex be published in Russian translation. She insisted it was published in the language it was written. It became a bestseller, paving the road for waves of contemporary Ukrainian literature.

Laiuk characterised the dominance of Russian book imports as a kind of colonialism. “It should be compared to how Russians invested in Ukrainian media outlets, Ukrainian TV channels, Ukrainian newspapers and magazines.” It was a conscious policy, she argued. “This is how Russians think: when they arrive on tanks, everything will be ready for them because they already have this information space.”

But in 2022, Ukrainian booksellers abruptly stopped selling Russian imports, in line with the rupture of all commercial ties between the countries. At the same time, swathes of the Ukrainian population switched their day-to-day language from Russian to Ukrainian.

They switched reading matter, too, and Ukraine’s publishers fed the appetite with new editions of classic Ukrainian literature from the 1920s, poetry, translations, and new Ukrainian writing. The country’s publishers may publish Russian-language books, as long as at least half their titles are in Ukrainian; in practice the social barriers to doing so, at the moment, would be prohibitive. (Death and the Penguin author Andrey Kurkov, for example, writes his novels in Russian, but they are published only in Ukrainian translation; he writes nonfiction and children’s books in Ukrainian.)

“People began to understand that the Russians came here to kill people simply because they were Ukrainian,” Laiuk told me in 2023. “So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are.”

Oleksiy Erinchak opened the first of his chain of Ukrainian-only bookstores, Sens, in 2021. In 2024, while the city was under fire, he opened a second, in a huge building on Khreshchatyk, Kyiv’s grandest boulevard, to which he has recently added a third floor, with an expansive events space. He has another branch in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk and he has just opened a fourth, in a former cinema in Lviv.

“When you go to a bookstore like Sens,” said Laiuk, “you feel that you have dignity. You have the right to buy a new book and to choose which one you like. And when you have drones above your head, it gives so much space, inner space in your heart and soul, and in your mind.”

The rapid expansion of Sens is a symptom of something unlikely: a Ukrainian publishing boom amid a full-scale invasion of the country. And now, that boom is threatened by the force and frequency of Russian attacks.

Kateryna and Artem Sova started their imprint in 2023, in the thick of the new Ukrainian publishing boom. By then Artem had been in the army for nearly a year and Kateryna was several months pregnant, living in her hometown of Kremenchuk, on the River Dnipro in central Ukraine. It was their dream: they had both worked in bookstores and at arts festivals for years. Part of the point for Artem was to keep some chink of his old self alive. “I realised,” he said, speaking in Zaporizhzhia during a break from his military duties, “that I was detached from everything I love.”

They began with Lonely City, a nonfiction work about art and the experience of urban isolation, by the British author Olivia Laing. They had loved it since they read it a decade ago, and were bemused it was not already translated. They wrote to Laing’s agent asking whether they could acquire the rights.

“We tried to explain why this book is important for Ukrainians now, and to me personally,” Artem said, recalling. “This experience of being lonely is kind of universal, but it has been multiplied because a lot of people went into the army, and there are so many displaced people in Ukraine: separated couples, destroyed lives.”

Laing, to their surprise, agreed: only then did they actually go through the legal process of setting up the company. They called it Krapky – Ukrainian for “ellipsis”, the three dots being their favourite punctuation mark, signifying, said Kateryna, as she sipped coffee in an independent bookshop in Kremenchuk, that they wanted reading their books “to be an ongoing conversation. Something that doesn’t stop when you close the book.” Their aim was for every book they published to be expertly translated and wonderfully illustrated.

In 2025, they finally went to Kyiv Book Arsenal – the great annual gathering for publishers, writers and readers in the capital – with a beautifully designed edition of Lonely City. By this year’s Book Arsenal they had several titles already out, and translations of Laing’s To the River and Karen Blixen’s classic, Out of Africa, in the pipeline. In preparation were also works by Flannery O’Connor, among others. “We wanted to get to a position where we were publishing eight to 10 titles a year,” said Kateryna.

Recently, they had signed a contract with Nova Poshta, the Ukrainian postal service, to handle fulfilment – so that Kateryna was not sending out the books herself to customers and bookstores. She was driving her sister to university on the morning of 28 August when Artem rang. The warehouse where their books were held, on the periphery of Kyiv, had been attacked. Kateryna had to pull off the road in her distress. At the Lviv BookForum, a fortnight later, their stand was empty but for a QR code so visitors could preorder their forthcoming titles. They had nothing physical to sell. All of their books had been destroyed.

Ranok is now rushing to reprint textbooks and bestsellers, hoping to get precious teaching materials into schools – and plug the shortfall in cashflow with sales of popular titles. Vivat, a large Kharkiv-based publisher, which lost 16m Ukrainian hryvnia (about £270,000) worth of books in a hit on one of its warehouses this summer, is doing the same. “We’ll definitely continue publishing Ukrainian authors, and the schedule for 2027 is already finalised,” said Vivat’s spokesperson, Kateryna Ilchuk, between events at Lviv BookForum. “But probably yes, it will mean going with more mainstream titles.”

Small literary publishers such as Krapky are the most vulnerable in the current crisis. Another small independent press, Who is That?, recently announced a pause in its operations until the end of the war, after the destruction of all of their stock this summer in two separate airstrikes.

For debut authors, or writers of less commercial or more experimental titles, this is a bleak moment. Even before the summer drone hits, there had been delays in some books’ publication owing to attacks on printing infrastructure. Ksenia Shpak’s debut young-adult novel – an urban fantasy about a girl internally displaced from eastern Ukraine to the Carpathian mountains – was originally due out in February 2025. It was finally published, by the imprint Zhorzh, in November.

But half the print run was in the Ranok warehouse in Kharkiv when it was attacked. “I must say that it’s sad because it was my first published book,” said Shpak, “and now my publisher will focus on their bestsellers, and only after that if they get enough money will they reprint my book.” She mentioned other factors that had lately cooled the Ukrainian publishing boom: a levelling out of demand; the rise in the cost of living. “It feels like there is a snowballing of bad things for our publishing industry,” Shpak added.

“It’s shaky,” said veteran poetry editor, poet and children’s publisher Ivan Malkovych. His premises – in central Kyiv, shared with a male-voice choir, the sound of whose rehearsal wafted through the editorial offices as he spoke – presented an absolute contrast to the desolation of the Ranok warehouse. In one room, a wall of shelves displayed ranks of exquisitely illustrated children’s titles, and handsome volumes of poetry. He began his company amid the economic chaos of the early 1990s, starting with a Ukrainian alphabet book, printed on board a supplier let him have on the vague promise he’d pay for it in six months (the book was a success, and he did). The alphabet began, “A is for Angel”, and the angel has been the publishing house’s good luck charm ever since.

Malkovych has published many children’s books, but none in such quantity as Harry Potter. His editions hit the shelves faster, and were better translated, than the Russian versions (“We Ukrainianised a lot of children that way,” he said.) He lost 40,000 books in the same Nova Poshta warehouse attack that destroyed Krapky’s stock – about $500,000 (£377,800) of losses. “We were always proud of our delivery service – you could order a book at 4am and it would arrive by midday. Now we face big delays,” he said. He was particularly worried about the next Harry Potter release, on 6 October. There had been a lot of pre-orders and he wanted delivery to be synchronised with the rest of the world, despite the full-scale invasion.

For publishers like Malkovych – whose staff have elected not to leave Kyiv, despite the oncoming winter and the new Russian jet-powered drones – the task now is to adapt: they will now spread stocks of book in smaller warehouses across the country, at the expense of super-fast delivery times. There is hope for Krapky too: Nova Poshta may reimburse it for some of their lost stock; there has been an outflowing of support from readers who have preordered forthcoming titles; and it has received a grant from an NGO towards reprinting costs.

When Laiuk visits Frankfurt book fair this October, she will be promoting a ministry of culture and Kyiv School of Economics fundraiser for small Ukrainian publishers like Krapky. But she will also urge global publishers to translate Ukrainian titles. “It’s important to see that the industry is suffering and to see the devastating pictures of burned books. But that is not the whole story. The whole story is that Ukrainian literature is rich and diverse as never before. The best way is to see that is to translate, and to bring new voices to the discourse in your country.”

As for Kruglov, despite the devastating loss of 8m books, he was, somehow, optimistic. Surveying the absolute ruin of his Kharkiv premises, he said, “I think that we will rebuild everything. And I even know how to do it better.”

Star Wars actor John Boyega on the day his 10-year-old school friend Damilola Taylor was killed: ‘It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy’

The Guardian Sun, 04 Oct 2026 05:00:19 GMT

The star was just eight when his friend was stabbed. Decades on, he’s ready to talk about that day – how it shaped him, and how, as he becomes a father himself, it will shape him as a dad

“I feel a bit nervous,” confesses John Boyega, as he sits down in front of the camera. “Speaking about it could possibly help. I haven’t revisited this in a long time. Yeah, my heart is just beating.” The Attack the Block and Star Wars actor is talking in the opening scene of a new BBC Two documentary about the killing of 10-year-old schoolboy Damilola Taylor.

On 27 November 2000, Damilola was stabbed in the leg with a broken bottle and left to die in a concrete stairwell, attacked as he walked home from an after-school club at Peckham library in south London. It took six years and three separate trials at the Old Bailey, costing a total of £16m, to secure a manslaughter conviction. His death shocked the nation not only because he was so young, but because all the suspects were also children. Boyega was one of the last people to see Damilola alive. The pair had enjoyed a close friendship since Damilola’s move to the UK from Nigeria in August of that year.

Watching the film at a Bafta screening a few weeks before its premiere, it’s striking how young and vulnerable the 34-year-old actor looks as he talks about the death of his friend. Boyega is more often seen looking assured and confident, be that his impassioned, impromptu address to thousands of people at a Black Lives Matter protest in Hyde Park, posing for the Pirelli calendar, or portraying an African king in a Hollywood movie. Usually he stands tall, with broad shoulders supported by a proud stance. But in revisiting the memories of that day, it feels as if he has almost reverted to the eight-year-old child he was nearly 26 years ago when he found out his friend had died.

A couple of hours later I reconvene with him at BBC New Broadcasting House to discuss the show. In person, Boyega is unassuming, with a calm demeanour and a welcoming smile. He has just returned from a trip to New York fashion week and looks surprisingly fresh-faced for somebody who has not long stepped off a transatlantic flight.

Boyega is sitting comfortably with his father Samson, his mother Abigail and an older cousin. It’s a lively space – Boyega lives in Los Angeles now and I get the impression that everybody is excited to snatch a bit of time with him while he’s in London. We immediately get into a five-way conversation about the criminal proceedings around Damilola’s death. Everybody is talking at once.

The first trial collapsed after the judge ruled that the prosecution’s key witness was unreliable and there was controversy about items of crucial evidence that were excluded from the proceedings. The family closely followed all three trials – in the second, the jury failed to reach a verdict for two of the three defendants on a charge of murder – and there is a sense of frustration at the opportunities missed when it came to bringing the killers to justice.

“You would have thought the influence of the Stephen Lawrence case would have been way stronger, if they had actually learned something. It didn’t come across like that,” Boyega sighs. The police investigation was heavily criticised after it was found to have made a number of significant mistakes.

The whole Boyega family knew Damilola; but the actor has previously said very little about him in public. Boyega has worked consistently since his 2011 debut in sci-fi cult classic Attack The Block, including a gamechanging role as a lead in Disney’s Star Wars franchise. His most recent projects, The Woman King (2022) and They Cloned Tyrone (2023), were both critically acclaimed. He has said that his professional success is in no small part due to being inspired by the way Damilola lived his short life.

He has been deeply involved in the documentary. “The first time I watched a rough cut I was in my living room and it was bright out. Since then, we’ve been watching daily edits, y’know, on a phone, on a laptop, on a little TV. But viewing it in the cinematic setup hits different – it was an emotional hill to get over, seeing the film like that. I feel really impacted by it.” Throughout the 75-minute screening, crying and sniffling could be heard around the room. “It’s one of those films I wouldn’t watch multiple times because of my personal relationship to it, but it’s definitely a film I will refer to – when my child comes of age I will show him this film. You need to know the realities of your lineage.”

On Damilola Taylor’s first day at Oliver Goldsmith primary school in Peckham, shortly after his arrival in the UK, a teacher assigned Boyega’s sister Grace to be his chaperone. She says in the documentary: “My teacher was like, ‘Grace, there’s a new guy and he’s from Nigeria and obviously you’re Nigerian so you understand the language – you can show him around.’” They became a trio, because Boyega and his sister were inseparable at the time.

“The only reason I was around him a lot was because I was always with my sister – I inherited Damilola,” Boyega tells me, laughing. “I stayed because I found him hilarious.”

His father chimes in with a poignant memory: “John don’t have many friends – at least not boys. John had girls surrounding him. And I remember asking, ‘John, why are you hanging around girls?’ and he said, ‘Dad, boys are dangerous – they’ll beat me up.’” At lunchtimes, the three of them would run around the playground together.

Boyega describes the day Damilola died as a transformational moment for him. “The psychological impact is something that definitely stayed with me, but now it’s expressed through appreciation. Every time I wake up and I’m here, I appreciate it.” He smiles as he says of talking to his friends: “I’ll tell my boys, ‘Hey, a bullet don’t look at you and be like, “You’ve done movies before,” and swerve you!’” As a child, though, his thoughts were less positive. “When I would hear that anybody had been stabbed or whatever, it just felt like it was getting closer and closer and that awareness became part of day-to-day life. I was very scared of that.”

Boyega was eight when Damilola was killed; he had previously thought that death “only happened to old people”. He was bewildered by it – “like when babies fall and everyone goes, ‘Oh my gosh!’ and then the baby [seeing the response] decides to cry? It was like that.” As the news sank in, he found it difficult to comprehend that bad things could happen to good people. “I was trying to compute what that meant. I thought about the practicality of it. The last breath. Does it hurt? I remember with Grace we would have conversations where I’d be like, ‘Do you think death is sleep?’ or, ‘Maybe they go for 20 years and then, they come back?’ It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy, y’know?”

In the aftermath of Damilola’s death, Boyega spent a lot of time at home in his bedroom. Sometimes friends would knock for him and he would tell his mother to relay the message that he didn’t want to go out. “The hand of death is influencing kids to kill kids. I’m like, ‘Damn, I’m a kid, let me stay where I feel the most safe.’ I had a home that granted extreme safety and my parents didn’t shy away from showing concern.”

This played out in many ways, including their choice for his secondary school. Instead of the options in their home borough, he was sent to Westminster City School – almost an hour away by bus. Was getting out of the area a response to Damilola’s death? Boyega’s father answers: “Before John says anything, I went to his teacher when he was going to secondary school and he said to me, ‘Mr Boyega, why do you have to choose Westminster?’ And I never said to him what I saw: that the environment here will corrupt this guy,” he says, pointing at his son. “I saw what was coming, that in the future this environment is going to be very, very dangerous.” This was in 2003. By the end of the decade, 188 teenagers had been murdered on the streets of London.

I direct the conversation back to Boyega. Did he have therapy back then? He lowers his chin and looks at me with a furrowed brow. What he appears to be conveying is there’s no such thing as therapy in an African household – especially not a 1990s African household. We both laugh. At this point I am conscious that my question could easily be construed as a criticism of his parents, who are sitting on the sofa opposite us in the suddenly quite claustrophobic room. We quickly move on.

Over the years there have been numerous documentaries focusing on various aspects of Damilola’s killing, from a 2002 BBC Panorama special to most recently one fronted by broadcaster Yinka Bokinni to mark the 20th anniversary of Damilola’s death. This latest project focuses much of the narrative on the 24 hours leading up to his killing.

We hear from a number of people who were critical to the investigation in its early stages, including the estate maintenance worker who first found Damilola as he lay bleeding in the stairwell. There were several months of discussions between Boyega and the director, Alex Thomas – who also directed the award-winning Sky Original documentary Bibaa and Nicole: Murder in the Park, about the 2020 killings of Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman. “It fell to me to decide who was coming from my world to sit down and talk,” says Boyega. “That’s when I decided that Grace would be more appropriate to discuss Damilola than me because that was her direct friend – they were around the same age. And I think her perspective on it was quite important.”

after newsletter promotion

That was the easy part. More difficult was deciding how to address the ecosystem of bullying and fear on the streets of Peckham that led up to and ultimately underpinned Damilola’s killing. In the final edit, much of this element of the storytelling is omitted.

It doesn’t go unnoticed. During a Q&A after the screening, a Bafta member in the audience queries the lack of backstory included about the lives of the two boys convicted of Damilola’s manslaughter. In August 2006, brothers Danny and Ricky Preddie were each sentenced to eight years in youth custody after the third trial. The questioner pointed out that the brothers appeared at the Old Bailey unattended by any family. “I’d love to know why you left that out,” they said, referring to the brothers’ troubled childhoods. It was well known that their single mother struggled immensely while raising them. The pair were eventually placed in a local authority children’s care home. “We did look at the option of interviewing the two brothers,” said Boyega, who explained a general concern within the team that it might be viewed as being too empathetic to the perpetrators. In the end, the decision was made not to approach them.

But Boyega agrees that some elements of their backstory do have a place in the narrative, in particular when it comes to the debate about how to end youth violence. “Family. Discipline,” he says decisively. “The fact that you don’t have an adult at home that holds you accountable is a very important thing, especially for boys. Especially for boys.” He repeats the last sentence a little slower to emphasise its importance. “But y’know, you could have two parents at home and the child still goes out and does what they need to do, so there’s obviously a more nuanced conversation. Even in the sense that someone showed you that they loved you, that they cared about what you did or whether or not you made a mistake. What that person [in the screening Q&A] said made me think about what it meant – that they didn’t have that. Not even a social worker.”

There’s an extended silence when I ask Boyega what was difficult about making the documentary. “Poverty,” he replies, eventually. He means it brought back memories of the poverty he experienced as a child. Growing up, he lived in a small flat on Sceaux Gardens estate just off Peckham Road, with both his parents and his elder sisters – Grace, who appears in the documentary, and Blessing, who generally keeps a much lower profile. His mother was a care worker and his father a Pentecostal minister. “I didn’t know I was poor until I was in year 7. When you’re super-young, you’re not really thinking about that. And then when you get to school, you start to see where you are in the food chain of life, and that’s when you start to compare yourself with other children and other kids.” The process of filming the documentary brought that world back into focus.

Boyega recalls being keen not to stand out for the wrong reasons in his first year at Westminster City School, and begging his mother to buy him a pair of Kickers. She took him to Barrie Howard, a shoe shop on East Street in Walworth – a strategic rite of passage for any south Londoner who hoped to survive the brutal transition from primary to secondary. But once he had the shoes he felt bad, because he could tell how much it cost her. “I never asked for Kickers from my mum again – I wore Clarks for the rest of school.” Recounting these memories, plus seeing the archive footage of Peckham and the burgundy Oliver Goldsmith school sweater, brought back the distinct feeling that he had so much less than many of his peers. “I did work hard to get out of that. In making this film I had to revisit who I used to be, and that bothered me.” The interviews took place while he was on location in the Isle of Skye making a supernatural horror movie, The Punishing, in which he stars alongside Cara Delevingne (it is currently in post-production). The surroundings served as a physical reminder of how far he’s come in life.

Boyega had some reservations about being involved in the project. His main concern was that he wanted to make sure that Damilola’s brother – Tunde Taylor, chair of the Damilola Taylor Trust – was happy with the way Damilola’s life is portrayed. “I’ve been in the public eye for a minute now and from my experience, you have to be very careful, because you don’t know which journalist is being stressed by an editor. You don’t know which person wants to grab a story and not use it with the right intentions. You don’t know if they’re gonna be respectful to the people who are really involved.” But he was reassured by meeting producer Nelson Adeosun, a childhood family friend, and fellow contributor Leroy Logan. Logan is the founder and former chairman of the Black Police Association, whom Boyega portrayed in the film Red, White and Blue, from Steve McQueen’s 2020 anthology series, Small Axe. The performance won him a Golden Globe award.

Settling down thousands of miles away from Peckham has inevitably changed Boyega’s relationship with the place that made him who he is. “South is still familiar, but if I go now, people have to guide me … it’s so, so different,” he says, referring to the gentrification of the area. For him, though, the heart of the place is in the people who remember what it was like when he was growing up. We do a little reminiscing about which legendary hangouts have survived. He is pleased to note that Bagel King is on the list.

Somebody pokes their head round the door to tell us we need to wrap up. Boyega’s on a tight schedule. I ask a final question. Tell me about your jewellery, I say, indicating towards his left hand. “Oh yeah, this is my wedding ring,” he says casually. “I’ve been married for coming up to two years now.” He doesn’t give any detail about his wife, but does say they had a small ceremony, joking that he got married the way Braveheart did, while miming the action of planting a sword in the ground. He continues by reaching to the deepest depth of his vocal range and bellowing, “Will you come with me?”

His eldest sister has now joined us and the room has erupted into a chorus of unrestrained laughter. I note that the ring he is wearing is different from the one he wears in the documentary. “Yeah, this is our very sentimental ring,” he says of the two-toned band. “This is the one we decided to pick up spontaneously because I just wanted the ring on my finger, so we went to Walmart to get this. It was a lovely trip to Walmart. Shout out, Walmart Canoga Park!” he laughs. I am surprised to learn that he didn’t have a traditional Nigerian ceremony. “I would love to have a wedding celebration. We both like the idea of celebrating something established, rather than celebrating the entry. And by then, we’ll have to shut Nigeria down!”

It occurs to me that the child he mentioned earlier in the conversation may not be hypothetical. Are you about to hard launch a baby, I inquire tentatively. “My baby’s on the way. We got a baby cooking.” And you said my son earlier – is that because you’re having a boy? He confirms this and that he also has a young stepson. “So, you know, my life is completely, completely fulfilled in terms of family. It’s been so nice with the timing.”

Getting used to the new dynamic away from the public eye has obviously served him well – and perhaps this is why he is now ready to speak publicly about his friendship with Damilola. “I do think it’s important to reach back and tell people the grounded realities of your origins, because it wasn’t until I knew the grounded realities of other people’s origins that I decided to pursue something more.” When thinking about the kind of father he wants to be, it’s all still sinking in. “Us being parents is funny! I just want to make sure I’m present, I’m consistent and full of love.”

These personal milestones explain why he’s been less visible in recent years. “I’ve tried to as much as possible – especially following periods when I’ve worked a lot – to de-centre my career. There have been certain moments when I’ve known that this is a time for family. Y’know, there’s stuff to do.” In this moment he’s clear that his purpose is to love his wife and sons and invest in the support system that he knows he is lucky to have had.

Damilola: The Untold Story is on BBC Two and iPlayer from 5 October

Tories would expand free childcare to high earners, Badenoch says

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 21:00:09 GMT

Kemi Badenoch says those earning more than £100,000 should not be discouraged from working more

The Conservatives have unveiled a proposed £700m childcare giveaway for high earners ahead of their annual conference, saying they would end the “cliff edge” where free entitlement ends at salaries above £100,000.

The plan, set out the day before the event begins in Birmingham, follows the earlier proposal by Kemi Badenoch’s party to abolish most stamp duty, another change to taxation that would disproportionately benefit wealthier people.

Under the current system, put in place under Rishi Sunak’s government, families with young children in England are eligible for 30 hours a week of free childcare, but this cuts off if one parent earns more than £100,000, irrespective of another parent’s salary.

Under the Conservative plans, this limit would be abolished, with all parents working 16 or more hours a week able to claim the childcare.

The party says it would cost aabout £700m a year, which it says would be paid for by cutting jobs at organisations such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.

In comments released to promote the idea, Badenoch said the current system was “absurd” and a disincentive to work more.

She said: “Conservatives believe that you shouldn’t be punished for working more, but this childcare cliff edge does exactly that.

“I’m a mum-of-three and I’ve had to make the same choices many families have had to make on work and childcare. Those choices are difficult already, government should not be making them harder.

“No one should be turning down a promotion or a pay rise because they literally cannot afford to earn more.

“It is often women who end up carrying more of the childcare responsibility so a system that makes it harder for them to progress in their careers is not helping families, it is not helping women and it is definitely not helping the economy.”

A Labour spokesperson said: “It tells you everything you need to know about the Tories that the first of their own tax policies they want to unpick is one helping higher earners. They clearly don’t want to admit that they set the thresholds in the first place.”

The idea of abolishing stamp duty on people’s primary residences in England and Northern Ireland was unveiled by Badenoch at last year’s conference, costing an estimated £9bn a year.

While some economists have argued that stamp duty can have a drag on the housing market and even the economy, as it disincentivises moving, scrapping it rather than reforming the tax would disproportionately benefit better-off people and those in London and south-east England.

The other main policy set out ahead of the conference was a plan to build 50,000 new prison spaces in England and Wales, a 50% expansion in capacity.

This would be paid for in part by slashing overseas aid to £1bn a year, a 90% cut on current plans. Under Keir Starmer, Labour said they would reduce aid from 0.5% of GDP to 0.3% by 2027, but even that lower proportion would still amount to £9bn a year.

When Reform UK announced plans to cut aid to £1bn a year, aid groups warned that this would not cover existing contributions to global bodies such as the UN and World Bank, shredding Britain’s international influence.

From Digger to The Strokes: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 03 Oct 2026 05:00:52 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Tom Cruise transforms in Alejandro Iñárritu’s heavyweight satirical comedy, while the NYC indie rockers are in the UK for an arena tour

DiggerOut now Tom Cruise is back, but he’s giving flyboys and secret agents a rest in favour of a transformation into a powerful oil tycoon, in director Alejandro G Iñárritu’s 2027 Oscar bid. But here’s the kicker: it’s not a sober, serious Oscar contender, but a wild and comedic big swing. Dig in.

The WeightOut now As character motivations go, the need to be reunited with your child is a powerful one. That’s what’s driving Ethan Hawke in this Depression-era historical thriller, in which a convict must transport gold illegally through the wilderness if he’s to be allowed to see his young daughter again. Also starring Julia Jones and Russell Crowe.

VerityOut now Anne Hathaway’s golden era of psychological thrillers (see also: Eileen, Mothers’ Instinct, Mother Mary) keeps on trucking. In this Colleen Hoover adaptation she plays an unstable novelist who may or may not be a murderer. Josh Hartnett plays her husband, and Dakota Johnson the ghostwriter caught up in a nightmare.

Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman RushdieOut now Prolific film-maker Alex Gibney directs a documentary about the aftermath of 24-year-old Hadi Matar’s 2022 attack on Salman Rushdie. Based on the literary titan’s own bestselling memoir, it contains footage filmed by his wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths. Catherine Bray

Beyond the Music MediaCity, Salford, 7 to 9 October As well as offering an industry talks programme, the annual Beyond the Music conference showcases new talent over three days. This year’s lineup includes Jamaican-Irish rapper JayaHadADream and noisy sister duo Alt Blk Era. Michael Cragg

The Strokes6 to 28 October; tour starts London Having galvanised gen Z via 2020’s The New Abnormal, New York’s premiere indie rockers arrive in arenas in support of their new album Reality Awaits. Single Going Shopping should slot nicely next to Reptilia, Last Nite and Someday. MC

Leonkoro Quartet Wigmore Hall, London, 6 October Impressive new quartets appear constantly in classical music, but this group are the real deal. Their first recital as Wigmore Hall associate artists combines Beethoven and Schubert with the UK premiere of a new work by Finnish composer Sauli Zinovjev. Flora Willson

Arbenz, Neame, Osby, Churchill Watermill Jazz, Dorking, 6 OctoberDorking is the last UK stopover for Swiss drums original Florian Arbenz’s European tour with US sax star Greg Osby, UK piano virtuoso Ivo Neame and resourceful UK singer Immy Churchill. Neame also plays 1000 Trades in Birmingham on Friday with his own trio. John Fordham

Painting the French Riviera Royal Academy of Art, London, to 31 January Timed perfectly to coincide with the weather turning miserable, the Royal Academy is taking a warm, summery look at the Côte d’Azur and what made it such a destination for the artists who shaped modernism, such as Picasso, Matisse, Renoir and Raoul Dufy. It might make you very, very jealous.

The 90s: Art and Fashion Tate Britain, London, 8 October to 14 February Tate Britain’s big autumn show is a dizzying exploration of life in the UK during the hedonistic, hectic, drug-addled, rave-filled, Britpoptastic party decade that was the 1990s, with art by the likes of Juergen Teller and Sarah Lucas, all curated by former Vogue editor-in-chief Edward Enninful.

Living Labyrinths: Art and Fungi Royal Albert Memorial Museum, Exeter, 3 October to 21 February Uncover all sorts of mycological marvels in this exhibition about the “culture of mushrooms”, featuring fungi-focused watercolours by Beatrix Potter, collages by Cy Twombly and mycelial art by a whole host of contemporary artists.

Mike Nelson Modern Art Oxford, 3 October to 11 April The master of large-scale, terrifying, atmospheric installation art returns to this Oxford institution 22 years after his last show here, this time tackling themes of belief, freedom, protest and memory. Eddy Frankel

Rent Tom Stoppard theatre, London, to 27 March A high-voltage new take on Jonathan Larson’s powerful musical, starring Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo. Set in 80s New York in the midst of the Aids/HIV crisis, the show focuses on a group of young artists forging a living and falling in love. Miriam Gillinson

London City Ballet Arts theatre, Cambridge, ouring to 24 OctoberIt is only two years since artistic director Christopher Marney revived this ballet company, and he’s taken it swiftly from 0 to 60. It lands in Cambridge with a programme including Glen Tetley’s Firebird and a rarely seen work by Jerome Robbins. Lyndsey Winship

King Lear Royal Exchange theatre, Manchester, to 15 November David Threlfall tackles the mighty theatrical challenge that is King Lear – and stars alongside a rich ensemble cast, including musician Nadine Shah and Shakespearean pro Jonathan Slinger. MG

Finlay Christie Guildford, 3 October; Peterborough; Sun; Chelmsford, Wed; Maidenhead, Fri; touring to 9 January It sounds counterintuitive, but leaning into poshness can be a very effective way for comedians to connect with the public. It’s a tactic Christie uses in his latest show, Champagne Casanova, which combines riffs on privilege with the tale of a New Orleans mugging. Rachel Aroesti

The Reluctant Vampire BBC One & iPlayer, 4 October, 6.40pm The neglected Sunday teatime slot gets a much-needed boost courtesy of this very cute adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s 1982 novel about a boy who discovers he’s a different beast from the rest of his bloodsucking family. Below Netflix, 8 October This ominous new thriller sounds a bit like a Canadian Widow’s Bay minus the irreverent humour. Josh Hartnett plays a weathered fisher whose tiny coastal town is beset by a monstrous sea creature, a mysterious iceberg and some increasingly unsettling behaviour from the locals.

Carrie Prime Video, 7 October Television’s ongoing reliance on familiar IP plus the current vogue for horror means it was only a matter of time before we got a new version of Stephen King’s celebrated tale of a tormented teenage girl with telekinetic powers – now updated to include a grim cyberbullying plotline.

Damilola: The Untold Story BBC Two & iPlayer, 5 October, 9pm It has been a quarter of a century since 10-year-old Damilola Taylor was killed in south-east London. This documentary reflects on the violence faced by young people at that time and hears how tragedy killing shaped the lives of Taylor’s family and friends, including actor John Boyega. RA

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve PC, PS5, Xbox; out nowOn the face of it, this aerial combat game takes itself extremely seriously. It looks expensive, featuring a large cast and a dramatic military story. But it is also full of explosions and unselfconscious cheesiness. People who love Ace Combat really love Ace Combat.

End of Abyss PC, PS5, Xbox; out nowThis science fiction horror game has shades of Limbo, Inside, Little Nightmares, and Dead Space. You’re a space-suited investigator in a gloom-shrouded compound full of horrid things, dwarfed by the architecture and the scale of the monstrosities. Keza MacDonald

Johnny Marr – The Age of EverythingOut now While his erstwhile colleague continues to swing a wrecking ball at his legacy, Marr has quietly built a solid solo career that peaks with this fifth album. Inspired by our overwhelming and oversaturated lives (hence the title), songs such as the bouncy Spin try to make sense of it all.

Victoria Monét – Frequency of LoveOut now The multiple Grammy winner, fresh off a Bruno Mars stadium support slot, follows up 2023’s Jaguar II with another suite of luxurious R&B and soul. Working alongside regular producer D’Mile (HER, Silk Sonic) and Kaytranada, songs such as Juicy and Reach Out showcase Monét’s caramel vocals and melodic flair.

Walt Disco – Walt DiscoOut now Alt-rock quintet Walt Disco return with their third album after a period of personal evolution. Musically influenced by the likes of Bowie and 00s indie discos, lyrically there are reflections on identity, growing up and, on the widescreen Lies, frontwoman Jocelyn’s struggles as a trans person.

Logic1000 – Confirmation!Out now Christine and the Queens, Jam City and Kučka guest on Australian DJ-producer Samantha Poulter’s second album as Logic1000. Featuring warm, house-adjacent bops such as All in for You, as well as club heaters (Jersey), the album peaks with The Only One’s ethereal ode to the next generation. MC

The Questlove ShowPodcast Drummer and film-maker Questlove hosts this in-depth interview series with his musical friends and inspirations. On the roster of intriguing guests are rapper Maseo from De La Soul and the R&B singer Eric Benét.

Why Do Some People Have a Better Sense of Direction Than Others?YouTube As someone who often finds themselves lost, this is a useful explainer on the existence of our “internal compass” and how those with a bad sense of direction can hone theirs to work more effectively.

Artworks: Roleplay Radio 4, 6 October, 4pm This charming series tasks actors from around the world to explain theatre’s great roles and their experiences playing them. This week, Fiona Shaw and Liz Carr are among the guests discussing Brecht’s gruelling Mother Courage. Ammar Kalia

Five Great Reads: ICE 2.0, millennial motherhood, and skinny-dipping with Christine Baranski

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 22:08:31 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

The Guardian’s range was on display this week across these five very different stories. Grab a coffee and dig in, digest, and reflect on harrowing accounts of Trump’s immigration crackdown, investigations into modern motherhood and masculinity, and for a bit of weekend fun, we leave you with some celebrity gossip.

Enjoy.

At the peak of Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, armoured vehicles occupied neighbourhoods, while masked agents violently pulled people from the streets. After officers killed two US citizens during the raids in Minneapolis, public backlash prompted Trump to try a new approach. Now, ICE arrests have hit record levels. In this series, ICE 2.0, Guardian reporters track how, despite the administration’s change of tactics, ICE is everywhere.

Notable quote: “Before, they were storming around, making a lot of noise Now, they are moving more quietly.”

The violence continues: People are arrested while pumping gas, leaving behind their empty cars. They are arrested on their way to work, or on their way home. Recently, an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in Texas. That same day, in Grand Rapids, Michigan, a Guatemalan man died in a fiery crash while fleeing federal immigration agents. ICE is now detaining more immigrants than ever before, despite the new secretary of homeland security, Markwayne Mullin, promising to avoid negative headlines by cutting the flash and fanfare.

How long will it take to read: Under four minutes.

Further reading: All the stories from the series ICE 2.0: inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet.

Women today are more educated, more employed and more engaged in childcare arrangements than ever before. But research shows that the expectations facing modern mothers continue to grow. In Australia, the statistics illuminate a global phenomenon. New research shows that the cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year. The cost of keeping a family afloat has increased by 134% in two decades, while household income has grown by only 102% in the same period.

Between juggling rising costs and managing careers, is there any way out of the total overwhelm?

A problem with no solution: In this personal piece, Kate Lyons writes that millennial women no longer feel trapped in their homes like generations before, but rather, by the impossible juggle of managing their career, relationships and children. Lyons recounts a friend reaching out for advice late one night after their five-year-old had a meltdown before bed. Another woman Lyons spoke to got so desperate she turned towards ChatGPT, asking the AI chatbot how to make her life work. But solutions are not easy to come by. After Lyons assessed the state of her living room, which, “looks as though someone has taken the contents of a laundry basket, a toy box and a nappy bag and Jackson Pollocked the floor with them”, all she could offer was solidarity.

Notable quote: “It’s not that I want to be at home five days a week. I don’t want to be exactly like my mum was. But I want to pick them up from school and take them home and calmly wind down the day with them. There’s absolutely no way I can do that.”

How long will it take to read: Just under six minutes.

Further reading: Why birthrates are plummeting, and why workplaces were built for men.

Polls show that Donald Trump is losing support with the bros that got him elected. As the midterms approach, the cost of living and the war on Iran have left male voters increasingly disillusioned. So how does one win them back? The health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, and the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, seem to think the hormone testosterone, often known simply as “T”, is the answer. Or as Sam Wolfson explains, Trump is hoping that “the male populace will vote not with their heads or their hearts, but with their hogs”.

The testosterone dog-whistle: Testosterone is found in the bodies of men and women, with a low amount all that is needed for normal function. But the hormone has emerged on the frontlines of the Trump administration’s many culture wars. While the war in Iran causes problems for Trump back home, Hegseth has shifted the military message to one of machismo. On the campaign trail, he said, “We’re reminding our warriors that their sole purpose is to be the most lethal fighting force on the planet. Full stop. We’re not here to do social engineering, or social justice, or gender-bending, or DEI, or dudes and dresses.” But Wolfson writes that Hegseth’s testosterone push is a “sciencey” way to dog-whistle his sexist message.

Notable quote: “Everything has been politicized in the United States. Vaccines are liberal and TRT is Maga. The needle is apolitical but the content of the syringe is decided by who you vote for.”

How long will it take to read: eight minutes.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Further reading: The Pentagon and “incel” slang, plus RFK Jr’s “peptide wild west”.

Patricia Nilsson was determined to bring porn industry leaders out of the shadows. For five years, she subjected the adult industry to forensic analysis in an effort to reveal who was getting rich through porn and how they were doing it. For decades, the owners of these companies have escaped scrutiny, and they have often enjoyed relative anonymity. But porn is everywhere, and for many young men and women, adult content can be their default sex education. Nilsson argues the owners of businesses that are recalibrating our sexual culture deserve further investigation.

Notable quote: “My argument is not that we should be neutral towards porn, but that we need to accept and understand it as a real industry, and ask what its growth and popularity says about the state of our economy and the world of work.”

The story of porn is the story of the internet: Nilsson argues that even if you do not consume explicit content online, the industry has shaped the way you interact with the digital world. We have porn to thank, she says, for high-quality video streaming and the way influencers sell their online personas. “Staring at content that is algorithmically engineered to arouse you is a perfect metaphor for our relationship with our devices and the internet and social media,” Nilsson says.

How long will it take to read: About five minutes.

Further reading: The malignant rise of OnlyFans managers and the rise of deepfake pornography in schools.

Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant have stories to tell. The actors have joined forces for the first time in a London production of Noël Coward’s comedic play Hay Fever. The Guardian sat down with the actors to get a glimpse of the tall tales told backstage.

Notable quote: When asked if she has ever worked with Grant before, Baranski wryly says: “Regrettably not. We could have had some good fun a few decades ago. A girl could have got into some real trouble. But here we are, and now we’re the veterans.”

Skinny dipping in the dark: Recalling her “marvellous house” on a lake in Connecticut, Baranski recounts an evening spent with Mark Rylance when the pair went skinny-dipping and ended up howling at the moon till four in the morning. Pressed on whether taking your clothes off is a prerequisite for visiting, Baranski says: “I encourage people only if they’re comfortable and if it’s pitch dark.”

How long will it take to read: five minutes of gossipy joy.

Further reading: How Richard E Grant ended up on Celebrity Traitors.

USA v Mexico, Nations League, F1 in Malaysia and NFL – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:50:06 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

David Tindall and John Brewin have all the breaking news and more for your essential launchpad to the weekend’s football. There’s bound to be more fallout from the Manchester City furore, but they’ll be fully attuned to the tantalising Nations League feast on offer. First up is England’s next stop in their busy schedule: a meeting in Rijeka with familiar foes Croatia at 5pm. Later, Scotland journey to Skopje for their League B Group 1 clash with North Macedonia, and they won’t be ignoring the other game in England’s group as Spain lock horns with Czechia in Oviedo. Plus Leagues One and Two fixtures. If the National League is your passion and you are travelling to a match, they would love to hear from you. Send your thoughts and observations to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

F1 fans will be rising early to follow qualifying, with Billy Munday at the wheel of our live blog. The championship battle takes an intriguing twist as Mercedes teammates Kimi Antonelli and George Russell renew their rivalry at an unlikely venue⁠. Although Sepang remains a permanent fixture on the MotoGP calendar, it has not hosted a grand prix since 2017 after the Malaysian government said it could no longer justify the ⁠hosting costs given the declining ⁠returns. But the Mercedes duo will now be fighting for supremacy there after the original Bahrain race was relocated from Sakhir due to the Iran war and ⁠tensions elsewhere in the Middle East.

England travel to Rijeka to take on Croatia before rounding off their four-match international splurge against Czechia at Wembley next Tuesday. So far, a defeat by Spain, a 2-0 win over Czechia, and Harry Kane and Anthony Gordon the Three Lions’ standout players. That victory was England’s eighth straight away win in all competitions, so there’s the tantalising prospect of setting a national record. The last time England won nine away games in a row was back in the 1960s when the Beatles, the Bee Gees and Engelbert Humperdinck were topping the singles charts – between December 1965 and October 1967, under World Cup-winning manager Sir Alf Ramsey. There’s a landmark beckoning for England’s No 1 goalscorer too: Kane could become just the fourth England player to score in six consecutive away games. The others? James Windridge (six from March to June 1908), Tom Finney (seven from September 1946 to May 1948) and Stan Mortensen (six from May 1947 to October 1948). Scott Murray helms the blog.

Anyone seeking a sporting fairy tale this weekend can look to events unfurling at Old Trafford. Sporting immortality awaits Trinity’s players if they can complete a transformation from top-flight also-rans to Super League champions. The club’s glory days were back in the 1960s, when the likes of the Fox brothers, Don and Neil, and half-back Ken Rollin were among league’s biggest names. Those times appeared long gone until last week’s seismic semi-final win over Wigan lifted the club’s modern counterparts to within 80 minutes of erasing well over half a century of hurt. Daryl Powell’s Wakefield team have been built around experienced former finalists such as Tom Johnstone and Mike McMeeken, but also bolstered by overseas players like Caius Faatili, Caleb Hamlin Uele and Jazz Tevaga, who arrived as relative unknowns but have helped form a thrilling and free-scoring spirit. It’s been quite a hiatus for title glory too for Warrington, with Sam Burgess’s Wire seeking to end their 71-year wait for a league title. Lee Calvert hosts our Grand Final blog.

Luke McLaughlin is on clockwatch duty as Scotland fans search for some uplift after the 3-0 defeat by Switzerland at Hampden on Tuesday when an early red card for Jack Hendry effectively rendered Sebastien Pocognoli’s home debut a write-off. The Scots have now gone four matches without a goal for the first time in 55 years but have an ideal opportunity to put that right in their third Nations League B1 encounter. North Macedonia have conceded five goals without reply in their opening two games and have also failed to score in their six matches since a 7-1 defeat to Wales last November. With just one point and no goals from their opening two Nations League fixtures after a 0-0 draw in Slovenia, this match in North Macedonia takes on an added weight for the new manager and his squad.

There’s little love lost between these North American sporting rivals and this international friendly at State Farm Stadium in Glendale sees Mauricio Pochettino’s USMNT measure their progress against Concacaf’s leading nation. The USA are on a hot streak coming out of the World Cup, where they fizzled in the group stage but came to a shuddering halt against Belgium. A 4–1 win over Peru and a 4–2 victory against Chile in St Louis sees Poch’s collective in fine fettle, with teenagers Julian Hall and Mathis Albert making an impact. Rafael Márquez’s El Tri venture to Arizona following a pair of 1–1 draws against Colombia and Peru. We’ll be live-blogging the match, with Jeff Rueter reporting.

With Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton trailing Kimi Antonelli by 103 points in third, the title fight has effectively become a straight duel at the top and George Russell arrives in Malaysia brimming with the momentum. Baku was the Briton’s weekend as he became only the seventh driver on the grid to achieve a grand slam – pole position, leading in every lap, clocking the fastest lap and taking the victory, his third of the season. A championship fight that once seemed to be slipping away from the Mercedes driver has suddenly become a realistic proposition. The question remains, however, whether Russell can turn one extraordinary weekend into a sustained challenge or if Antonelli will respond immediately with eight rounds remaining in the 23-race season. With Red Bull’s four-time world champion Max Verstappen and Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc charging hard in practice, a crackling race beckons. Join Yara El-Shaboury for lap-by-lap updates.

John Brewin and Rob Smyth share the blogging duties in the buildup to more Nations League fixtures, with the Republic of Ireland, Wales, Germany, Netherlands, Portugal and Norway all engaged in compelling fixtures. Breaking news, fun facts, wildly divergent opinions – join the footballing fray by emailing your notes and queries to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

Renée Slegers’s Gunners already trail WSL leaders City by seven points and a defeat would leave last season’s runners-up 10 points off the top after only five games following a 1-0 defeat at Chelsea last weekend. Arsenal let slip a two-goal lead in their midweek Champions League match against Paris FC, the 2-2 draw memorable for a bizarre mistake by Leah Williamson, who gave away a late penalty by putting her hand on the ball from a goal-kick. Slegers’ side did at least score twice for the first time in six fixtures, but they have only registered two wins this season. A win then is vital for Slegers and her side at the Etihad, where the furore around the club’s devastating guilty verdict on more than Premier League 100 charges has cast a pall over the hosts’ season. The women’s team is not implicated in the systemic breaking of financial monitoring rules and impressed on Thursday in their 1-1 Champions League draw with Real Madrid. Rob Smyth keeps the updates flowing.

Daniel Gallan has his hands full for an evening of Nations League games, and the clash of Republic of Ireland against Israel behind-closed-doors match in Serbia is certain to be dogged by political fallout between the two nations over the conflict in Gaza. The 2-2 draw with Austria leaves the Republic third in their group at the halfway point, three points behind leaders Austria and level on four with second-placed Kosovo after beating Israeli 3-0 in the reverse fixture in Debrecen, Hungary. Wales upset the World Cup finalists Norway 2-1 in Nations League A on Thursday night and next face Denmark in Cardiff, seeking to avenge last weekend’s 2-0 defeat in Copenhagen.

After covering Indianapolis Colts v Washington Commanders at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (the first of nine games being played outside the United States this season), Graham Searles resumes his blog post for Sunday evening’s clutch of NFL clashes. Winless Miami Dolphins face unbeaten Minnesota Vikings while elsewhere Denver Broncos meet San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs take on Las Vegas Raiders and Los Angeles Chargers meet Super Bowl champions Seattle Seahawks.

Saudi-Backed Yemeni Government Declares War Against Houthis

The New York Times October 04, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The announcement follows weeks of fighting with the Iran-allied armed group and threatens to deepen U. S. involvement in the widening Middle East conflict.

By Vivian NereimEric Schmitt and Saeed Al-Batati

Vivian Nereim reported from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Eric Schmitt from Washington, and Saeed Al-Batati from al-Mukalla, Yemen.

The Saudi-backed government of Yemen on Sunday announced a major military campaign against the Houthi militia, a key Iranian ally, plunging the Middle East deeper into war.

The new operation threatens to open a new front in the U. S.-Israeli war with Iran and further entangle the United States in the widening regional conflict that it began more than seven months ago.

In a televised speech, Rashad al-Alimi, the leader of the internationally recognized Yemeni government — which depends heavily on Saudi Arabia for financial and military support — said that his armed forces were seeking to reclaim the territory lost to the Houthis over the past 12 years.

In a statement hours later, Maj. General Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for a Saudi military coalition in Yemen, said that Saudi Arabia had the right to defend itself from Houthi attacks and pledged “full operational support” to the Yemeni military to fight the militia until it is “eliminated.”

Asked about the campaign, Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a Houthi political official, accused Saudi Arabia of waging war in Yemen to “impose its tutelage and interfere in sovereign decision-making.”

The announcement marks the second time that the Yemeni government has sought to fight the Houthis with Saudi support. In 2015, a Saudi-led intervention devolved into a grinding war that contributed to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people from violence, hunger and disease, and failed to defeat the Houthis.

Last time, the campaign hinged on U. S. support and weaponry, and Saudi officials have sought American assistance this time, too. Last month, President Trump rebuffed the Saudi requests.

But the U. S. is providing intelligence, planning and targeting assistance to Saudi Arabia to help its Yemeni allies, according to one current and one former U. S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters. Saudi Arabia has sent military advisers into Yemen to coordinate a ground offensive by the government’s armed forces, they said.

More than 200 U. S. intelligence and military analysts are aiding the Saudi government in command centers inside the kingdom, helping to analyze and select targets, the officials said. The United States is also providing aerial refueling for Saudi warplanes conducting defensive air patrols, they added.

U. S. Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, declined to comment.

Mr. al-Bukhaiti, the Houthi official, warned that whenever Saudi Arabia strikes Yemen, the Houthis would strike back by targeting the kingdom’s oil facilities.

Asked about Iran’s role in providing support to the Houthis, Mr. al-Bukhaiti said that the militia views Yemeni sovereignty as a “fixed principle” and declared that “any hand that reaches out to violate Yemen’s sovereignty will be cut off, whether it is Saudi, Iranian, or otherwise.”

It is still unclear how the new Saudi-Yemeni campaign will differ from the last one. The Houthis have made significant gains on the battlefield in recent weeks and have substantially developed their military capabilities over the past few years.

“It’s an open question if the Saudis and their Yemeni allies are any more capable of success on the battlefield versus the Houthis than the last time they took up this fight,” said Dan Shapiro, a former top Mideast official in the Pentagon.

But it is clear that the Houthis “can do some damage in Saudi Arabia,” he added.

The Yemeni government and the Houthis have been engaged in fierce battles in recent weeks, after the militia took control of the country’s Red Sea coast, increasing pressure on shipping routes and energy markets.

The Houthis and Saudi Arabia have also attacked each other directly.

Mr. al-Alimi’s remarks appeared to end any hope that a truce would be reached soon, saying that the military operations would continue “until the country is liberated.”

The Houthis also say that they are fighting to liberate Yemen, and have dismissed government fighters as Saudi mercenaries. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said in a statement on Sunday that the group’s fighters “will not stop carrying out further painful operations against the Saudi enemy.”

Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when the Houthis took over the capital, Sanaa, and forced out the government. A Saudi-led military coalition intervened on behalf of the government but failed to defeat the Houthis, who created a de facto state in northern Yemen.

A truce in 2022 established a fragile peace, until the conflict reignited this year.

The Houthis have accused Saudi Arabia of launching hundreds of airstrikes in their territory in recent weeks, most of which Saudi Arabia has not acknowledged.

But the Saudi government’s involvement is integral to the Yemeni government’s military campaign, analysts say. Much of the Yemeni government operates from Riyadh, and Saudi officials assert a significant say over many matters inside Yemen.

“You can’t ignore the fact that this is probably happening with the Saudis,” said Adam Baron, a fellow focused on Yemen at New America, a Washington-based research group. He added that Mr. al-Alimi’s announcement echoed previous government efforts to “put more of a Yemeni face on joint military actions.”

In his statement, Maj. General al-Maliki, the Saudi spokesman, said that the Houthis had targeted Saudi ships and cities across Saudi Arabia and that the militia posed a threat to the freedom of navigation as well as regional and international security.

The kingdom will “stand with Yemen” until Yemen’s state and institutions are restored, and the threat posed by the militia is ended, he added.

The latest cycle of violence began in July, after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa’s airport. The Houthis responded by launching drone and ballistic-missile attacks inside Saudi Arabia. They also declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, a key alternative route for oil shipments from Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters, during the Iran war.

The Houthis have made significant gains on the battlefield since the fighting resumed, including seizing territory beside the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a choke point near the southern tip of the Red Sea.

On Sunday, the Houthis moved closer to encircling Taiz, one of Yemen’s largest cities. Their forces captured Al-Turbah, a government-held town south of Taiz on the main road linking the city to Aden, the temporary seat of Yemen’s government, according to two Yemeni officials who requested anonymity to discuss sensitive military deployments.

Control of the town gives the Houthis control over a crucial supply route and leaves Taiz increasingly isolated. The city is at a strategic crossroads between Houthi-held northern Yemen, the government-controlled south and the Red Sea coast — making it a major prize for both sides.

“We remain anxious and afraid, fearing that the Houthis may enter the city,” said Ala’a, a Taiz resident who asked that only his first name be used because of possible reprisals. “It is the first time I have seen my neighbors’ children still awake at 3 a. m. because of the bombardment.”

On Saturday, the Houthis claimed a missile and drone attack had caused fires at a facility owned by Aramco, the Saudi state-controlled energy company, in Riyadh. Videos verified by The New York Times showed a fire at an oil refinery in the city belonging to the company.

Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, rejected the Houthi account in comments to the Saudi-owned newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat, calling the group’s claim to have targeted Riyadh “misleading.”

Houthi-run media reported that Saudi Arabia had carried out a fresh attack on Sanaa, the Yemeni capital. Saudi officials did not comment.

The new fighting has compounded the humanitarian crisis in Yemen. More than 800 people have been killed since early August, according to the World Health Organization, while the World Food Program says more than 150,000 people have been displaced.

Shuaib Almosawa, Euan Ward and Dylan Collins contributed reporting.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U. S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

After Week of Turmoil at Cornell, a Heavy Cloud Hangs Over Student Life

The New York Times October 04, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

As the weekend arrived, much of the nightlife in the upstate New York college town was subdued. But there were still some students looking to cut loose.

By Maia Coleman

Maia Coleman reported on Cornell University’s nightlife scene from Ithaca, N. Y.

Weekend descended, somewhat reluctantly, on Cornell University.

As the evening sun set on Ithaca, N. Y., students across campus dropped their backpacks and headed for the doors. Some lingered over beers at quiet cafes. Others swiped on mascara and laced up their boots, headed for the noise of the city’s bar scene. Still others stayed tucked out of sight in the library’s dense stacks.

But by all accounts, it was a weekend like none other.

As new information emerged this week about Cornell’s internal investigation into allegations of a 2024 sexual assault on campus, the Ivy League university has been consumed by the incident, its tentacles reaching nearly every corner of the sprawling upstate New York campus.

A wave of anger and horror has gripped the school, as students question the university’s handling of sexual assault allegations against seven male students at the Chi Phi fraternity house, and what they see as its failure, both then and now, to properly meet the moment.

There have been public meetings. Event moratoriums. Informal gatherings of support. There have pleas for accountability and university statements that have only ignited more anger. And there have been conversations, seemingly endless ones, in classrooms and living rooms, over lunch and on the phone.

Earlier this week, fraternity presidents voted to suspend nightlife for the weekend, scrambling plans on a campus where Greek culture has long been a key, if troubled, fixture. Off-campus gatherings and trips to bars in Ithaca’s downtown lulled, too.

Still, after a week of revelations that seemed to bring the university to a halt, students, from eager-eyed freshman to world-weary seniors, grappled with how to spend their nights off.

“It felt like you had to take a break from it — the story has kind of been all- consuming,” Hal Stokes, a Cornell senior, said from his perch at a metal table behind Collegetown Bagels, a local hangout that serves food and coffee and operates a small bar. Mr. Stokes said he had come to the cafe with his friend, Anna Diorio, in search of a low-key night.

Around him, in a courtyard behind the shop, students chatted over glasses of pale pink sangria and plastic cups of beer. The mood was mellow, tired even, though still warm under the glow of string lights above.

“I think that it’s going to be a quieter year,” he said, reflecting on the pause on Greek life this weekend. “The vibe is different, at least for us. I would be very surprised if in a week, two weeks, three weeks, we were back to normal.”

“It’s hard to guess, though,” Ms. Diorio interjected. “Given how Cornell seems to respond to these situations, I wouldn’t be totally surprised if they didn’t enforce any regulatory things on Greek life.”

Nearby, dozens of students huddled together, debriefing the week. Most said that a sense of heaviness felt across campus had drawn them to their closest friends and roommates, rather than large parties. That, combined with the start of preliminary exams and the approach of fall break next week, had kept plans light.

But many said they couldn’t remember a weekend on campus this quiet — at least not since Nov. 8, 2024, when Cornell sent out an email alerting the student body that a female student had reported being sexually assaulted.

Despite the cloud hanging over campus, Ms. Diorio said she was still trying to find moments of levity this weekend.

“I really do think people are just, we’re living our lives,” she said. “Life moves on.”

One block away, on Eddy Street, evidence of that life was everywhere.

Outside two bars on the block, a growing crowd of students surged the width of the sidewalks, waiting to squeeze through the cramped doors. Young women in made-up faces zigzagged gleefully through the mass to find their friends. Young men waved vapes and, in one case, an inflatable beach ball, high in the air. They laughed. They gossiped loudly about their love interests and their hopes for the night.

The crowd, some students said, seemed larger than usual and more diverse. Members of fraternities who would normally throw parties seemed to have flocked to the area to blow off steam, as had several upperclassmen. The energy was high and tinged with a certain intensity.

“It’s so packed,” a group of girls could be heard saying as they made their way toward the gaggle of students.

In downtown Ithaca, where a smattering of bars typically draw students at night, things were notably quieter.

Just before 1 a. m., at Moonies Bar & Nightclub, neon lights flashed and bass lines rumbled into a deserted room. The bar is usually filled with students from Cornell and Ithaca College, which is a mile south of the city’s downtown. In her lawsuit, Jane Doe claimed she made an early stop there on the night of the assault and was served alcohol, even though she was underage.

But on Friday, two women, clad in boots and black outfits, bobbed and swayed on an empty dance floor. Two men floated around the room. A bartender said about half the number of usual patrons had come in.

“I’ve heard people say they’re being more cautious,” Sasha Belogortsev, a Cornell senior, said after emerging from Lot 10, a nearby nightclub.

Others said the sudden spotlight of national attention on Moonies and nearby establishments had made students more reluctant to visit.

Back on campus, outside the black-trimmed Tudor that was once home to the Chi Phi fraternity before it was barred from campus, a small commotion interrupted the quiet night.

A group of young men standing side by side stared up at the house, yelling and cursing at the defunct fraternity and the seven former members whom Jane Doe accused of assault. One of the men threatened to throw a rock through a window before his companions hustled him away.

The group moved on. But when they crested the hill, the man hurled a small rock down the center of the empty street.

It tumbled down, and down, past the thicket of trees, the house and all it has come to represent.

Maia Coleman is a reporter for The Times covering the New York Police Department and criminal justice in the New York area.
