Iran’s Top Security Official Warns of Dire Economic Crisis

The New York Times October 04, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The rare admission from Mohsen Rezaei, the security chief, came weeks after the U. S. tightened sanctions and its naval blockade.

By Erika SolomonSanam Mahoozi and Zane Irwin

Erika Solomon is the Iran bureau chief.

Iran’s national security adviser has warned that the rapidly deteriorating economy has plunged the country into one of the most difficult periods in its history.

Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s top security official, made the rare admission on Saturday at a high-level government meeting about how to stabilize the economy after more than seven months of war.

Iran’s currency, the rial, has plummeted since the United States and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. The decline has accelerated sharply in recent weeks, since the United States ratcheted up sanctions and enforced a naval blockade. That has made imports more expensive and deepened a longstanding cost of living crisis that sparked nationwide protests last December that the security forces crushed with deadly force.

Analysts say the U. S. naval blockade has also largely prevented Iran from exporting oil, depriving the country of its main source of revenue and causing a fuel crisis.

Mohsen Paknejad, the oil minister who said in July that Iran would continue exporting oil despite U. S. sanctions, resigned on Sunday. Seyed Mehdi Tabatabaei, a spokesman for President Masoud Pezeshkian, said on social media that Hamid Bovard, managing director of Iran’s national oil company, would be Mr. Paknejad’s interim replacement.

In recent days, government and private sector employees, including nurses and teachers, have taken to social media to say they were quitting their jobs because their salaries could no longer support them. Iranian local media has reported that retired government employees have held protests in the past few weeks because they said they had not received their full pensions.

In addition to Mr. Rezaei, the government meeting on Saturday included Mr. Pezeshkian and other senior Iranian ministers, according to state media.

State news outlets in Iran did not provide direct quotations of Mr. Rezaei’s comments. But Iran’s state news agency, IRNA, reported that he “described the circumstances as among the most difficult periods the country has faced” and told the meeting that Iran’s security council would provide whatever support it could.

Mr. Pezeshkian acknowledged the worsening economic conditions in a statement on social media on Saturday and said that the government “has adopted a new posture to manage the special conditions.” He did not specify what that would mean in practice.

The economic pressure on Iran has intensified as negotiations between Tehran and Washington have stalled, with both sides refusing to make concessions and signaling that they can outlast the other’s tolerance for economic pain.

In recent weeks, U. S. officials have argued that they are winning the economic standoff. Recent data showed oil shipments from the Middle East have returned almost to prewar levels.

But the price of oil remains higher than before the conflict, and some analysts have warned the crisis for the global economy is far from resolved. The strait remains dangerous to navigate and damage to energy infrastructure has hampered refining capacity and natural gas exports. Iran’s leaders hope that the pressure could hurt President Trump ahead of the U. S. midterm elections, according to analysts.

In addition to the blockade, the United States has blocked most civilian air travel between Iran and the rest of the world, adding a new layer of economic isolation that some sanctions experts have said could hurt critical imports, including medicine.

Shirin Hakim contributed reporting.

Erika Solomon is The Times’s bureau chief for Iran and Iraq.

Zane Irwin is an international reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Democrats Lead Governor Races Deep in Republican Territory, Polls Show

The New York Times October 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Democratic advantages in the races for governor in Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska reflect deep unhappiness with President Trump and the economy. A Republican leads in Kansas.

By Anna GriffinRuth Igielnik and Sejal Govindarao

One month until Election Day, voter dissatisfaction with the economy, concerns about political extremism and frustration with President Trump have Democrats within reach of flipping four Republican-held governorships, opening a wide lead in Iowa and an expanding advantage in Ohio among likely voters, according to new polls by The New York Times and Siena University.

In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican fixture in the state for decades, is now narrowly behind his Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa.

The Democratic candidate also has an advantage in the race for governor of Alaska. The only place surveyed where the Republican is ahead in the campaign for the governor’s office in Kansas, now held by a retiring Democrat.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Sept. Surveys

Among likely voters. Shaded areas represent the margin of error.

Note: Alaska’s result is from the final round of a ranked-choice simulation.

Based on New York Times/Siena polls of 504 voters in Alaska conducted Sept. 24 to Oct. 1, 606 voters in Iowa conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 1, 605 voters in Kansas conducted Sept. 22 to 30, 616 voters in Ohio conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 1 and 615 voters in Texas conducted Sept. 21 to 30.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

The polls also show Democrats with an advantage in the Senate in these states, with Democrats ahead in Texas and Alaska, and with the edge in Ohio, while the races in Kansas and Iowa are neck-and-neck.

While national attention has fixated on the fight for control of Congress, governorships will be important heading into a wide open presidential election in 2028. Not only will governors influence the electoral process, they will help shape the redistricting wars that are likely to spill into 2027 and beyond.

The polling results underscore how Democrats have been able to push into states that have traditionally favored Republicans, as voters have soured on Mr. Trump amid frustration over the economy, rising gas prices and a deeply unpopular war in Iran.

Still, the polls show that even as many of the Republican candidates for governor are at a disadvantage, they are outrunning the difficult political environment. Mr. Trump’s approval rating stands at just 40 percent across the five states. In four of five states surveyed, the Republican candidates for governor are doing better than the president’s approval ratings.

Democrats, meantime, are boosted by broadly well-liked candidates who are, for the most part, seen as more politically moderate than their Republican opponents.

In Texas, for example, just 28 percent of voters worried that Ms. Hinojosa was too far to the left, compared to 45 percent who were concerned Mr. Abbott was too far to the right.

Gov. Abbott was expected to have an easy path toward re-election in a state that hasn’t put a Democrat in the governor’s office since Ann Richards, who served one term before losing to George W. Bush in 1994.

Ms. Hinojosa, an Austin lawyer and former school-board president, has tried to turn the election away from national culture-war issues toward affordability, support for public schools and a backlash against the rapid construction of power- and water-hungry data centers.

Mr. Abbott retains an enormous financial advantage, but since a Times/Siena poll in June, Ms. Hinojosa has picked up support among white voters, Hispanic voters, voters younger than 45 and independent voters.

Mark Rios, a 38-year-old Republican from Dallas, said he is supporting Ms. Hinojosa because he wants a fresh pair of eyes in office. He said he supported Mr. Trump in three elections but has seen higher gasoline prices since the president took office. The economy seems to be getting worse, he said.

“There needs to be a change,” Mr. Rios said.

Ms. Hinojosa is viewed far more positively than negatively in the state, though about a third of voters said they had not heard of or did not yet have an opinion of Ms. Hinojosa. By comparison, Texans know Mr. Abbott well after 11 years as governor and another 12 as attorney general. Forty-seven percent of voters viewed him positively, and another 47 percent viewed him negatively.

“It’s baffling to hear him say, ‘Oh, I’m fighting this and this and this.’ Dude, you’ve been there more than a decade, and your party has been in charge for forever. You’re the problem,” said Jeanette Fierro, a Democrat and hospital marketing director in Odessa, Texas.

Ms. Fierro, the daughter of immigrants from northern Mexico, said she knew little about Ms. Hinojosa when the campaigns began but believes Texans, particularly Hispanic voters, will embrace her if she can find the money to compete: “The more I have learned, as a Latina and a single mom, the more I like,” Ms. Fierro said. “She’s a chingona, you know? A badass.”

The widest Democratic lead was in Iowa, where Rob Sand, the state auditor and the only Democrat holding statewide office, holds an advantage over Republican businessman and farmer Zach Lahn to succeed Gov. Kim Reynolds, a conservative Republican who is retiring after nine years in office.

Mr. Sand has built his campaign around a bipartisan persona and a promise to address government accountability and the economy. He’s benefiting from high voter appeal: more than half of Iowa’s likely voters view him positively, including more than 20 percent of Republicans.

Since June, Mr. Sand has grown his support across nearly every demographic group. He is now ahead among voters over 65, a group that typically tilts Republican.

Iowa hasn’t elected a Democratic governor since 2006.

In Ohio, which also hasn’t voted in a Democratic governor in 20 years, a summer of bad news for the president and his party has taken a toll on the Republican candidate for governor.

The June Times/Siena poll showed billionaire pharmaceutical entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy and the Democratic former state health director, Amy Acton, neck-and-neck. Now she has an advantage, including 11 percent of Mr. Trump’s 2024 supporters who say they intend to vote for Ms. Acton. She also has a significant lead with independent voters.

Alexandria Hensley, 27, described herself as conservative and voted for Mr. Trump two years ago, but said she wants a governor who will work toward “the middle ground.”

A domestic violence worker from Cincinnati, Ms. Hensley said her concerns were less about Mr. Ramaswamy and more about the economy, the spread of data centers and politics broadly. She said social issues such as whether transgender girls should be allowed to play on girls’ teams never mattered to her as much as politicians seem to think.

”Everyone seems to focus so much on what we disagree on, when I think we all tend to agree on more basic things,” she said.

In Alaska, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins led a crowded August primary field and has maintained that advantage over three Republicans, Bernadette Wilson, a businesswoman and conservative radio host; Dave Bronson, a former Anchorage mayor; and Treg Taylor, a former Alaska attorney general, the poll found.

A former state legislator who helped lead a bipartisan coalition in the statehouse and won repeatedly in a district carried by Mr. Trump, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins has promised his cabinet will include a balance of Democrats, Republicans and independents. All three of the Republican candidates are populist conservatives in the mold of Mr. Trump. Alaska’s current Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, is barred from re-election by term limits.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, but while Democrats have united around a single candidate, Republicans have not. Ms. Wilson urged Republicans to coalesce around one person, fearing that multiple candidates will benefit the Democrat. Mr. Bronson and Mr. Taylor declined, arguing that Republicans can use the system to their advantage as long as their potential voters don’t rank Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins.

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 504 voters in Alaska conducted Sept. 24 to Oct. 1. The first column shows initial vote choice, including undecided voters. The remaining columns simulate ranked-choice voting, excluding undecided voters, where each round eliminates the last-place candidate and shifts those votes to their supporters' next choice. Percentages reflect only active ballots.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

Anita Baker, a retired U. S. Army lieutenant colonel in Eagle River, Alaska, who supports Ms. Wilson, said she fears her fellow conservatives won’t understand the system. “You could add a couple of expletives to how worried I am,” she said.

Ms. Baker said she fears the damage a Democratic governor could do and still supports Mr. Trump.

“He might say things that make my eyebrows go up or make me scratch my head sometimes, but the policies are there,” she said.

The Times/Siena poll, which simulated the ranked-choice voting process, showed the three Republicans collectively winning a larger percentage of initial responses but Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins with a slight lead over Ms. Wilson after three rounds. He’s trying to become the youngest governor in Alaska history at 37 and the first Democrat elected to lead the state since 1998.

Republicans can hope for their own flip in Kansas, where outgoing Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, won tight races in 2018 and 2022 despite the state’s conservative leanings. The Times/Siena poll showed the Republican state senate president, Ty Masterson, with a four-percentage-point lead over the Democrat, fellow state lawmaker Cindy Holscher.

Chris Martsolf, a 53-year-old commercial general contractor from Wichita, Kan., said Republicans are about as disorganized as Democrats these days. But after eight years of Democratic control, the governorship needs to go back to Republicans, he said.

“If we don’t win midterms, there probably will be no more Republican Party,” he said.

Voters in Kansas were the least likely to say their state is headed in the wrong direction, and a majority of Republicans say the economy in Kansas is excellent or good.

Mr. Masterson also benefits from some crossover appeal. He has the support of 8 percent of voters who say they also plan to support the Democrat in the Senate race, the Rev. Adam Hamilton.

Right now, Republicans hold 26 of the nation’s 50 governorships, so this year’s elections could tip the balance of power in statehouses. States operate independently, and the political philosophies within either major party can vary greatly from state to state. A Democrat on the liberal West Coast is very different than one in the Midwest or Southeast.

Still, Democratic organizers believe holding a majority of governorships would give them an additional bulwark against Mr. Trump on policies that cross state lines, including immigration enforcement, House gerrymandering and the rollback of health care funding and environmental regulations.

Ruth Igielnik is a Times polling editor who conducts polls and analyzes and reports on the results.

Sejal Govindarao is a national reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Why Kansas Has Suddenly Moved to Center of the Fight for Senate Control

The New York Times October 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The state hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century. Economic challenges during President Trump’s second term, as well as other factors, have put it in play.

By Tim Balk

Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since before World War II.

But this year, this reliably Republican state has unexpectedly lurched toward the center of the battle for control of the Senate.

Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, a first-term Republican, is in such a competitive race that the top super PAC for Senate Republicans is diverting millions of dollars to the state that it would prefer to be spending in traditional battlegrounds.

With a month until Election Day, Mr. Marshall and his Democratic challenger, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, are roughly tied at 45 percent each, according to a New York Times/Siena University poll released this weekend.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report still grades the race as leaning toward Republicans. But Democrats have become more optimistic, and Republicans are increasingly nervous.

Here are three reasons Kansas is competitive:

Kansas’s farming-heavy economy has been buffeted by challenges both of the president’s making and out of his control.

Mr. Trump’s war with Iran has driven up the costs of gasoline and diesel.

The president, as part of his trade wars, has allowed a flood of ground beef imports into the United States with lower tariffs, squeezing Kansas cattle farmers.

And the administration’s immigration crackdown has rattled ranchers who rely on immigrants to keep the cattle supply chain moving.

Then there’s a deepening drought in the state that has hampered yields of soybeans, wheat and corn.

Put it all together, and the state’s farmers are in an anxious mood.

Mr. Hamilton is a strong fund-raiser from a well-populated part of the state — near Kansas City — who has led a politically diverse, thousands-strong congregation.

He is running on a centrist platform focused on getting the United States out of the Iran war, unwinding the president’s tariffs and regulating data centers.

Mr. Hamilton has deep roots in Kansas. His great-great-grandparents settled in Dickinson County, in the middle of the state, in the 19th century.

Among his backers are two Republican former Kansas governors: Bill Graves and Mike Hayden.

Arch Naramore, who won a fifth of the vote in a Republican Senate primary challenge to Mr. Marshall in August, has endorsed Mr. Hamilton, too.

Mr. Hamilton has positioned himself as someone who will “lead from the middle.” Mr. Marshall’s allies are trying to counter that pitch by branding Mr. Hamilton as an “extremist.”

Mr. Hamilton is less likely to be seen as “extreme” than Mr. Marshall, according to the Times/Siena poll.

Mr. Marshall has had a series of headaches.

Last month, The Times reported that he had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist and routinely charged patients an 18 percent annual interest rate. That has become a campaign issue.

Then there is the issue of his alignment with Mr. Trump, who has grown deeply unpopular in Kansas as economic conditions have worsened. Fifty-five percent of Kansas voters say they disapprove of the president, compared with 40 percent who approve, according to the Times/Siena poll.

Mr. Marshall is campaigning on an argument that he gets results for Kansas. His opponents say he has not stood up enough for Kansas against Mr. Trump.

Mr. Marshall has sought some distance from Mr. Trump. The senator has criticized the administration’s immigration enforcement actions, and his representatives have not said if he would be open to campaigning with the president. (Mr. Marshall campaigned with Vice President JD Vance last month.)

Still, half of Kansas voters say they think Mr. Marshall would support Mr. Trump too much, the Times/Siena survey found.

The Only Woman Charged With War Crimes in the Balkan Wars Has Died

The New York Times October 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Biljana Plavsic, a Bosnian Serb, pleaded guilty to one count of crimes against humanity. She later recanted and said she “would do the same again.”

By Andrew Higgins

Reporting from Belgrade, Serbia.

Biljana Plavsic, a Bosnian Serb biologist and ultranationalist political leader during the Balkan wars of the 1990s who expressed remorse and pleaded guilty to one count of crimes against humanity but later recanted and said she “would do the same again,” has died in Belgrade, the capital of Serbia. She was 96.

The death of Ms. Plavsic was announced on Thursday by Serbian state media. No other details were provided.

Ms. Plavsic, a former professor at Sarajevo University who studied in Zagreb, New York, London and Prague and wrote more than 100 scientific papers, became notorious in the 1990s for applying biology to politics when the multiethnic state of Yugoslavia disintegrated. She declared Bosnia’s Muslim population “deformed genetic material” and railed against mixed marriages, common before the war, as leading to “the degeneration of Serb nationality.”

Often coldly indifferent to the suffering of non-Serbs, she was known as the Iron Lady of the Balkans, a nickname inspired by Soviet descriptions of Britain’s Margaret Thatcher. But the name Ms. Plavsic relished most was a tribute that Serb fighters daubed on the side of their tanks: Empress.

“She was educated, a professor but a real hard-line nationalist,” recalled Laura Silber, the co-author of “The Death of Yugoslavia,” who interviewed Ms. Plavsic several times during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia. “She was prim and proper — school marmish in demeanor — so it was especially shocking to hear the ugly nationalist rhetoric coming out of her mouth.”

Olivera Simic, an Australian scholar from Bosnia who interviewed Ms. Plavsic for hundreds of hours in her later years, remembered her as highly intelligent but often blind to the suffering of non-Serbs. “She was not a monster and would express from time to time that she felt sorry for everyone — and then quickly start talking about Serb victims and cry over them,” Ms. Simic said in a telephone interview.

For nearly four years, Ms. Plavsic served as vice president of Republika Srpska, a Serb enclave in Bosnia that declared itself a separate state in 1992 and began a program of ethnic cleansing aimed at driving out Muslims, Croats and other non-Serb residents. In that role she worked closely with Radovan Karadzic, the self-declared state’s president, who in 2016 was convicted of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity by a United Nations tribunal.

She rejected the term “ethnic cleansing” in her interviews with Ms. Simic, a law professor at Griffith University in Australia, describing the separation of different peoples as a “natural process.” According to Ms. Simic, Ms. Plavsic believed that “everyone should live with their own tribe” and, as a result, “willingly turned a blind eye” to the suffering this caused when ethnic groups were separated at gunpoint “because she was only interested in protecting her own tribe.”

Testifying as a witness at The Hague trial of Serbia’s wartime leader Slobodan Milosevic, Vojislav Seselj, the founder of a far-right Serb political party, who was also charged with war crimes, said that Ms. Plavsic “held very extremist positions during the war, insufferably extremist, even for me, and they bothered even me as a declared Serb nationalist.”

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

After the war ended, Ms. Plavsic muted her anti-Muslim fervor, broke with Mr. Karadzic, accusing him of corruption, and in 1996 took over as president of Republika Srpska with support from the West, which viewed her as a partner for peace.

She was for a time hailed as a symbol of reconciliation after she expressed remorse during a 2002 sentencing hearing in The Hague. “I have now come to the belief and accept the fact that many thousands of innocent people were the victims of an organized, systematic effort to remove Muslims and Croats from the territory claimed by Serbs,” she said.

Serbs, driven by “an obsession to never become victims,” had “allowed ourselves to become victimizers,” she told the court.

Despite her strident ethnonationalism during the war, Ms. Plavsic later won plaudits in Washington and other Western capitals for supporting a peace settlement brokered by the United States in 1995.

Madeleine Albright, who served as secretary of state during President Bill Clinton’s second term, praised Ms. Plavsic at her sentencing hearing for breaking with Bosnian Serb leaders who opposed the peace deal. “She stood up for that at times when it was very difficult, when there were those who wanted to destroy the Dayton Accords,” Ms. Albright said at the 2002 hearing.

Ms. Plavsic was the only woman among more than 150 people indicted by the international court for war crimes in former Yugoslavia. In 2003, she received an 11-year sentence for persecution, a crime against humanity, as part of a plea bargain that allowed her to avoid a trial on charges of complicity in genocide.

In contrast with Mr. Karadzic, who went into hiding for more than a decade and, after his arrest, boycotted parts of his trial in The Hague, Ms. Plavsic surrendered voluntarily and cooperated with the tribunal.

After initially pleading not guilty, she later pleaded guilty on one count, acknowledging that Serb forces had committed crimes and her own responsibility for these. “The knowledge that I am responsible for such human suffering and for soiling the character of my people will always be with me,” she told the court.

The judge said that Ms. Plavsic had not conceived or planned the violent Serbian campaign of ethnic separation that killed tens of thousands of Muslims and Croats and expelled many more from their lands with “great brutality,” but that she had embraced, supported and contributed to it. “This is a crime of utmost gravity,” he said.

Victims of the war and some human rights groups criticized her sentence as too lenient. But others said the major issue in Ms. Plavsic’s confession and guilty plea was that they would make denials by other Serbian leaders more difficult.

“In a region where denial and revisionism are central and where the tribunal is seen with skepticism, Ms. Plavsic’s gesture is striking,” Alex Boraine, a member of South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, told the court.

Fellow Serb nationalists, appalled by the confession in The Hague, denounced her as a traitor for deviating from the narrative that Serbs were innocent victims. They embraced her as a hero when she later recanted and declared herself and Serbs blameless.

The grip that the narrative of innocence still holds on many Serbs was on ghoulish display in September when thousands, including Serbian government ministers and the son of President Aleksandar Vucic, turned out in Belgrade for the funeral of Ratko Mladic, a Bosnian Serb general convicted of genocide and known as the Butcher of Bosnia.

Ms. Plavsic’s contrition, if ever more than a ploy to avoid a lengthy trial and escape genocide charges, did not last long. Released early from prison in 2009 for good behavior, she settled in Belgrade and quickly retreated from what Ms. Simic, the author of the 2025 book “Madam War Criminal,” concluded was “fake remorse” in The Hague.

Divorced with no children, she lived alone in a modest Belgrade apartment decorated with Orthodox Christian icons and a wooden cross made for her by a fellow inmate convicted of genocide for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre.

“She believes she sacrificed herself for ‘her people’ and did not show any ability to critically reflect on her actions but persistently justified and rationalized her behavior, which she always perceived as highly ethical, moral and legitimate,” Ms Simic wrote in her book. “She told me on many occasions during our conversations that if the circumstances would arise again she would most likely respond the same way.”

Ms. Plavsic’s case in The Hague “raised fundamental questions about the delivery of international justice,” said Philippe Sands, a British human rights lawyer. He represented Croatia, also formerly part of Yugoslavia, in an unsuccessful genocide claim it brought against Serbia.

“On one level, justice was done,” he added. “She was convicted and did time.”

“But at another level the fact that justice was done catalyzed a whole other set of frictions, which nobody really thought through when the system was created,” Mr. Sands said, referring to the codification of genocide as a separate crime under international law after World War II.

The classification of certain crimes as genocide but others in different categories of criminality, he said, “ends up with a sort of Champions League of horrors” that leaves communities angry and resentful if horrors they suffered are not judged as “genocide.”

The debate rages in former Yugoslavia, where the 1995 massacre of Bosnian Muslims at Srebrenica has been legally recognized as genocide but atrocities committed by Serb forces against Croats in Vukovar in 1991 and by Croats against Bosnian Muslims in Mostar during a 1993-94 siege have been classified as war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Biljana Plavsic was born on July 7, 1930, in Tuzla, then part of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. She grew up in Sarajevo, to which her affluent family moved when she was 4. Her father was a prominent scientist who had been educated in Vienna, and she was raised on books and stories celebrating an infamous relative — Gavrilo Princip, a Serb nationalist who precipitated World War I in 1914 by assassinating Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo.

Eleven years old when Nazi Germany invaded Bosnia in 1941, she witnessed Serbs being executed in the street and lost dozens of relatives to brutal ethnic purges carried out by the Ustashe, a Croatian fascist group that led the Independent State of Croatia, a puppet state of Germany formed during World War II.

After the defeat of the Nazis, Bosnia became one of six republics in the newly declared Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Despite her family’s hostility to communism, Ms. Plavsic, who never joined the party, embarked on a highly successful academic career focused on plant virology. This included two years of botany research in the 1970s at Cornell University.

A popular biology professor in Sarajevo, she had a reputation as an exacting but fair-minded scholar who held all students, no matter what their ethnicity, to the same high standards. Elected dean of Sarajevo University’s faculty of natural sciences and mathematics in 1987, she turned to politics in 1990 when she became the Serb member of a collective, multiethnic presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then still part of Yugoslavia.

When Slovenia and Croatia, two other Yugoslav republics, broke away to declare independence in 1991, Bosnian Muslims began demanding their own state, too — a prospect that terrified Ms. Plavsic and many other Serbs.

In interviews with Ms. Simic, the Australia-based scholar, before her death, Ms. Plavsic often referred to 1991 as “the continuation of 1941,” a replay of the World War II conflict between Nazi-aligned Croats and antifascist Serbs that, she believed, “never finished.”

Convinced that conflict between different ethnic communities in Bosnia was inevitable after a March 1992 attack on a Serb wedding procession outside an Orthodox Church in Sarajevo, she left Sarajevo for Pale, a predominantly Serb town in the nearby mountains that served as the capital of Republika Srpska, the newly declared Serb statelet.

From there she helped organize what she called “humanitarian work” that aided refugees but also Serb soldiers and paramilitary gangs involved in clearing non-Serbs from ethnically mixed areas and in shelling Sarajevo, which was clamped in a siege that would last more than three years. Among those she worked with was a notorious gangster and soccer hooligan turned paramilitary leader known as Arkan, whose Serb Volunteer Guard, known as Arkan’s Tigers, committed multiple atrocities.

She told Ms. Simic years later in Belgrade that everything she did was motivated by a desire to avoid “the extinction of the Serb people.” Bosnian Muslims, Serbs and Croats all suffered and, Ms Simic said, Ms. Plavsic’s obsession with crimes against her own people was part of a bigger problem across former Yugoslavia.

“Everyone talks about their own victims, never their own perpetrators — no one,” Ms. Simic said. “This is the problem. Everyone wants to talk about their victimhood, never their perpetrators. They think nobody acknowledges crimes done against them, no matter how big or small.”

Andrew Higgins is the East and Central Europe bureau chief for The Times based in Warsaw.

As Democrats’ Midterm Dreams Grow, South Carolina Becomes a Test of the Possible

The New York Times October 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat, is hoping to defeat Senator Darline Graham. Even some of her most ardent supporters sense that her bid is a long shot.

By Emily Davies

Reported from farmers markets, playgrounds, grocery stores and a shrimp processing plant across the greater Columbia and Charleston areas.

Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democrat running for Senate in South Carolina, walked along a dock just off the coast of Charleston as Cindy Tarvin explained how her company’s shrimping season had been crippled by the high cost of diesel.

“We live on hope,” said Ms. Tarvin.

“Same,” said Dr. Andrews.

She might need it. Dr. Andrews, a pediatrician, is running for a seat that no Democratic candidate this century has come within nine points of winning. Even some of her most ardent supporters, in what may prove to be the most favorable midterm for Democrats in years, sense that her bid is a long shot.

Yet there is also some reason for optimism. Dr. Andrews is running against Senator Darline Graham, a political novice facing skeptics within her own party, at a time when the political environment is rapidly deteriorating for Republicans. Democrats are tied or in the lead in Senate races in five reliably Republican states, according to new New York Times/Siena University polls. That puts victories in Kansas, Mississippi and South Carolina within the party’s sight lines, if at their outer reaches.

Dr. Andrews will emerge next month as either a symbol of a massive Democratic comeback, or a cautionary tale of the limits of progressive optimism. Two weeks ago, the Cook Political Report shifted the race from solidly Republican to likely Republican. Only two years ago, Mr. Trump carried South Carolina by more than 17 points.

“I’m very hopeful,” said Daniel Chambers, 72, a retired program director at a hospital who attended a fund-raiser for Dr. Andrews on Tuesday. “But I’m not expecting her to win.”

Voter anger over high prices caused by Mr. Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran exists in South Carolina, too.

At Tarvin Seafood, a local market in Mt. Pleasant, all of the shrimp trawlers were on the water for the first time in weeks. Diesel had gotten so expensive that some fishermen had adopted a new strategy of waiting to set out until the tide was powerful enough to propel them into the Atlantic Ocean.

“We just always hope that we can weather the storms,” said Ms. Tarvin, who wore a belt with shrimp on it. “But there’s no guarantee.”

There are structural disadvantages for any Democratic campaign here. The state is deeply conservative, and in this divided era, only a sliver of the electorate has been open in recent elections to crossing party lines.

Although Dr. Andrews’s campaign has out-raised and outspent Ms. Graham’s, the main super PAC for Democratic Senate candidates has not invested in the race. And Republicans have only just begun airing attack ads against Dr. Andrews. Some Democrats fear a reprise of 2020, when Jaime Harrison, a former state Democratic Party chair, mounted an energetic campaign against Senator Lindsey Graham, Ms. Graham’s brother who died in July, but finished 10 points behind him.

Dr. Andrews has been traversing the state for 18 months, promising to reverse President Trump’s policies that have caused prices to rise, with a particular emphasis on health costs and children’s health care. She has also softened her language on past positions that could alienate South Carolina’s conservative electorate, including transgender policies.

A fast-talking, denim-loving mother of three, she has pitched herself as an anti-Democratic Party Democrat, a pediatrician with a work ethic who loves her job but is willing to set it aside to help her state. If elected, she has vowed to leave the Senate after two terms.

In 2022, she ran for a House seat against Representative Nancy Mace and lost by more than 10 points.

“I feel more optimistic than ever that there’s enough people in South Carolina who are ready for change, who see in me someone who’s actually going to be an independent voice for South Carolina,” Dr. Andrews said in an interview on Thursday, sitting atop a cooler near the dock in Mt. Pleasant, where she lives with her children. In case voters see Ms. Graham as an emblem of change too, Dr. Andrews likes to remind them that she “was really handpicked by Washington.”

Ms. Graham, a longtime advocate for people with disabilities, decided to run for Senate in July, days after Gov. Henry McMaster of South Carolina appointed her to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term. During a televised debate in the primary election, Ms. Graham acknowledged that she was “not that informed on national security” — a stumble that tapped into voters’ concerns about her eligibility.

She won the bruising primary with a heavy assist from Mr. Trump, but not without scars. Representative Ralph Norman, vice chairman of the hard-line Freedom Caucus who lost to Ms. Graham in a two-person runoff, initially encouraged voters to write in his name before backing down and endorsing Ms. Graham.

Republicans, for their part, said they expected Ms. Graham to need a financial boost to secure a win in the end. Asked if there would be more spending on her behalf, an official close to the White House, speaking anonymously to talk candidly about the race, said that Ms. Graham’s “allies are monitoring the race closely and will make sure she wins.” A second Republican official said there were “conversations about getting more help for Darline.”

President Trump is scheduled to visit the state again later this month, the second official said, granted anonymity to discuss plans not yet made public. John Thune, the Senate majority leader, is also planning to visit the state before Election Day.

As Dr. Andrews has covered the state this fall, Ms. Graham has spent much of her time governing in Washington.

Mark Knoop, Ms. Graham’s campaign manager, stressed that Dr. Andrews has benefited from weeks without opposition on television and “is still losing.”

“Just imagine how those numbers look when voters meet the real Annie Andrews,” he said. “This is South Carolina.”

Ms. Graham’s campaign has introduced a website with a virtual game called “Dr. Annie’s Waiting Room,” highlighting Dr. Andrews’s more progressive stances: her past support for an assault weapons ban; desire to restore Roe v. Wade, which protected abortion rights; and past support for transgender people.

Ms. Graham has called Dr. Andrews “one of the most radical people that has ever been the nominee for a statewide office in South Carolina.”

Dr. Andrews has supported prescribing puberty blockers and hormone treatment for children, but she says she opposes gender-transition surgery for those under 18. She previously argued against a bill that barred transgender athletes from girls’ and women’s sports but said in an interview on Wednesday that she did not “support biological men playing in women’s sports.”

To win, Dr. Andrews will need to win over some Republicans and motivate the state’s Democratic Party base, which showed up in force amid a redistricting fight this summer. After record turnout in the primary election in June, the South Carolina legislature blocked Mr. Trump’s effort to eliminate the state’s only majority Black district, which has been held by Representative James E. Clyburn since 1993.

Mr. Clyburn, who is known for his ability to turn out the state’s Black voters, said in an interview on Thursday that he would do everything he could to help Dr. Andrews win. He has recorded a radio spot that has aired statewide and said he planned to publish videos, make calls and host events on her behalf.

“I do believe Annie Andrews has a good chance of winning,” Mr. Clyburn said. “I just go by my feeling, and my feelings are not without cause.”

South Carolina is one of the nation’s fastest-growing states, and both campaigns are hopeful that new voters will fall their way. Republicans point to the boom in the Myrtle Beach area as a sign that the G. O. P. base is growing. Democrats point to Hilton Head, which has attracted some left-leaning newcomers in recent years, as a beacon of hope.

“It’s the perfect time for a different type of campaign, a different type of candidate, so we’ll see if she can pull it out,” said Donovan Malloy, an attorney and Democratic operative, over dinner in Columbia. “I still have my doubts because it’s a red state, but it’s a changing state.”

Jim Hodges, the last Democratic governor to win an election in South Carolina, said the political environment reminded him of the year he triumphed, 1998.

“People were very dissatisfied with the incumbent party,” he said. “They wanted candidates who were focused on dinner table issues.”

He praised Dr. Andrews for running a campaign focused on those issues and generating sizable crowds at campaign events.

At a farmers’ market in North Charleston on Thursday, Carolyn Lecque, 81, handed out fliers encouraging people to register to vote. A lifelong Democrat and breast cancer survivor, Ms. Lecque said she was particularly excited about Dr. Andrews because of her focus on health care.

“I think she’ll challenge Robert Kennedy with all this craziness he comes out with, like about vaccines,” said Ms. Lecque, referring to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

If she gets the chance. After more than an hour in North Charleston, a historically Black city, Ms. Lecque had handed out a few fliers but had not registered anyone to vote.

Back on the dock in Mt. Pleasant, Ms. Tarvin, the shrimper, took a minute to ponder the question of whether Dr. Andrews could win. She looked at the candidate, who stayed after the press event to buy shrimp for her kids.

“This is South Carolina,” Ms. Tarvin said. “But I hope so.”

An earlier version of this article misstated how the Cook Political Report has rated the South Carolina Senate race. It moved the contest to likely Republican, not lean Republican.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Emily Davies is a political correspondent for The New York Times.

Galliano Was a Fiasco. Bob Mackie Would Sparkle.

The New York Times October 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By David Colman

Mr. Colman is a critic and a former Possessed columnist for The Times.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute has yet to announce a replacement for its Spring 2027 exhibition, which was originally supposed to celebrate John Galliano.

That plan went down in flames. It became clear that many influential people were not ready to forgive and forget the designer’s past antisemitic statements, despite the fact that he still gets work in the industry and is a longtime friend of Met trustee and Vogue grandee Anna Wintour’s.

After this P. R. fiasco, the Met and Ms. Wintour should instead pick an underappreciated crowd-pleaser who understood, decades ago, the celebrity-first, red-carpet look that has taken over fashion: Bob Mackie, the Sultan of Sequins, who died last month at 87.

Mr. Mackie became famous as a Hollywood costume designer, not a member of Ms. Wintour’s inner circle. As Cher, one of his most well-known clients, put it in the 2024 documentary “Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion,” “Bob did costumes, and fashion people looked down on him for some reason.”

He won nine Emmy Awards — including the very first one ever awarded for costume design, which he shared with his then-partner Ray Aghayan — and was nominated for 23 others. He designed showstopping dresses for generations of performers from the 1960s to the 2020s: Tina Turner, Barbra Streisand, Dolly Parton. Madonna, Whitney Houston and Beyoncé. Some of his more comic expressions — including the Scarlett O’Hara curtain-rod parody dress he designed for Carol Burnett — are now in the Smithsonian. He designed the dress Cher wore to the 1986 Oscars after she was snubbed for her performance in “Mask.” “As you can see, I did receive my Academy booklet on how to dress like a serious actress,” Cher tartly quipped from the podium.

Mr. Mackie understood the viral-dress moment before there was an internet to spread it.

The fashion world just never quite accepted him as one of their own. He never had much success with ready-to-wear. In an oral history for Vogue, he recalled that the Council of Fashion Designers of America wanted to honor him with a prize in 2001: “They wanted to give me something, but they didn’t know what to do with me, so they gave me an award for fashion exuberance, which I still think is funny.”

“Costume designers have long been overlooked for the importance of their work in creating and influencing mainstream contemporary fashion,” the designer Tom Ford told Vogue. “I think he could never really get a footing in the fashion world,” his longtime design director, Joe McFate, also noted.

It’s time for Mr. Mackie to finally get his due.

Mr. Galliano and Mr. Mackie actually have a lot in common. Over their careers, they have both displayed technical brilliance, meticulous craftsmanship, wit and showmanship. But there are differences. Mr. Galliano is a part of the hierarchical fashion system, rooted in runway shows, haute couture, socialites, ready-to-wear collections, “It” bags, perfume launches and big advertising budgets. The single-designer shows mounted by the Costume Institute are usually more in step with Ms. Wintour’s runway-fashion-first perspective. More often than not, they spotlight a designer known for practicing haute couture — Alexander McQueen, Gianni Versace, Karl Lagerfeld, Coco Chanel.

One might argue that a man who has designed thousands of costumes for weekly television shows and made dresses that can show off (and stand up to) Tina Turner’s performances is practicing couture of the first order. It’s also worth noting that the Costume Institute (as its name suggests) has its roots in the theater world of the Lower East Side, not Paris. It was begun in 1937 as the Museum of Costume Art, led by the Neighborhood Playhouse founder Irene Lewisohn.

These days, the Costume Institute often wants to play in the pop-culture sandbox but can end up feeling like it’s been sanitized for the Bergdorf Goodman shopper. Outsider subcultures like “Punk” and “Camp” and “Superheroes” lose their grit and authenticity when they become themes. They sound fun and draw people in, but invariably feel prim and bloodless.

A Bob Mackie show could also help the tarnished profile of the Met Gala. The $100,000-a-ticket “party of the year” has started to seem to some people an absurdist display of modern-day wretched extravagance. That was brought into stark and unpopular relief when Jeff Bezos, the executive chair of Amazon, and his wife, Lauren Sánchez Bezos, were brought on as honorary co-chairs for this past spring’s gala, the theme of which was “Costume Art.”

Mr. Mackie is popular and populist. Both the Met and Ms. Wintour could use that. And unlike some of the head-scratching themes the Met has cooked up over the years (“Sleeping Beauties: Reawakening Fashion”; “About Time: Fashion and Duration”), a Mackie-themed Met Gala would be about the razzle-dazzle. It should be an easy sell to persuade someone like the self-professed showgirl Taylor Swift to host.

His dazzling kinetic dresses cost thousands of dollars and worked far better on dancing theatrical performers than idle cocktail guests. But in the business of show, he was an equal-opportunity glamorizer. His dresses were spectacularly flattering, get-out-of-the-way glam. You could be built like Bette Midler, or Tina Turner or Cher. What mattered was where you were going and how you looked when you got there. That is most true on today’s mother of all red carpets: the one at the Met Gala.

Another of Mr. Mackie’s clients, RuPaul, told Vogue, “It’s too bad that people have sort of put him in the costume realm because it really is high art, actually.”

Time to show it in the Met museum.

David Colman has been contributing to The New York Times since 1996.
