Cornell Case Carries Far-Reaching Implications for Hochul and James

The New York Times October 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The decision to intercede by Gov. Kathy Hochul and the New York attorney general, Letitia James, has raised questions of impartiality as both face re-election.

By Benjamin Oreskes

Just two months after Gov. Kathy Hochul assumed office, a well-known colleague — Letitia James, the New York attorney general — declared that she would challenge the governor in the Democratic primary.

Ms. James eventually reconsidered, and Ms. Hochul went on in 2022 to capture her first full term as governor of New York.

Roughly five years later, the two women find themselves locked arm in arm, both running for re-election as the closest of allies on a range of issues.

The latest evidence of this partnership came on Thursday, when Ms. Hochul named Ms. James special prosecutor to investigate a woman’s allegation that she had been raped inside a fraternity house at Cornell University in October 2024.

The governor’s decision to intercede in the matter by enlisting Ms. James as a special prosecutor may carry implications for the investigation and beyond.

For Ms. Hochul, appearing as a take-charge governor may help her counter accusations from her Republican rival, Bruce Blakeman, that she has been weak on crime. It also allows her to tell voters that she stands up for the state’s most vulnerable, whether they are immigrants or victims of sexual assault.

Ms. Hochul said on Saturday that it was important for New Yorkers to see two female leaders — Ms. Hochul and Ms. James are the first women to be governor and attorney general in New York — who “are fighters who won’t put up with any crap.”

“So I’ve heard from a lot of people,” Ms. Hochul added. “The image gives them comfort to know that two women perhaps are looking at this differently than men would in the same position.”

There are fewer immediate political implications for Ms. James, who is all but assured re-election next month. But Ms. James, who has frequently challenged the Trump administration’s policies, has also been the target of a multiyear pursuit by the Justice Department to prosecute her on a range of charges.

Her involvement has added a layer of complexity to the investigation, as her stance as a legal bulwark to President Trump has already led to questions of impartiality.

After the office of the Tompkins County district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, said earlier this week that he would revisit the 2024 sexual assault accusations, Ms. James wrote on social media: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable.”

Asked by a reporter on Friday whether it was appropriate to affirm the victims’ allegations before she had looked into them, Ms. James said: “I will not comment on a Facebook post.”

Ms. James’s opponents were quick to attack her and to impugn her work this week, with Mr. Trump saying on Friday that the attorney general was a “corrupt person.”

“I feel badly for whoever she’s looking at because they won’t get a fair shake,” the president said in Washington.

Ms. James has been locked for years in a multipronged legal war with Mr. Trump, which has included suing both his administration and his businesses on multiple occasions. When Mr. Trump’s lawyers appealed a half-billion-dollar judgment in a civil fraud case, they pointed to Ms. James’s past comments maligning the president as reason she should not have brought that case.

The penalty was thrown out last year by a divided state appellate court. In their ruling, several of the justices denounced Ms. James for having called Mr. Trump’s presidency “illegitimate” and promising to investigate him while she was campaigning in 2018. Some of the justices said there was no merit to Mr. Trump’s assertion of political persecution, even as they criticized Ms. James.

“Her habit of basically making statements about matters and individuals she is investigating does call into question her discretion as a prosecutor to not prejudge things and to actually handle these matters fairly,” said John Faso, a former Republican congressman and lawyer who has endorsed Ms. James’s opponent in this fall’s election.

“I mean, let’s face it,” Mr. Faso said. “Tish James is a politician, not a prosecutor.”

Ms. James insisted that she would be impartial and that she would allow the facts to dictate her decisions.

“My office enforces our state’s laws to protect all New Yorkers,” she said in a statement released on Saturday. “I am committed to leading a comprehensive investigation they can trust, guided only by the facts, the evidence and the law.”

This is not the first time that Ms. James’s ability to be impartial has been questioned as she investigates a politically charged issue. In 2021, Andrew M. Cuomo, then the governor of New York, asked Ms. James to appoint an independent counsel to investigate allegations of sexual misconduct against him, which he denied.

The resulting report led in part to Mr. Cuomo’s resignation. He later filed an ethics complaint against Ms. James, arguing that the final report was misleading and that it had been brandished for political cudgel by the attorney general in her brief run for governor against Ms. Hochul.

“AG James cynically manipulated a legal process for personal, political gain,” Mr. Cuomo’s lawyers wrote in their complaint.

Ms. James’s campaign for governor lasted about a month in 2021 before she dropped out to run for re-election. Ms. Hochul said in an interview on Saturday that apart from “that one month, we’ve been tight.”

Ms. Hochul and Ms. James were slated to appear together on Saturday morning at a campaign event for canvassers in the Bronx. The attorney general ended up leaving before the governor arrived, which spokeswomen for both campaigns chalked up to packed schedules and overlapping events across the city.

That Ms. James and Ms. Hochul were to appear so soon after the announcement of Ms. James’s appointment at a political event speaks directly to concerns about the politicization of this case and others handled by the attorney general.

Last month, the Cornell student, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, sued the university, her sorority, the fraternity and the seven men she claimed had been involved in the assault. None of the accused have been charged with a crime, and all have denied wrongdoing. Four said they had consensual contact with the woman at a party, and the others denied that they had been involved in the assault.

Ms. Hochul insisted on Friday, and again on Saturday, that Ms. James would follow the facts, and that she could be trusted to handle the case with integrity.

“She knows how to do her job,” Ms. Hochul said in an interview on Saturday.

The symbolism of having two women leading the state in this tense moment was woven through the remarks of Ms. Hochul, Ms. James and others.

“With the current events, the person that we needed the most right now has been appointed to oversee a very serious case,” Nathalia Fernandez, a Democratic state senator whose district includes the southeast Bronx, said on Saturday at the campaign event.

“We all know what’s happening at Cornell University,” she added.

Benjamin Oreskes is a reporter covering New York State politics and government for The Times.

The ‘God Gap’ Is Narrowing in Texas

By David French

Opinion Columnist, reporting from across Texas

Robert Jeffress, the senior pastor of First Baptist Dallas, a 16,000-member congregation, stepped to the microphone at the Republican Party’s midterm convention last month and issued what sounded like a declaration of a religious cold war:

“The beliefs of James Talarico are certainly wrong. But they’re more than wrong. The beliefs of James Talarico are blasphemous. They are evil, and they are not beliefs that any true Christian could support. Ever.”

Talarico is running for Senate in Texas, and he has a chance to be the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the state since Lloyd Bentsen defeated a Republican congressman named Beau Boulter in 1988. Republicans are worried, and as a consequence their rhetoric is getting wilder and wilder.

According to Talarico’s critics, he’s a heretic. He’s a wolf in sheep’s clothing who will lead God’s people astray. President Trump calls him “Talafreako,” and he’s apparently so dangerous to Republicans that, as The Wall Street Journal reported last month, right-wing podcasts are mentioning Trump less and less while attacking Talarico more and more.

He’s young, he’s polished and he is, heaven forbid, a seminarian (on leave from his studies at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary). Talarico is running one of the most faith-forward campaigns in the country, along with other Democratic candidates like Adam Hamilton in Kansas (a pastor running for senator) and Rob Sand in Iowa (running for governor).

Democrats have run a version of this playbook before. The Rev. Raphael Warnock has prevailed in two Senate elections in Georgia, winning a partial term in a 2021 runoff against Kelly Loeffler and then a full term in 2022, against a MAGA favorite, Herschel Walker. Democrats nationwide are trying to close the “God gap” that has been the Republican Party’s not-so-secret weapon since the 1970s and the advent of Ronald Reagan.

Talarico’s Christian faith, though, is more liberal than the Christian faith of many Republicans. It’s more liberal than mine (which isn’t hard). But for many fundamentalists, Talarico’s theology makes him the wrong kind of Christian. And to some, no Christian at all.

His opponent is Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general of Texas, whose wife is divorcing him for infidelity and who was impeached by the Republican-led Texas House of Representatives for misconduct that included bribery, obstruction of justice and disregard of official duties. (The Texas Senate acquitted him.)

Trump calls him “the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”

This frontal assault on Talarico’s faith comes after much of the right has spent more than a decade telling voters that they’re electing a president and not a pastor, that they should pay no attention to the religious beliefs (much less the personal conduct) of the Republican president they love. But now the message has changed. In Texas, one of the candidates — Talarico — is treated more like a pastor than a potential senator, and his theology is treated as the true threat to our Republic, and to our souls.

Paxton? He gets a pass. Just like Trump.

The race between Paxton and Talarico could be the most consequential in the country. If Democrats win in Georgia and North Carolina, that’s to be expected, this time around anyway. If they win in Ohio and Maine, it’s troubling for Republicans, but hardly catastrophic — Maine leans blue, after all, and Ohio was a swing state until recently.

But Texas? A Democratic win there would be monumental. It’s not just that Texas is red — Trump won by more than 13 points in 2024, and he won convincingly in 2016 and 2020 as well. It’s not just that no Democrat has won statewide office in more than three decades. It’s that Texas is arguably the cornerstone of both Republican and evangelical political power in the United States.

Its 40 Electoral College votes are indispensable to the party. Were Texas to go or even trend blue, G. O. P. presidential victories would become far more difficult.

It’s the Republican state with the largest economy, and it’s arguably the most important culturally (though Tennessee would like a word). It has long been a magnet for internal migration. The South tends to dominate the G. O. P., but it’s a Texas-flavored version of the South. To quote the country singer Ella Langley, when it comes to finding a home in Red America, an extraordinary number of Americans are “Choosin’ Texas.”

But Texas isn’t just a symbol of Republican power; it’s also a symbol of Democratic defeat. Democrats used to run the state, and the story of Democratic decline in Texas is also a story about religion. When the religious right emerged as one of the most potent voting blocs in the nation, it ultimately routed Democrats in the South.

And yet, as of Friday, a key polling average has Talarico leading Paxton by three points. And he’s leading in poll after poll. Beto O’Rourke — the last great blue hope — never achieved such lofty polling heights in his Senate race against Ted Cruz. Is the era of Democratic decline at an end?

But there’s a question that’s even more important: Will Talarico’s religious faith help put him — and his party — over the top?

To try to answer that question, I went on a reporting trip that became a journey — from Zoom calls in my home office to meetings in coffee shops in Austin to walking the streets of Beaumont, which is where I met Brady, a shirtless Marxist-Leninist in a kilt.

But I’m getting ahead of myself. To understand the religious dynamics of the Texas race, it’s important to absorb the true depths of the “God gap” in American politics. That gap isn’t just about white evangelicals (although it certainly is partly about them), and it’s one of the Democrats’ chief obstacles to obtaining a durable political majority.

Any discussion of the God gap does have to begin with white evangelicals. Their numbers are vast (far more than twice as large as Black Protestants, the most loyal religious Democratic voters), and they vote in lock step.

In 2024, white evangelicals voted for Trump by a 65-point margin, 82 percent to 17 percent. Trump lost all other voters by 18 points, 58 percent to 40 percent.

Lost, however, in that top-line number is an additional fact that should disturb Democrats: In 2024, virtually every Christian denomination — evangelical, mainline and Catholic — shifted to the right.

Last year, Ryan Burge, a political scientist who is one of the nation’s foremost statisticians of religion, published an analysis of 22 Protestant denominations, and he found that all but four shifted to the right from 2020 to 2024, and some of them shifted rather significantly.

The predominantly Black National Baptist Convention had an immense rightward shift. In 2020, 10 percent of its members voted for Trump. By 2024, that percentage almost tripled, to 29 percent.

And what about the Catholic vote? In Texas, 22 percent of the adult population is Catholic, the only religious group that comes close to evangelicals, who represent 27 percent of Texas adults. Nationally there was a 13-point Catholic swing toward Trump.

There are two ways of looking at this data. One is deeply depressing for Democrats: The religious vote is sliding away, and in a country as religious as the United States still is, despite recent declines in religious faith and practice, losing the religious vote means losing elections time and time again.

The other is a bit more hopeful. The religious vote is sliding, but that’s recent — and reversible. Joe Biden, though well past his prime in 2020, did substantially better than Kamala Harris. People of faith may not be lost to Democrats forever so much as they’re punishing Democrats — warning with their votes against the secularization and social radicalization of the far left.

As I talked to Paxton supporters, angry anti-Paxton Republicans and wary but hopeful Democrats, a picture began to emerge. Talarico can win his race, but it will take MAGA pushing Christians out and Talarico pulling Christians in. Anger at Paxton alone won’t be enough for Talarico to prevail.

My first conversation was with Robert Jeffress. I reached out by email, and he graciously agreed to chat, even though we’ve been on opposite sides of the conservative civil war for a very long time. He’s been one of Trump’s most prominent evangelical supporters since 2016; I — to put it mildly — have not.

When we connected via Zoom, he was a bit less fiery than he was on that stage in Dallas, but he still made his beliefs crystal clear. First, he emphasized that “I don’t endorse and haven’t endorsed anybody in this race. I don’t endorse, except for president.”

So, if he’s not endorsing, why did Jeffress speak to the Republican convention in Dallas? “Because of some of the erroneous things Talarico said that I don’t reconcile with the New Testament,” Jeffress said. “And I was criticizing him not for his political beliefs, but his religious beliefs.”

“His religious beliefs certainly don’t disqualify him from being a senator,” Jeffress continued. “They do disqualify him from being a follower of Christ.”

I asked Jeffress to specify his religious objections to Talarico, and he named three key issues — that Talarico had “said that he believes there’s a spectrum of genders,” that Talarico’s spiritual mentor had said that he’s uncomfortable using words like God and Father, and that Talarico had “very recently indicated that all religions were basically different paths that led to the same truth.”

If that seems like thin gruel to you to condemn someone to hell, you’re not alone, but that’s not the central flaw in Jeffress’s analysis.

If conservative Christians are supposed to reject Talarico’s religious views, what are they supposed to make of Paxton’s conduct, and isn’t his conduct both in and out of office more relevant to voters than Talarico’s theology?

Paxton has reportedly cheated on his wife more than once, and his wife, a Texas state senator named Angela Paxton, has filed for divorce, citing “biblical grounds.” (Even the divorce filings in Texas invoke the Bible.) He was recently spotted overseas, during the thick of the campaign, with a woman who appears to be his current girlfriend.

And his misconduct isn’t just private. Paxton was impeached after seven of his top deputies at the attorney general’s office blew the whistle on him, claiming that he’d engaged in bribery and abuse of office to provide favors for an investor named Nate Paul.

Paxton was accused of providing favors to Paul, including providing him with “highly sensitive information” about an F. B. I. raid on Paul’s home. In exchange, Paul reportedly helped Paxton remodel his home, and Paul employed a woman who was Paxton’s mistress at the time.

But Paxton isn’t just corrupt. As The Associated Press detailed in a report last week, he lives a “jet-setting lifestyle” that takes him across the country (and the world) and leaves immense blank spaces in his official calendar.

Earlier in his tenure as attorney general, The A. P. reported, Paxton’s “official calendars were packed with job-related duties. In 2021, more than 90 workdays were blank — a number that reached 112 in 2024, the last full year The A. P. had records for.”

“Over a two-year period ending in 2024,” The A. P. noted, “Paxton flew to the Caribbean, Israel, India, Taiwan, South Africa; made three trips to Europe; and hit five different ski towns in the Rockies, including numerous visits to Park City, Utah, among other destinations, records show.”

Here’s one way to think of Paxton — he possesses all of Donald Trump’s corruption and none of Trump’s charisma.

These details are supposed to matter to Southern Baptists. In 1998, at the height of the scandal surrounding Bill Clinton’s relationship with Monica Lewinsky, the Southern Baptist Convention passed a resolution on the moral character of public officials, and a key clause said, “Tolerance of serious wrong by leaders sears the conscience of the culture, spawns unrestrained immorality and lawlessness in the society, and surely results in God’s judgment.”

I asked Jeffress about that resolution and its impact on Southern Baptists today, and his response confirmed the views of skeptics who believed that Baptists cared more that Clinton was a Democrat than they cared that he had cheated on his wife.

“What was going on in 1998?” he asked, and then answered his own question: “Monica Lewinsky and Bill Clinton, and that was an emphasis on that, and I think it could have been partisan, very much a partisan reaction to that.”

And what is his own view? The Book of Romans, he notes, “teaches that God has given government the role of protecting society.”

“And I’ve said before,” he continued, “when I look for somebody who does that, I don’t want somebody with a demeanor of Jesus necessarily — be nice if they did — but I want the meanest, toughest S. O. B. I can find.”

Raise the subject of Ken Paxton to a conservative supporter of Senator John Cornyn, the incumbent Paxton defeated in the Republican primary, however, and you’re very likely to get a much different reaction.

Trump endorsed Paxton late in the primary race, and Paxton won by a stunning 28-point margin.

Many Cornyn supporters are still furious. Why mount a primary challenge to a man who almost always voted with Trump? Why risk a Senate seat to put a corrupt man in Washington?

The answer, it seems, is a version of a MAGA purity test. Cornyn has been with Trump almost all the time, but it’s the “almost” that counts. Cornyn, for example, supported a modest gun control compromise after the massacre at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas. Perhaps most important — to Trump at least — is that Cornyn voted to certify Biden’s election.

Paxton, on the other hand, abused the power of the attorney general’s office to file one of the most specious and frivolous lawsuits I’ve ever read.

In December 2020, he sued Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin to try to block them from voting in the Electoral College. The suit was so frivolous that Texas’ respected solicitor general, Kyle Hawkins — who was appointed to the post by Paxton — refused to add his name to the complaint. The Supreme Court dismissed the case without even granting it a hearing.

The Texas Republicans I talked to were divided on whether Trump’s endorsement was fatal to Cornyn, or if Cornyn was going to lose no matter what Trump said. Karl Rove seems to think Trump made a difference. During a conversation at the Texas Tribune festival in Austin, Rove not only attacked Paxton for his record of corruption but also said that tracking polls showed Texas Republicans breaking toward Cornyn before Trump’s endorsement, a trend that decisively reversed itself when Trump weighed in.

As Matt Mackowiak, a former senior Cornyn campaign official, told me, Paxton’s supporters were “trying to exterminate RINOs” — referring to the ultimate Republican insult, “Republican in name only” — “but they’ll turn the state blue.” Though Cornyn, he hastened to add, was no RINO: “Cornyn cannot be a RINO if he voted 99 percent with Trump.”

I asked Mackowiak about the idea I mentioned before, that anger at Paxton alone won’t do the trick for Talarico. It’s not enough for Paxton to merely push voters out; Talarico has to pull them in.

His answer focused on “permission structures.” By emphasizing his own faith and — perhaps more important — by trying to explicitly welcome disgruntled Christians into his coalition, Talarico was creating a permission structure for Republicans to support his candidacy.

The more I talked to Cornyn Republicans and dissenting evangelicals, the more I realized that Jeffress’s theological attack was missing the mark. The permission structure that Talarico was creating had little to do with theology and everything to do with decency. Voters were less interested in what Talarico believed (they weren’t seeking to join his church) than how he behaved.

It’s almost as if they’d listened to the words of Jesus Christ in Matthew 7: “By their fruit you will recognize them.”

As the head of an Austin-area evangelical nonprofit who insisted on anonymity for fear of retaliation told me, “I’ll bank on basic character, and the ability to actually listen and respond.” Talarico, he said, “seems like a genuinely good guy.” In a Christian version of the beer test, he said, “I’d like to have a coffee with him.” Or as a former Republican and former Texas public official told me, “I would want him as my neighbor.”

It was difficult to find any conservative evangelical leaders who were willing to go on the record with their support for Talarico. As that same former Republican told me, “there is a massive social barrier” to saying that you’d vote for a Democrat.

Evangelical cancel culture is real, and there are few better ways to land in its cross hairs than saying nice things about James Talarico.

I wasn’t content, however, with talking only to pastors, consultants and public officials in the Texas political elite. I wanted to see the race at the grass roots. So I got in my rental car and drove down to a neighborhood in Beaumont, in southeastern Texas, to walk along and listen as Talarico volunteers and local Democratic Party candidates and officials went door to door trying to turn out the vote for Democrats.

(I contacted the Paxton campaign also, but my messages went unanswered. Neither candidate would speak to me about the issue of faith — or any other issue.)

I met the Talarico crew in the parking lot of a local seafood joint. The day was hot, but not too hot, and the volunteers who’d gathered there were excited about Talarico. They were also nervous, maybe very nervous.

They’d been through 2018, when they thought Beto O’Rourke might win. And they’d been through many more drubbings when the Democrat never had a ghost of a chance. As Samantha Bartley, a member of the Hardin County Democratic Party, told me: “I’m praying we aren’t like the Dallas Cowboys, OK? We can beat some booty until the fourth quarter, we got two minutes left, and we can drop the ball and lose every time.”

But they still had hope. Shannon Heath, a precinct chair in Hardin County, said that membership in the local party had doubled, and that while she wasn’t seeing any movement in what she called “Mega MAGA,” the core of Trump’s base, Democrats were focusing on “Republicans who are still Republicans, and a lot of them have changed their minds.”

I walked with Bartley and Heath through a working-class neighborhood in Beaumont. They both said they were still at least a tiny bit nervous. It’s socially awkward to knock on a person’s door.

But there was no cause for concern. Real-life contact with these ordinary Texans was as different from online political conversations as Venus is from Mars.

Everyone was unfailingly polite and gracious, but in one key way my (admittedly anecdotal) grass-roots experience was identical to my conversations at the grass tips. Republicans were everywhere, but actual Ken Paxton supporters — people willing to say nice things about him — were hard to find.

The neighborhood was surprisingly ideologically diverse. We encountered roughly equal numbers of Republicans and Democrats, and most of the time that was the extent of the conversation — a person pleasantly identified as being Republican or Democratic and that was that.

But two voters stood out — Sharon and Brady (I agreed not to use the voters’ last names). Sharon was an older woman who said she leaned Republican. She listened patiently to the Talarico volunteers but interrupted them to say that she’d supported Trump. He’s “rude and crude,” she said, “but things had to change.”

She paused for a moment, however, and blurted out, unprovoked, “I hate Ken Paxton.” She didn’t commit to Talarico by any means, but she had no affection for Paxton at all, and in the intensity of her feelings you could see the difference in at least some Republican perceptions of the two men.

Trump was “rude and crude” but had his uses. Paxton? There was nothing good to say about him.

Brady was the shirtless man in the kilt I mentioned earlier. He was the last house of the day, and he was delighted to talk to the Talarico volunteers — and to me. Before our brief interview he dashed inside to put on a shirt. He identified himself as a “Marxist-Leninist” who “chronically doomscrolls” on social media and votes Democratic.

He was unconvinced, however, that people were changing their stance. “Everyone’s kind of dug in,” he said. “Everyone’s doing what they’ve been doing.”

In 15 minutes I felt like I’d met the two farthest poles in the Talarico tent. To win, his campaign had to capture all the Sharons, all the Bradys, and everyone in between.

That sounds like a daunting task, and it is. I can see the polls showing Talarico in the lead, but I keep hearing a voice whispering in my head, “This is still Texas.”

At the same time, something is stirring. It’s hard to take evangelical attacks on Talarico’s theology seriously when evangelicals have flooded the polls to support Trump, a man without a visible theology other than the worship of the self, and whatever else we say about him, Donald Trump is no god.

It’s also hard to take seriously the attacks on Talarico’s pastor for his supposed heresy when Trump’s most prominent faith adviser, Paula White-Cain, is also a person whom many Southern Baptist and other evangelical supporters of Trump would consider a heretic. She preaches a form of the prosperity gospel — the belief that if you have the right kind of faith (and donate to her ministry) that health and wealth await you.

But there is something else in play — something that was a common theme in every conversation I had with a disgruntled Republican. They’re not just tired of Paxton, and they’re not just growing tired of Trump. They’re especially tired of Trump’s most zealous supporters, the people who are happy to blow up the Republican Party to make sure that MAGA stays in charge.

Some of these disgruntled Republicans could swallow Trump, but not the mini-Trumps. Amid all the arguments about policy and ideology, some religious voters are willing to try decency for a change. As one evangelical told me about supporting Talarico, a man he admired but disagreed with on some important things: “It’s an experiment. Let’s see what happens.”

There was one more thing that caught my attention — a surprising hint of grace from all sides. And I wonder if that hint of grace might doom Paxton more than any policy or scandal. His movement feeds off the fear and fury of its members. That’s what causes them to overlook — or perhaps even cheer — his cruelty and corruption. There are no lines he won’t cross to take on the people he hates. He is indeed a mean S. O. B.

But what if hatred starts to fade?

One of the Talarico supporters who showed up at the seafood place in Beaumont was Julie Stephenson, a pastor at First Christian Church in Beaumont. Her church is part of the Disciples of Christ, a mainline denomination, and like most mainline congregations, hers has red and blue members. But “there’s no animosity,” she said. “It’s not red against blue in our congregation.”

Nor did I hear an insulting word from any Talarico volunteer I spoke to. I asked Heath, the Democratic precinct chair, if she was angry at MAGA supporters, or if she had any serious conflicts with people on the other side, and she looked at me with a hint of incredulity.

“They are our neighbors,” she said.

There was even a glimmer of hope and reconciliation from Pastor Jeffress. Throughout my conversation with him, he was certainly unsparing in his criticism of Talarico’s religious beliefs, but he also repeatedly said that Christians should vote their conscience.

“What if a parishioner comes to you and says, ‘My conscience is telling me Talarico’?” I asked.

“Follow what you feel like God’s leading you to do,” he responded. “Period. I wouldn’t hesitate to tell them why I’m not voting that way and made sure they were aware of some of the statements he had made about Jesus and the Bible, but if they say, you know, ‘I just can’t overlook the other. This is the way I’m going’?

“I’d say, ‘Fine, I’ll see you in church next Sunday.’”

How Cornell Punished Each of the 7 Men Accused of Sexual Assault

The New York Times October 04, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

Summaries obtained by The New York Times offer a detailed look at the discipline meted out to the men accused of sexually assaulting a fellow student at Cornell University.

By Sharon OttermanHurubie Meko and Debra Kamin

The lightest punishment called for writing a paper and completing training. The most severe was expulsion from the school.

After a woman attending Cornell University accused seven fraternity members of sexually assaulting her in 2024, the university convened a closed proceeding to determine what had occurred and whether those men should face discipline.

Since then, the sanctions imposed on each of the men, and the reasoning behind those decisions, have remained secret. The school has said little.

But detailed summaries of the punishments obtained by The New York Times provide the first look at how Cornell administrators apportioned blame for the alcohol and drug-fueled gathering that the woman has said left her shattered and degraded.

Two of the fraternity members were expelled. Another, who had already graduated, was barred from campus. Two more were suspended. The remaining men were handed lighter punishments, the summaries show.

All of them have denied any wrongdoing, and the Tompkins County district attorney declined to prosecute in 2024. None of the men have been charged with a crime. Their fraternity, Chi Phi, has been banned from campus.

Still, since allegations from the woman who has become known as Jane Doe surfaced in a lawsuit on Sept. 16, they have touched off intense anger over sexual abuse on campus and why more is not done to punish those responsible. Others have criticized what they see as a rush to judge the seven men involved.

In her lawsuit, Jane Doe claimed that, from the start of her encounter involving the seven fraternity members, she was incapable of consent because she was severely intoxicated. The lawsuit inflamed particular ire by stating that the defendants were all “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell,” an assertion Cornell has said did not accurately reflect what occurred.

Combined with more than 1,000 pages of interview transcripts, police reports and other records gathered by Cornell investigators and previously obtained by The Times, the discipline summaries show that the university based its decisions on a broad and complicated body of evidence.

In the end, the punishments handed out by the three-member panel, which met on Zoom over 12 days in May 2025, varied widely. The panel, which enforces federal civil rights at the university under Title IX provisions, did not conclude that Jane Doe was sexually assaulted by all the men she had accused, according to the discipline summaries.

The university investigative files outline in excruciating detail what the fraternity members were accused of doing on the night of Oct. 19, 2024.

It was Matthew Ingalls whom Jane Doe originally went to visit at the Chi Phi fraternity house at about 11 p. m. She walked there alone from a bar to see him, with her intoxication level from drinking through the evening at about a 5 out of 10, she told investigators.

After she arrived, Mr. Ingalls asked her if she wanted to have a threesome with Jonathan Newell, Jane Doe said. During that encounter, she said, the men gave her ketamine and alcohol. Eventually, other men engaged in sex acts with her without her consent and while she was incapacitated, she said.

At the end of the night at the fraternity house, when Jane Doe was near hallucinating, there was more sex, she told investigators.

Expulsions were handed to Mr. Ingalls and Mr. Newell — the man who sent a Snapchat message to other fraternity members encouraging them to enter the bedroom where Jane Doe was undressed, the discipline summaries show.

The discipline summaries show that the panel found Mr. Ingalls responsible for sexual assault, judging that he was willing to manipulate, exploit and endanger Jane Doe for his own self-interest and the entertainment of others.

A lawyer for Mr. Ingalls declined to comment.

Mr. Newell was also accused of sexual assault, the university files show. Jane Doe told police on Nov. 14, 2024, that he had struck her buttocks with enough force during intercourse to leave bruises, and that he had manipulated her to ingest ketamine.

It was not clear whether Mr. Newell had hired a lawyer, and he did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Suspensions and disciplinary probation were given to Winston Lee and Gillio Lopes. Jane Doe had accused Mr. Lee of inhaling ketamine off her body and forcing oral sex on her. She alleged that Mr. Lopes had sex with her without her consent.

Mr. Lee was suspended for two years, with several semesters of disciplinary probation upon his return; Mr. Lopes received a three-semester suspension and two years of probation, the discipline summaries show. Both men also were ordered not to contact Jane Doe, and were required to study sexual harassment and to write reflection papers.

Lawyers for Mr. Lee and Mr. Lopes did not respond to requests for comment.

A persona non grata order was issued to Diego Sarabia, who had graduated by the time of the discipline panel’s ruling. Mr. Sarabia, whom Jane Doe accused of forcibly kissing her, was barred from campus for three years.

The remaining two men, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar, were ordered not to contact Jane Doe, to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write “reflection papers.” They were accused of being part of a group of men who entered the room after reading Mr. Newell’s Snapchat message.

A recently unsealed lawsuit filed by Mr. Kretzschmar against Cornell shows that he was not found responsible for sexual assault. Instead, Cornell ruled that he had committed a lesser offense of attempted sexual exploitation.

Jeremy Saland, a lawyer for Mr. Kretzschmar, said in a statement on Friday that the discipline his client received showed that he was “never accused of, nor found responsible for, rape.”

“He was not even present during any sexual activity,” Mr. Saland said.

It was not clear whether Mr. Norris was represented by a lawyer, and phone calls and text messages to numbers listed for him and his family members went unanswered.

Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said in a statement on Friday that the punishments “did not reflect the severity of the charges.”

“With the exception of two of these men, all of them will be able to graduate with a Cornell diploma and live their lives reaping the benefits of this coveted degree,” Mr. Giuffra said. “In contrast, as of today, it is doubtful whether Ms. Doe will even graduate college or ever live a normal life due to what these men did to her.”

A spokeswoman for Cornell declined to comment, citing federal laws protecting student privacy.

Earlier this week, and in the wake of Jane Doe’s lawsuit, Gov. Kathy Hochul ordered an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case. On Thursday, she appointed the New York State attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor with the power to bring criminal charges.

Sharon Otterman is a Times reporter covering higher education, public health and other issues facing New York City.

Hurubie Meko is a Times reporter covering criminal justice in New York, with a focus on the Manhattan district attorney's office and state courts.

Debra Kamin is an investigative reporter for The Times who covers wealth and power in New York.

Whatever AI Safety Is, It’s Not This

Wired October 01, 2026

Here’s a fun history lesson for you. Don’t worry, we’ll make it quick! In 1966, nearly 51,000 people died on US highways. The overwhelming evidence suggested that many lives could have been saved with modern seat belts, which by then had been around for several years. The automotive industry responded by rallying together, and, in a triumph of self-regulation, voluntarily put the safety feature in every new vehicle that rolled off the line.

Kidding! Of course they didn’t do that. In the fall of 1966, Congress established the Department of Transportation and then passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act as well as the Highway Safety Act, giving the federal government sweeping new authority to set safety standards. By 1968, seat belts were required in every new car. Despite a massive increase in highway traffic in the last 60 years, far fewer fatalities happen on the road today.

I was thinking about this while watching various AI CEOs huddle around US president Donald Trump on Tuesday, congratulating themselves and each other on having signed an AI safety accord. My colleague Maddy Varner wrote about the specific stipulations here, but the short version is that it’s largely up to the AI labs to keep themselves in check.

Or, as Trump put it even more succinctly in the Oval Office on Wednesday: “They’re gonna police, and they’re gonna police each other, and they’re gonna self-police, they’re gonna police themselves. It’s going to work out very well.”

So this is the current state of AI safety regulation. On one side are the AI executives, employees, and tech luminaries, who are all saying that there need to be clear, thoughtful, tactical rules introduced to avoid potential disaster. (Bill Gates, for instance, has been on a media blitz playing Cassandra about an AI apocalypse.) On the other side is Trump’s magical thinking that if you say something enough times, it must be true.

That’s not to say any of this is simple or easy. The question of how to properly “pace the frontier,” as some of those same executives like to say, remains open. Even if all of the major AI labs were to agree to a slowdown, there’s no good way to keep them to their word, and China would likely continue on its own path regardless. The US economy is increasingly propped up on the AI industry, which itself has become an ouroboros of financing deals and circular investments; any meaningful crackdown risks major instability that reaches well beyond Silicon Valley.

The automotive industry is also admittedly an imperfect analogy for all kinds of reasons. There’s no seat belt equivalent for AI, no straightforward solution that can demonstrably reduce risk overnight. (It also took decades for the majority of states to pass laws mandating that people actually wear them.) The potential harms are less certain and less quantifiable. AI doomers will tell you the technology could result in human extinction in a decade; skeptics argue that’s sci-fi marketing malarkey.

We’ve talked about various AI risk scenarios before, but no one can say for certain what’s going to happen next. If you’re looking for data points to calculate your own personal p(doom), I’d point to a recent CNN report about how the US military supposedly nearly boarded a Chinese ship in part because a false AI-generated report said it was carrying nuclear materials. What, if anything, does the AI accord accomplish to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future? Unclear.

The correct answer to all this uncertainty surely isn’t “I guess we’ll find out.” But that’s exactly what self-regulation encourages. To its credit, OpenAI has delayed and even canceled the release of its most advanced models over security concerns. But not before they went on various, extensive hacking sprees, new details about which are still trickling out at a steady pace.

In an interview with TIME published on Thursday, Trump suggested that the Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation were sufficient “guardrails” for the artificial intelligence industry. Are they? It’s far from clear if AI companies can even be held legally responsible when their models go rogue. And it’s not like AI agents themselves are being served subpoenas.

The truth is, no one knows how to solve for AI safety right now. It’s going to take massive amounts of coordination, resources, and regulatory authority to develop the right framework and enforce it, which is exactly the kind of thing governments are designed to provide. Instead of even attempting to work through any of that, the Trump administration is getting out of the way and telling everyone to step on the gas. Don’t bother buckling up.

This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

He was like, "It's going to be great because previously restaurant reservations were first-come, first-serve, and now your agent can say if it's your birthday or an anniversary and then the restaurant can prioritize you." I was like, "You only have to think about this for two seconds to realize that then everyone will just say it's their anniversary or birthday. What do you mean?" Anyway.

So yeah, when we have this world where everybody has their own AI agent looking out for their best interests, negotiating with other AI agents to figure out who gets the best result, I think we're going to run into some really interesting unintended consequences.

Tim Heidecker Is Bringing His Joe Rogan Parody Show to The Onion

Wired October 01, 2026

As satirical news outlet The Onion continued to wage a legal battle to acquire the assets of Infowars out of bankruptcy this summer, it launched a streaming program that spoofed the brand and its bellowing conspiracist ringleader, Alex Jones.

Comedian Tim Heidecker took the reins of the operation, adopting Jones’ guttural and paranoid bluster as he investigated, among other unconfirmed reports, whether Jones himself had exploded in his car after eating too much Whataburger.

But Heidecker wasn’t about to stop there in his quest to transform the Infowars brand into a gonzo comedy network along the lines of Adult Swim. Now he’s taking aim at another high-profile target: Joe Rogan, the bro podcaster whose rambling, misinformed conversations with everyone from Vice President JD Vance to [checks notes] Yakov Smirnoff have somehow kept his long-running series, The Joe Rogan Experience, at the top of the charts for years. Heidecker’s companion show, The Tim Heidecker Podcast, premieres at 8 pm ET on Thursday night, and WIRED can exclusively reveal that the debut episode includes lots of complaining about pronouns, wildly dumb speculation around AI, and plugs for a supplement called “Crab Salts” that makes your “head hurt” and causes you to shout.

A representative for Rogan did not immediately return a request for comment.

Heidecker first lampooned Rogan’s discursive and disorganized interviews in 2021, with a viral 12-hour podcast (in reality, one hour of footage looped a dozen times) covering topics including psychedelics, cancel culture, and whether Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson would run for president. His guests for that show, comedy duo and Onion contributors Rajat Suresh and Jeremy Levick, return for the new episode, offering their “expert” takes on hot-button topics. (The pair have essentially perfected the art of fake celebrity web content and once even got Justin Theroux in on the joke for a mock Hollywood Reporter-style actors roundtable.)

“What is essentially happening is, in place of Christianity, we have the 10 commandments of woke,” Levick says during a discussion of DEI policies on the first episode of The Tim Heidecker Podcast. The chat veers into concerns that bearded men are dressing as princesses to visit Disneyland. Heidecker then abruptly informs the boys that he’s planned a weekend trip to Glasgow “for Scotch wrestling.”

In 2026, it’s more difficult than ever to exaggerate the absurdities of the right-wing media ecosystem, with its fact-free moral panics and bizarre alternative medicines. Though if anyone is up to the task, it’s the endlessly inventive Heidecker—who will have no shortage of grifters and lunatics to go after once he’s done with his run as a Rogan type. Luckily for him, few of those potential impressions are as rough on the voice as Alex Jones.

Amazon Alexa Devices Are Already on Sale, but the Deals Aren’t All as Good as They Look

Wired October 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Amazon's Prime Day has returned for its fall edition, and the Amazon Alexa-powered devices are already on sale. But are the sales actually any good?

There's already the question of whether you want Alexa in your house, and now it's a question of whether the sales are more of a mind game than a real discount. That's thanks to Amazon raising prices across its device categories at the end of August, leaving us with the same product lineup but a worse case to recommend it. Some devices are already on sale right now ahead of Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days for $40 off, but went up in price by $20 just a few weeks ago, cutting that discount into something that feels barely worth the spend.

If you're interested in Amazon's device sales but want the real picture of what the discount is and which devices are worth it, I've got you covered. I've been testing Amazon Alexa speakers since they launched in 2012, and I am also WIRED's resident Kindle tester, which gives me almost too much insight into the price games Amazon plays with these devices. Here's my full breakdown.

Right now, Amazon's Alexa-powered Echo speakers and Fire TV sticks are currently on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days next week (October 6-7). These devices saw price hikes at the end of August, so some of the deals aren't as good as in the past. They do seem to be permanent price changes, though, so if you're certain you want one of these models, this is the best time to buy.

So far, most Kindles aren't on sale yet, but all three Kindle Kids models (the Kindle Kids, the Kindle Paperwhite Kids, and Kindle Colorsoft Kids) are already on sale. (Amazon also announced new versions of these Kindles today, along with the rest of its lineup, so it's up to you whether you want the current on-sale model or to preorder the new one!) If you're looking for a Paperwhite and Scribe, they aren't on sale yet as of this writing. Neither are Eero routers.

But I expect most of those models will be discounted once the event begins. Both Kindle and Eero products also saw price hikes at the end of August, so I recommend buying them only on sale (even if the sales aren't as good as they used to be, since they're similar discounts but on higher prices).

Not all deals are great, especially given the recent price increases. If you're set on getting a new Amazon Alexa-powered speaker, though, here are the discounts (and devices themselves!) that are still worth it.

Amazon

Amazon

Best Buy

The best deal in Amazon's early device deals is easily the second-gen Echo Spot, revived in 2024. It's 50 percent off its new price, and it's still a solid discount off its original price of $80. I really like this fun little smart speaker. It works great as a bedside alarm, shows when your next alarm is set, and can display the weather or your calendar details when you ask Alexa. Best of all, you get the fun benefits of a screen without a camera to worry about.

Amazon

Amazon

The only new Amazon Alexa speaker that didn't get hit with a price change is the second-gen Echo Studio. It still sits at $220, which is not only its original price, but also the original price of the first-gen model. It's a nice thing to see. Its discount isn't huge for Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days, but it's $40 for powerful, room-filling sound that could extend across great rooms without getting muddy.

Amazon

Amazon (65-inch)

Amazon (55-inch)

The Amazon Ember Artline TV is another rare device from Amazon that didn't see a price hike at the end of August, maintaining the $1,099 price it had at launch (and now has a $300 discount off that). It's a well-priced art television that is more accessible than its more expensive competitors, and comes with handy features like built-in Alexa+. I'm usually not a fan of the Fire TV devices, but this one keeps catching my eye and is already on sale for Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.

Amazon’s New Kindle Lineup Is Lighter, Thinner, and More Metal

Wired October 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The Kindle will turn 20 in 2027. Amazon says it plans to celebrate the milestone throughout the year, but to kick things off, it's starting with an entirely refreshed Kindle lineup.

On Thursday, the company introduced a handful of new Kindle models: a new 6-inch base Kindle, a 7-inch Kindle Paperwhite, and a 7-inch Kindle Colorsoft. You can buy Signature Editions of the latter two and Kids versions of the entire range, which include artist-designed kids cases, a year of Amazon's worry-free guarantee for damage, and a year of Kids+, the company's subscription service that offers unlimited access to ad-free, child-appropriate books.

The highlight is Amazon's use of aluminum for the Kindle's construction rather than traditional plastic. The starting tier is plastic, but you can upgrade to an all-aluminum model (Amazon uses 80 percent recycled aluminum) if you prefer that Kindle model and you just want something more robust.

It can get a little confusing with all the different SKUs, so here's a quick rundown:

The base Kindle, the aluminum version, and the Kids Kindle are on sale starting today. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft are available for preorder on a rolling basis and will launch at the end of October.

The Kindle's screen offers 30 percent faster book opening than its predecessor, Amazon says. The build is a whole millimeter thinner at 6.8 mm, and Amazon cut the weight by around 18 grams to 140 grams. The Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft are both similarly lighter (204 grams) and thinner (6.8 mm), retain the waterproof design, and feature adjustable warm reading lights. Like before, the screen has a higher pixel density that makes text appear sharper.

Amazon says the new Kindles are also compliant with the European Union’s new battery regulations, meaning the batteries should be easier to remove and replace.

Upgrading to the Signature Edition for the Colorsoft and Paperwhite nets you the aluminum build, an ambient light sensor that adjusts brightness automatically, and an accelerometer that lets you turn the screen to landscape orientation and have the pages adjust accordingly. The upgrade also adds the ability to use a double-tap gesture to turn pages.

Uniquely, the Signature Editions feature pogo pins that let you charge via Amazon's new $60 dock, which props the device up as it charges. There's also a new Page-Turn Cover ($80)—a case with physical page-turn buttons that magnetically attaches to the back of the devices and pairs via the pogo pins, which Amazon says offers page-turn buttons to the vocal minority that still loves them (around 5 percent of Kindle users) without adding unnecessary bulk to the device.

Don't worry, you don't need the case, the Signature Edition, or even a new Kindle if you just want page-turn buttons. Amazon is debuting its own Kindle Click, a $35 page-turn accessory that pairs over Bluetooth for the non-Signature (and older) Kindle models.

The Kindle business is booming. Amazon's Kevin Keith, vice president of devices, says Kindles have seen double-digit growth over the last three years, with 2025 being the highest sales year in more than a decade. He says 60 to 65 percent of people buying new devices have never had a Kindle before, with Gen Z, millennials, and even Gen Alpha driving the lion's share. This past January saw the highest single-month Kindle reading volume in history.

At the same time, Kindles are more expensive than ever. “Memory pricing is a little bit crazy,” Keith says, referring to the memory shortage behind the general price bump on all electronics. Amazon upped prices of existing Kindles earlier this year; the new devices match those prices.

Part of the redesign aims to lower overall manufacturing costs and standardize the hardware. Take the refreshed display on the base Kindle—Keith says many of the improvements trickle down from the development of the Kindle Scribe. For the first time, the base Kindle has a display that sits flush with the body, just like its pricier counterparts. (It previously had a raised plastic bezel around the screen.) That whole front panel is also available in a new color: Ube (purple).

While Amazon has made Kindles with colorful fronts (like the matcha green Kindle from 2024), it hasn't done this with flush displays. That's because simply coloring the front would make the Ube color, for example, scatter around the screen as the frontlight reflects it, casting a purple hue on the display. To counter this, Keith says Amazon developed a new “edge-to-edge” color technology that prints two different colors under the cover lens: the Ube color backed by a layer of black. The black absorbs the light, which solves the problem. Amazon says it perfected this tech in the Scribe and ported it down here.

Color is important. Keith says alternative colors typically make up just 15 to 20 percent of sales—the rest being classic options like black or white—but the matcha green model captured a surprising 55 percent. Amazon also chose that color because, at the time, it noticed a general increase in the popularity of matcha in drinks and sweets (it also noted that folks on #BookTok are reading in coffee shops). Hence the new ube color, which is based on the popular purple yam of the same name.

“We've been tracking food trends, and two years ago, ube just exploded—ube was growing 200 percent year over year,” says Chris Green, Amazon's vice president of design. “We expect it to do far better than the matcha.”

For the aluminum housing, instead of milling the device's frame from a block of aluminum and using a lot of water in the process, Amazon stamps a flat sheet, which then goes into a forge that presses down to create the backplate and sides. The process supposedly takes seconds compared to the hours it can take to machine a single aluminum device frame (like an iPhone or MacBook), saving material and energy. It helps lower the Kindle's carbon footprint, which is now equivalent to 11 hardcover books.

Green says these improvements bring down the device's density. The density of the average human body is around 1 gram per cubic centimeter; an iPhone is around 2.2 grams per cubic centimeter. The new Kindles are around 1.2 grams. Lowering that number can help make the hardware “disappear” during prolonged use.

“I truly want people to never think about the Kindle,” Green says. “I just want them to think about the magical world that the author has created inside of this device.”

For Green, who has designed nearly all of Amazon's hardware in his 19-year tenure at the company (and yes, he says he's embarrassed by the Fire Phone), chasing that 1.2-grams-per-cubic-centimeter target is all about getting the gadget out of the way so the Kindle can mimic the analog calm of physical print.

“More people are reading on paper, more people are reading on Kindles,” Green says. “Is it a backlash to AI? Probably. People are trying to find things more authentic—we're in a crisis of authenticity.” Surveys have shown that overall leisure reading is down across the US, but the people who are reading are buying more than ever.

As for the 20th anniversary of the Kindle in 2027, Keith says the company may roll out a significant refresh to the Kindle's user interface, though he didn't share more. Expect special anniversary editions of some Kindles. When I asked whether we could expect the return of the Kindle Oasis—an asymmetrical e-reader with physical page-turn buttons—Green chuckles.

“The first Oasis was one of my passion projects,” he says. “I loved that. I really, really loved that product. But I was a vocal minority on that—most of the people wanted slabs.”

So, probably not.

Correction on October 1, 2026 at 2:30 pm: We've updated this story to correct an incorrect statement about page-turn speed that Amazon initially provided (along with Kevin Keith's title).

I Found the Best Kindles to Take Your Library Anywhere

Wired October 01, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

There’s a lot to love about a Kindle if you’re a reader. If you’re looking for the best Kindle, you really can’t go wrong with any of the models. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or get free books from your local library. Our guide will help you decode the differences to find which Kindle is right for you.

I've owned all kinds of Kindles, from the newest Kindle Scribes to hand-me-down base Kindles without a front light. The latter came from a friend who noticed I had spent my entire postpartum summer glued to library books on my phone, and I still have it to this day. But after trying all of the latest Kindles, I can say it's easy to spot the best one.

Read on to find out my favorite overall Kindle and my favorite Kindles for specific uses and younger readers. You can also check out my other buying guides made for readers like me, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.

Updated October 2026: I've added details about the new Kindles announced today.

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon (Signature)

You came here to find out one thing: What is the best Kindle? The Kindle Paperwhite is Amazon's most popular Kindle and our favorite after testing every model, thanks to its great range of features. You'll get a large display with high resolution and warm lighting, and the technology inside has fast and smooth performance. Amazon launched the 12th-generation Paperwhite in late 2024, and it's been our new favorite ever since. Whether you want to read more or are tired of carrying physical books, all the extra features are worth the price. The basic Kindle may seem enticing, especially with the fun new colors it offers, but the Paperwhite will serve you better in the long run, especially if you're a nighttime reader like I am. The warm lighting is a great option on the eyes before bed.

If you already have a Paperwhite, the update isn't so major that you need to upgrade to the newest model, but it's the best to choose if you're shopping for a brand-new Kindle. You'll get a slightly larger screen and the highest contrast ratio on any Kindle, not just of the Paperwhites. The battery life also increased from two months to three months, and it has the thinnest form factor yet. The 12th-gen Paperwhite has two versions: the standard and the Signature Edition. The latter comes with auto-adjust brightness, wireless charging, and double the storage at 32 gigabytes. The regular Paperwhite is more than enough and easily one of the best Kindles to buy, but if you plan on buying the model without lock-screen ads, you may as well pay the extra $30 for the Signature Edition.

Speaking of price differences, both the Kindle Paperwhite and the Paperwhite Signature Edition recently became more expensive after Amazon increased some of its prices. The base Paperwhite went up $40 to hit $200, while the Signature Edition went from $200 to $250. I'm curious how much cheaper they'll be during fall sale season; we might now see the old base price as the new sale price. I'd wait for Prime Day or Black Friday to purchase either version of the Paperwhite.

Amazon

Amazon (16 GB)

Best Buy (16 GB)

Students who want something digital to take notes on but who also love to read will love a Kindle Scribe. While there's a new version of the Scribe out that's also great, the best one is still the second-generation Kindle Scribe from 2024.

This model has the same 10.2-inch (300 ppi) paperlike display as the first iteration, but it has a white border for a more notebook-style look, and the new Premium Pen is not only included but also has a soft-tipped eraser at the end. Personally, this is my most-used Kindle because I love to scribble notes and ideas all day long. It's easily my most-used Kindle and digital notebook because of the long battery life (12 weeks!) and the convenience of grabbing it for both my reading and note-taking needs. While I don't have as many options and layouts as I would on a true digital notebook, the Kindle Scribe still offers a handful of options to help me free up most of the ideas jumbling around in my brain, and solid options for students.

The second-gen Scribe also packs new software capabilities, even if it's the slightly older model. Active Canvas lets you write directly in the book you're reading, though it won't work like true annotation—instead, the notes will appear in a small square on the screen like a Post-It note. That means it'll always be there if you resize the screen, but it didn't feel as natural as our testers would've liked. There are now Expandable Margins as well that let you write notes in the side panel of books, which feels a little more intuitive, but still isn't the full annotation experience you might want.

There are also a couple of generative artificial intelligence features. The Refined Writing tool transforms your notes into a script font, while Summarization will quickly summarize pages of notes into bullets with a script font that you can then share from the notebook tab. Both features work well, but I never find myself reaching for them. These new software features can be downloaded onto first-generation Kindle Scribes if you already have one, or you can wait for an over-the-air update to hit your device. There are now three new Kindle Scribe models, which I detail below, but I still prefer this model. It also didn't see a price increase like other Kindle devices did, but that's true across the Kindle Scribe category.

Amazon

Amazon (Colorsoft)

Amazon (Colorsoft Signature Edition)

Amazon now has two versions of its colorful Kindle. There's the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, which came out last year and was Amazon's first-ever model with a color screen, and now there's a basic Kindle Colorsoft. It competes with colorful models we’ve already seen from Kobo and Boox, so while it’s new for Amazon, it’s not new in the world of e-readers. Both models have a 7-inch display with an oxide backplane for speedy performance and higher contrast for both color and black-and-white content. The front light has also been changed to include nitride LEDs, which enhance color and increase brightness.

The Colorsoft Signature has a few extra features, but it also comes with a higher price tag. You'll get twice the amount of storage—32 GB to the base Colorsoft's 16 GB—wireless charging, and an auto-adjusting front light. It's a nice set of add-ons to get for just $20 more if you know you'll use the wireless charging and want an auto-adjusting light, but unless you already have a wireless charger you love, you'll probably be just as happy spending $20 less. It's already a hefty increase for the color screen and no other new features. The good news, at least, is Amazon did launch Dark Mode for Colorsoft, which it previously didn't have.

Amazon also raised prices of the Kindle Colorsoft and Colorsoft Signature Edition, bringing both up $40 to $290 and $320, respectively. I'm curious to see what sale prices both of these get come Prime Day and Black Friday—I'd hold off buying anything until then.

I’m a parent of a young kid, and the books in our house are very, very colorful. We're still getting started on reading, but pulling up a book on the colorful Colosoft Kids is a much more fun experience than a black-and-white option. The color makes everything more engaging: The bookshelf of your books! The options to choose from on Kids+! The pages in the illustrated books themselves! Having a colorful option is something a lot of users want, but I think kids of all ages have the best chance of really getting the most use out of it. They can enjoy everything from picture books to graphic novels with full-page color, and add colorful highlights to books they want to annotate or study. It's not quite as vibrant as a digital screen or color on paper since it's an E Ink screen, but it's still a fun feature that adds to the reading experience.

You can technically turn on Kids mode on any Kindle, so you don't necessarily need a Kids-branded model (there's both a basic Kids ($180) and a Paperwhite Kids ($230) model) to have your kiddos read books separated from adult ones. But the real benefit is that Kids models, whether it's the Colorsoft or a black-and-white model, come with free access to Kids+ for six months to a year. Kids+ is Amazon's subscription service that features tons of age-appropriate books. The Colorsoft Kids gets the longest access, a full year, while the other models will only receive six months. That extra six months, plus colorful pages, really make going for a kid-specific model worth it. The Colorsoft Kids is also waterproof and comes with a colorful cover (you get to choose between two fun designs).

It's no surprise that the Colorsoft Kids also went up in price like the regular Colorsoft models, as did the rest of the Kindle Kids line. This one went up $30 to hit $300, while the Kindle Kids is now $180 (up $50) and the Kids Paperwhite is now $230 (also up $50). My recommendations may change soon based on how expensive the color version has become.

Amazon

Amazon

If you're looking for something lightweight and affordable, Amazon's 11th-generation Kindle is your best bet. It was updated in 2024 and builds upon the 2022 update that added more storage, a higher-resolution screen, and USB-C charging. The 2024 model has a few nice updates, including a higher-contrast-ratio screen, a brighter front light, and a faster page-turning rate.

You still won't get a warm lighting feature, so if you want that, you'll have to upgrade to the Paperwhite or Colorsoft. But otherwise, you'll still get dark mode on this device (unlike the Colorsoft) and a snappy overall performance and nice screen brightness for the price point. Former WIRED reviewer Brenda Stolyar said the performance was a big improvement over the 2019 Kindle model she was previously using. If you have room to spend a little more, we still prefer the Paperwhite, since you'll also get a longer battery life and a waterproof build, along with the warm lighting, but this is a good Kindle for the price.

But not as great as it used to be since Amazon raised its prices, including this Kindle model. The 11th-gen Kindle used to retail for $110 and was often on sale for under $100, but now its starting price is $150. I'm curious how good the sales will be this fall, but I fear we won't see it fall under $100 anymore.

Amazon announced today that there's a whole new generation of Kindles coming, with every model getting a new version. Here are the details; I'll be updating this guide soon with thoughts as we review each model.

That's not all Kindle has coming out. There will also be a handful of new accessories, including the Kindle Click ($35) Bluetooth remote that will work with Kindle models as early as 2024, a Page-Turn Cover ($80), a Charging Dock ($60) designed to work with the pogo pins on the Signature Editions, and new Kindle covers in a variety of colors and textures. I'm most excited about the remote; I will update this guide and our Best Kindle Accessories guide with my notes as I test.

Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only the recent Kindle Scribe models with the original price tag. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. It's interesting that none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it's also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.

Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There are now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light. Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.

All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, a slightly slimmer form factor, and an updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.

Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.
